[1] The Hacker News - WhatsApp Patches 3 Security Flaws, Including Android Bug Suspected of Use in Scams
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 23:27:20 +0530
Link: https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/whatsapp-patches-3-security-flaws.html

[TAM METİN - 474 kelime]
Meta-owned WhatsApp has addressed security vulnerabilities, including one impacting its Android app that it suspects may have been exploited in connection with scam messages.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-23871 (CVSS score: 3.5), has been described as a case of incomplete validation of external ad-reply URLs in WhatsApp for Android and WhatsApp Business for Android before 2.26.17.4.

The issue could have "caused a target's device to reveal its IP information to an attacker if an attacker sent media from an attacker-controlled URL when a crafted Click to WhatsApp ad-reply message was rendered and displayed in a message thread," WhatsApp said.

The messaging platform said it may have been "abused in conjunction with specific spam messages." Internal researchers on the WhatsApp Security Team have been credited with discovering and reporting the issue.

When reached for comment, a WhatsApp spokesperson told The Hacker News that the vulnerability was discovered while disrupting a scam campaign. "We believe a scammer was using it to make their scam message seem more credible," the spokesperson added.

WhatsApp did not disclose the scale of the activity, and if those efforts were successful.

Also addressed by the company are two other flaws -

CVE-2026-102769 (CVSS score: 6.8) - An SQL injection vulnerability in WhatsApp for Android prior to version 2.26.35.74 that occurred when a recipient tapped on a specially crafted "order details" message sent from an unofficial client, causing locally-stored WhatsApp files to be deleted.

CVE-2026-44908 (CVSS score: 4.8) - A trust-validation vulnerability in WhatsApp's certificate verification mechanism for Meta AI's confidential computing infrastructure that affects WhatsApp for iOS before 2.26.24.72, WhatsApp Business for iOS and WhatsApp for Mac Desktop before v2.26.23.72, WhatsApp for Android before v2.26.23.74, and WhatsApp Business for Android before v2.26.23.70.

Interestingly, CVE-2026-102769 is also capable of leaking one bit of information through a timing-based side channel if the user is online at the time of receipt of the malicious message.

It "leaked one bit of information asked by the attacker about the user's chat database via an induced-crash delivery receipt timing side channel," WhatsApp added. There is no evidence the vulnerability has been exploited in the wild.

Successful exploitation of CVE-2026-44908, on the other hand, could have allowed a bad actor positioned within Meta infrastructure to bypass the hardware root of trust using a Versioned Chip Endorsement Key (VCEK) certificate not signed by the hardware manufacturer's key.

"Any such VCEK Cert would first have to be published to the third-party binary transparency ledger used by WhatsApp Private Processing," WhatsApp noted. "The ledger shows that every published VCEK certificate chains to the hardware root of trust, confirming no exploitation."

WhatsApp is advising users to keep their apps and devices up to date to ensure optimal protection. The company also said that it continuously works to strengthen its systems and acknowledged the bug bounty community's contributions towards keeping the platform secure.

[2] The Hacker News - Bazuka Android Malware Uses Fake Screen Overlays to Hide Credential Theft and Device Control
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 22:28:16 +0530
Link: https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/bazuka-android-malware-uses-fake-screen.html

[TAM METİN - 1458 kelime]
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a previously unknown Android malware framework called Bazuka that offers large language model (LLM) integration for victim management and control at scale.

Dutch mobile security company ThreatFabric said it discovered the threat in late October 2026 during an investigation into an NFC-relay banking Trojan.

"Bazuka is a full malware framework," ThreatFabric said in a technical report. "A dropper/downloader, a core, and 23 modules cover overlays, keylogging, 2FA and SMS interception, remote control, and crypto-address swapping."

One notable aspect of the malware that distinguishes it from the rest is a novel overlay technique that allows the trojan to take a screenshot of the home screen or lock screen, and display that as an overlay on demand to cover up malicious activities taking place in the background.

Another perhaps not-so-surprising element is the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in the control panel to help operators identify victims of interest and manage infections. It supports both locally hosted models and models accessed through an API.

One of the sample prompts provided by the author refers to a score, indicating an operator can likely request the AI model to score victims and determine how attractive they are as targets. The panel also supports the following capabilities -

Create accounts for traffers, who are cybercriminals responsible for driving victims to malware using various lures

Build droppers containing the malware with options to choose the kind of permissions specified in the Android manifest file likely in an attempt to bypass Google Play app review process

This indicates that the dropper apps can be distributed via at least two distribution channels: through traffers, who can use social media ads or bogus sites to trick users into downloading them, and Google Play Store.

One of the droppers containing the malware masquerades as a premium, adult-friendly version of TikTok (package name: "com.tiktok.premium"). Two different variants of the Bazuka attack chain have been observed -

A dropper, which asks the victim for permissions to install applications from third-party sources and then proceeds to download a standalone APK ("com.tiktok.premium.pro") that serves as the stager

A downloader that directly downloads the main payload

It's suspected that the stager is the same as the downloader, whose main responsibility is to retrieve the core and supplementary modules necessary for a particular campaign, and then launch them.

"Once the core and required modules are loaded, Bazuka operates as a keylogger and a classic overlay trojan, monitoring the text entered by the victim and displaying an overlay at the right moment," ThreatFabric said. "All functionality is controlled by commands from C2 [command-and-control]."

The core module is the orchestrator, maintaining communication with C2, loading additional DEX modules, dispatching commands, collecting device information, and managing permissions and component updates. Like other Android trojans, it abuses Android Debug Bridge (ADB) shell commands and the operating system's accessibility services to request permissions and grant them automatically.

"Important components of the core include mechanisms for enabling Wireless Debugging and completing the pairing process," ThreatFabric explained. "The core can open the system settings screen, find the relevant menu, enable Developer options, and then enable Wireless Debugging."

"When this mode is enabled, it also intercepts the PIN, which is then used to establish a TLS connection to the ADB daemon."

Furthermore, the core component counters detection by Google Play by disabling the protection component through the accessibility services API. It is also equipped to launch a self-destruct mechanism that clears local storage, deletes the database, and disables the application completely.

Communication with the C2 server takes place over two WebSocket channels -

Control, which is used to issue commands

Data, which is used to exfiltrate data and screen capture streams

Bazuka supports 23 modules that enable comprehensive data and cryptocurrency theft -

call_forwarding, to manage call forwarding through USSD commands

clip_monitor, to act as a clipper and substitute cryptocurrency wallet addresses copied to the clipboard with attacker-controlled ones

contacts, to collect contact information

device_control, to manage the device over the ADB bridge and execute commands as shell commands

file_manager, to access the file system

input_recorder, to act as a keylogger and capture all text entered into a target application, as well as identify bank card numbers, wallet addresses, and passwords in user input

location, to determine a victim's location using GPS, cell tower positioning, and Wi-Fi

media, to capture photos and stream camera video and microphone audio

oem_power, to open system and OEM settings for power saving, background operation, and autostart

optics, to facilitate remote control, screencasting, and phishing overlays

preflight, to perform preliminary checks of the runtime environment

proxy, to implement a reverse TCP proxy

push, to create and manage local Android notifications

screen_control, to capture the lock screen PIN, text password, and unlock pattern through accessibility services

self_adb, to implement an embedded ADB client

session_ui, to display phishing HTML overlays

smsmessage, to access SMS messages and extract potential verification codes, send SMS messages, and attempt to delete messages from the device

system_checker, to check the runtime environment and implement anti-analysis measures

tapread-nfc_module, to interact with contactless bank cards

toast, to display text messages on the device's screen

twofa, to capture one-time verification codes

uninstall_shield, to counter attempts to uninstall or force-stop the application

ussd, to send USSD requests from the victim's device and receive responses from the mobile operator

The malware has not been attributed to any known threat actor or group. However, the panel has been found to display UI elements in a mix of English and Russian.

"ADB bridging is becoming a standard feature of modern banking trojans," ThreatFabric said. "While it is not there yet for Bazuka and its current architecture, this is a very concerning sign, as it allows malware to obtain various privileges covertly and deploy independent modules that can survive removal of the host application."

"Another equally concerning feature is the use of LLM chats directly within the control panel. AI agents are used to identify victims of interest."

ArcticRAT Android Malware Uses LLMs to Extract High-Value Data

Bazuka is not the only Android-focused threat to integrate an LLM into its workflow. Last week, Zimperium zLabs research team detailed another sophisticated and rapidly evolving Android malware called ArcticRAT that supports 129 distinct commands and incorporates LLM APIs into its data exfiltration pipeline to extract high-value financial intelligence from stolen SMS messages and app data.

"What initially began as a targeted spyware operation aimed at users of 11 specific cryptocurrency apps has morphed into an enterprise grade, AI-powered, Remote Access Trojan (RAT)," researchers Rajat Goyal and Fernando Ortega said.

Infection chains make use of malicious sites impersonating Google Play app listings to convince users to install the dropper app. Unsuspecting users are redirected to these pages through malvertising, smishing, or third-party forums. The apps masquerade as popular brands (e.g., Amazon and TikTok), cryptocurrency applications, and generic file managers.

Once installed, the app abuses Android accessibility services to establish remote control, automate fraudulent activity, and leverage AI to parse and "clean" exfiltrated data. It uses TCP sockets to communicate with the C2 infrastructure.

An initial reconnaissance step is used to build a host profile, which then dictates the C2 server to dynamically select the relevant attack payloads to deploy. At a high level, the malware supports the following features -

Initiate a real-time video transmission from the compromised device

Abuse accessibility services for full remote control

Serve fake extortion overlays and deceive victims into making cryptocurrency payments

Make use of LLMs to process harvested SMS messages and look for financial, banking, and trading apps through hard-coded prompts that ask the model to take the role of a professional SMS analyzer and device app analyzer, respectively

Capture credentials, authentication codes, and private communications

Serve overlays to steal device lock screen pattern, PIN, or password

"The malware requests VPN service privileges to null-route network communication on the victim's device, effectively blinding Google Play Protect telemetry during the staging phase," Zimperium said.

"To prevent the user from interfering with these operations, ArcticRAT employs a defense evasion tactic known as a "Black Screen" overlay. When the attacker is navigating banking apps via Hidden VNC (HVNC) or auto-approving system permissions, the malware draws a completely black, un-dismissible view over the screen and drops the brightness to zero. To the victim, the device appears locked or powered off."

Recent versions of ArcticRAT have also been found to abuse the native Wireless Debugging mechanism to initiate a privileged shell session on the victim machine and execute commands, including enabling or disabling accessibility permissions, verifying lock screen PIN or pattern, and displaying a black screen to conceal background operations.

"By abandoning hardcoded attacks in favor of real-time Hidden VNC (HVNC), raw TCP command-and-control (C2), and aggressive defense evasion overlays, the malware achieves complete device takeover," Zimperium said.

[3] The Hacker News - Linux KVM Flaw CVE-2026-99312 Lets Guest VMs Access Host Memory on AMD Hosts
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 17:50:00 +0530
Link: https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/new-linux-kvm-flaw-cve-2026-99312-lets.html

[TAM METİN - 1013 kelime]
A flaw in KVM, the hypervisor built into the Linux kernel, let researchers read about 127 GB of a cloud server's memory from inside a virtual machine of their own on DigitalOcean.

On a shared server, that memory can include other customers' virtual machines. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-99312, affects only hosts with AMD processors and nested virtualization enabled.

Fixed kernels shipped upstream on Tuesday, the day before the research went public. The provider patched its own fleet with a live patch, telling Droplet customers: "No action needed on your part." Operators who run their own KVM hosts on AMD hardware need to update the host kernel or turn nested virtualization off.

Oren Yomtov, a researcher at the security firm Terra Security, found the flaw and reported it through the provider's bug bounty program. The provider confirmed the exploit worked on its own hosts and treated it as critical, and the Linux KVM maintainers, told on October 21, merged a fix on November 2.

In the test on one of its Droplets, the first thing to come back was the host's kernel version banner, followed by about 127 GB of the host's RAM, mapped read-only, the provider said in a disclosure post yesterday.

The write test ran on the researchers' own bare-metal AMD server, with no other customers attached. There, the guest wrote 32 chosen bytes into a live page of the host kernel's memory, and a witness module loaded into that kernel confirmed the change.

Both tests started with root access inside a VM controlled by the researchers. An attacker would need the same position: control of a guest on a vulnerable host, not just network access to it.

Intel-based KVM hosts are not affected, because the vulnerable code exists only in KVM's support for nested virtualization on AMD. Many cloud providers the researchers surveyed were not vulnerable because they had not enabled nested virtualization on AMD.

There are no reports of the flaw being used outside research, according to VirtFusion, a virtualization platform vendor that is tracking the issue for its operators. No exploit code has been published either, and no guidance exists for detecting a past attempt.

Severity ratings disagree. The Linux kernel's CVE team scores the flaw 8.8 out of 10, with high impact on confidentiality, integrity, and availability, while Red Hat's preliminary security assessment rates it as Moderate at 5.6 and treats the impact as denial-of-service only. The provider treated it as critical for its own shared cloud.

Terra's technical analysis, published on Wednesday, describes a pointer left pointing at freed memory. KVM confines each VM with a table, the nested page table, that translates the VM's memory addresses into the host's real memory, and the processor finds that table through a pointer kept for each virtual CPU.

Some hosts let a VM run a VM of its own, a nested VM. When a reset signal called INIT stops the nested VM, KVM skips restoring the outer VM's pointer, leaving it pointing to a page of memory the kernel has already freed.

Once the kernel reused that freed page, the guest could fill it with entries of its own choosing, and the processor followed them as if they were the real table. The forged entries could name any physical page on the host, which is how about 127 GB of the server's RAM came into reach of a guest that was never given it.

The fix makes KVM reset that memory-management state on every INIT.

The flaw was created by a security fix. A 2022 patch for a different nested-virtualization bug, CVE-2022-3344, switched a reset path back to the outer VM's control block but missed the page-table pointer, the researchers say, and the error then sat in the kernel for just under four years.

In earlier work called PatchSlop, the team found that the fix for another one introduced 3.2% of kernel vulnerabilities.

The fix lives in the host kernel. Updating the operating systems inside the VMs changes nothing, and a host keeps running its old kernel until it is rebooted.

Upstream, the fix shipped on Tuesday in stable kernel 7.3.5 and in the long-term kernels 6.18.64 and 6.12.118, the kernel team's CVE announcement shows. The affected code goes back years: it entered the 6.1 kernel in 2022 and was carried into the 5.15.81 and 6.0.11 releases, so older kernel lines and the distribution kernels built on them are in range.

Distribution kernels mostly do not have the fix yet. As of publication, Debian's security tracker lists the kernels in all of its releases as vulnerable, with a fix only in unstable, and Ubuntu's CVE tracker rates the flaw High and lists its kernels as vulnerable with no fixed package released. Red Hat lists the Enterprise Linux 9 and 10 kernels as affected with the fix deferred, and the Enterprise Linux 8 kernel as not affected.

Until a fixed host kernel is installed and the host rebooted, the only available protection is to turn nested virtualization off. That closes this path completely, but VMs can then no longer run VMs of their own, so warn tenants who depend on that before making the change.

Nested virtualization is on by default in the kernel's kvm_amd module, according to VirtFusion's operator guide, so an unpatched host is exposed unless the setting was deliberately changed. To check and change it:

Check the setting with cat /sys/module/kvm_amd/parameters/nested. A value of 1 or Y means nested virtualization is on.

If the host cannot be updated yet, add options kvm_amd nested=0 to the host's module configuration.

Reboot the host. The setting cannot change while VMs are running, and a newly installed kernel does not protect the host until the reboot either. Confirm with uname -r and by reading the nested setting again.

The flaw is the latest in a series of KVM isolation failures disclosed this year, after a 16-year-old flaw in KVM's shadow memory management that affected both Intel and AMD systems, and the PwnEscape flaw in Linux's networking code, which let a guest read host memory in Vercel's live sandboxes in October.

[4] The Hacker News - The Path to AI Autonomy in the SOC
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 17:30:00 +0530
Link: https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/the-path-to-ai-autonomy-in-soc.html

[TAM METİN - 1762 kelime]
Security leaders are about to hand AI agents a lot more authority. In a recent a16z survey of CISOs at organizations with more than 1,000 employees, 36% said they are comfortable today letting AI agents act autonomously on low-risk security actions. In 12 months from now, 60% expect to be comfortable at that level. Overall, AI SOC was the highest ranking initiative for 2027.

The pressure behind the shift is easy to see. In the same survey, the most common worry was AI-accelerated attacks outpacing the team's ability to respond, selected by 55% of respondents. Analyst time is the scarcest resource in the SOC, and every alert still means pulling evidence from several systems, reconstructing what happened and deciding whether it matters.

The same respondents are cautious at the top end. Only 1% are comfortable with agents acting autonomously on most actions today, and only 7% expect to be a year from now. Most teams want more autonomy, just not all of it.

Discussions today frame autonomy as a single slider that runs from "AI suggests" to "AI acts," and that exact framing is why so many programs stall. Autonomy is a set of decisions made per stage of the workflow and per action, and the teams that get it right treat it as something an agent earns with evidence.

Autonomy is not “all or nothing”, but rather a spectrum

The question "how much do we trust the AI" is too broad to answer. Researchers worked this out decades ago, in a framework later applied widely in aviation and air traffic control, long before anyone was building SOC agents.

In a widely cited 2000 paper, Parasuraman, Sheridan and Wickens proposed that automation applies to four broad functions. Those are information acquisition, information analysis, decision and action selection, and action implementation. Each function can sit at a different level of automation, from fully manual to fully automatic, within the same system.

Mapped onto security operations, the four stages look like this.

Evidence collection. Querying the SIEM and EDR, pulling process trees, enriching indicators, gathering identity and cloud context.

Analysis and verdict. Correlating what was collected, reconstructing what happened and deciding whether the alert is a real threat.

Response recommendation. Proposing what should happen next, such as containing a host, resetting credentials or closing the case.

Response execution. Actually changing something in the environment.

This split gives security leaders a cleaner set of choices. A team can automate the first two stages heavily, since that is where analyst hours go and where mistakes are cheapest to catch. The same team can stay conservative on the fourth stage, where a wrong move disrupts the business. As the a16z report itself puts it, gathering logs is different from changing a production system.

Human IN the loop vs. Human ON the loop

Once autonomy is split by stage, teams need a shared way to describe how much of it each stage gets. A useful vocabulary comes from researchers at the University of Washington, who define five levels of agent autonomy by the role the human plays.

The authors make a point every SOC leader should take to heart. Autonomy is a deliberate design choice, separate from how capable the agent is. A highly capable agent can still run at L2 if the stakes call for it.

Read through this lens, the a16z data describes a market moving from roughly L2 today toward L4 for low-risk actions within a year. Gartner offers a complementary distinction between a human in the loop, who approves each action, and a human on the loop, whose oversight is strategic.

Enterprises evaluating AI SOC vendors should make sure that both models can be applied as appropriate, across their entire operations.

How to decide where and how much autonomy to grant an AI SOC

The levels mentioned above tell you what the options are. Deciding where each SOC action belongs takes a rubric, and three questions do most of the work.

Reversibility. If the agent gets this wrong, how quickly and completely can it be undone?

Blast radius. How many users, systems or business processes does the action touch?

Receipts. How strong and verifiable is the evidence behind the decision? An action backed by forensic proof of what was executed deserves more latitude than one backed by an LLM hunch about what looks suspicious.

Scoring real actions against those questions produces a map that most security teams will recognize.

The exact placement will differ by organization, and that is the point. The rubric forces an explicit decision for each action, instead of a single policy that is either too loose for the dangerous actions or too tight for the safe ones.

When human approval becomes a rubber stamp

According to the a16z survey, 52% of CISOs want agents to act only with human approval. It sounds like the safe choice, and in many cases it is. It also hides a failure mode that rarely gets discussed.

Human approval is only as good as the context the reviewer receives. When an approval step arrives without clear evidence or criteria, reviewers start clicking through requests to keep the queue moving, and oversight quietly disappears.

If the AI shapes how every investigation is framed, the human approving the final action is approving a conclusion they never saw being reached.

Only when the reviewer can actually check the AI’s logic and work along with hard, forensic evidence that conclusively points in one direction or another, is the approval actually worth anything.

In practice that means every approval request should show three things.

The evidence the agent collected and where it came from.

The reasoning that connects that evidence to the verdict.

What the agent checked and ruled out along the way.

A useful test if this is working, is time spent. If a reviewer cannot verify a verdict in a minute or two, the approval step is ceremonial and the team is paying for a human-in-the-loop without getting it.

Autonomy you earn, autonomy you lose

The OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications gives this approach a name. It extends least privilege into least agency, granting agents only the minimum autonomy needed for safe, bounded tasks and letting that autonomy grow as it is earned.

Earning it requires criteria that are set before the pilot starts. Otherwise autonomy expands on vendor promises and gut feel. A practical set of graduation criteria for moving an action class up one level looks like this.

Measured agreement. Track how often the agent's verdicts match analyst review over a defined period and alert volume, and set the threshold in advance.

Dry runs first. Run new actions in a test mode that executes the logic but mocks every write, so the team sees what the agent would have done before it does anything.

A complete evidence trail. Every decision at the new level must be auditable after the fact, including what the agent looked at and why it concluded what it did.

A rollback path. Define how the action is undone and who owns that before expanding scope.

Autonomy should also move down. A drop in agreement rates, a major change in the environment such as a new EDR or cloud migration, or a single serious miss should trigger a demotion until the criteria are met again. Teams that only ever ratchet upward are building risk they cannot see.

Your SOC agent is an agent too

Every level of autonomy granted to a SOC agent has a second effect. It raises the damage that agent can do if it is wrong, manipulated or compromised.

Security leaders already feel this risk across the enterprise. In the a16z survey, 46% of CISOs listed AI agents acting outside their intended permissions, or compromised agents, among their five biggest worries, and 29% cited prompt injection or data leakage through AI applications. Meanwhile 55% already run MCP servers or other agent-to-application integrations in production, and 34% run autonomous agents with tool access or write permissions.

The lesson for the SOC is that autonomy itself is a risk factor, scored alongside the vulnerability. Treat the AI SOC agent the way you would treat a new privileged identity.

Give it its own identity, never shared credentials.

Scope its permissions to the actions it is approved for at its current level.

Log every tool call, query and action in a form a human can review.

Watch it with the same detections you would apply to a new admin account.

A playbook for the next 12 months

The move from 36% to 60% will happen with or without a plan. Security leaders who want the capacity gains without the incident that sets their AI program back a year can start with five steps.

Inventory every action. List everything your AI SOC agent can do today, from read-only queries to response actions, and place each one on the reversibility, blast radius and receipts rubric.

Automate investigation aggressively. Evidence gathering and analysis consume most analyst hours and carry the least risk. This is where full autonomy pays off first.

Gate disruptive response with real evidence. Keep approval on high-impact actions, and make sure every approval request carries proof a reviewer can verify quickly.

Write graduation and demotion criteria now. Agree on the accuracy thresholds, test periods and rollback paths before the pilot starts, so autonomy expands on data.

Govern the agent like a privileged identity. Scope it, log it and monitor it, because its autonomy is also its blast radius.

Crossing the trust threshold

Every SOC that adopts AI agents will eventually face the same question for each action. Is the agent's work trustworthy enough to act on without a human checking it first?

A helpful way to think about it is a trust threshold. Below it, AI assists analysts, and humans still validate every conclusion. Above it, teams can safely hand off execution and supervise outcomes instead of steps. What moves an action across that line is depth and proof. An agent that can show what actually executed, where it came from and what it did, gives a human something real to verify, and gives the organization a defensible reason to extend its autonomy. Forensic-level investigation, the approach Intezer’s AI SOC is built on, is what moves an action across that line.

That is what earned autonomy means in practice. The agent gets more authority one action class at a time, each step backed by evidence the team can inspect, and each step reversible if the evidence stops holding up.

Note: This article has been written and contributed by Zev Schonberg, PMM at Intezer.

[5] The Hacker News - SonicWall Warns Gen 6 Firewalls Won't Get Security Patches, Even for Critical Flaws
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 16:08:22 +0530
Link: https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/sonicwall-warns-gen-6-firewalls-wont.html

[TAM METİN - 548 kelime]
SonicWall has urged all customers still running Generation 6 firewalls to retire and replace them immediately and stop exposing the devices on the internet edge, citing security risks fueled by AI-assisted attacks.

"Attackers now use automation and AI to find and exploit unsupported edge devices faster than ever," SonicWall said. "We expect internet-facing Gen 6 firewalls to be actively targeted. Treat any Gen 6 firewall still in service as a high-risk exposure, and migrate to a supported Gen 8 firewall running SonicOS 8."

The affected products running SonicOS 6.x include -

TZ350, TZ350W, TZ500, TZ500W, SOHO 250, SOHO 250W

NSA 4600, NSA 5600, NSA 6600

NSa 4650, NSa 5650, NSa 6650

TZ400, TZ400W, TZ600, TZ600P, NSA 3600

SOHO, SOHO W, TZ300P, NSa 9250, NSa 9450, NSa 9650

NSv 10 to NSv 1600 (Gen 6 virtual)

SuperMassive 9200, 9400, 9600, 9800

NSsp 12800, NSsp 12400

In recent years, threat actors have increasingly targeted edge devices as a launch point to obtain initial access, even as the window between disclosure and confirmed exploitation has collapsed significantly, in part driven by threat actors' use of automation and AI to scan the internet for unsupported devices, analyze patches and vulnerability disclosure announcements, and build working exploits faster.

According to Google Mandiant's M-Trends report published in March 2026, the mean time to exploit vulnerabilities has turned negative, reaching an estimated -7 days, meaning exploitation, on average, begins before a patch is available, down from 63 days in 2018 and -1 day in 2024.

"This trend is compounded by threat actors' evolving interest in security appliances and networking infrastructure," Google said. "Because these assets provide critical inspection of data ingress and egress points, they grant significant visibility and permissions to those who gain access to them."

Cisco Talos' 2025 Year in Review report has also found that 23% of CVEs discovered in the year directly impact network devices like VPN appliances, next-generation firewalls (NGFWs), load balancers, routers, and others.

"Since these systems sit at the perimeter of enterprise environments, compromise may lead to direct access to the critical networks," Talos said. "This aligns with real-world trends from CISA'sKnown Exploitation Vulnerability (KEV) catalog, where exploitation consistently favors edge devices because they are internetfacing, often lag in patching, and provide direct operational leverage once compromised."

With Gen 6 no longer being actively supported and receiving patches, even for critical flaws, users are recommended to follow the steps below without any delay -

Inventory every Gen 6 firewall in the production environment and retire them.

Prioritize units that are exposed to the internet or provide remote access.

Replace them with a Gen 8 firewall running SonicOS 8

Contact an authorized SonicWall partner to plan the migration

Until the firewall is replaced, it's advised to take the below actions to minimize exposure -

Disable WAN management (HTTPS, SSH, and SNMP on WAN interfaces).

Disable SSL VPN, or restrict it to known source addresses.

Enforce multi-factor authentication on every remaining remote-access and admin account, and reset local passwords.

Disable services and interfaces not in use.

Monitor logs closely for unusual logins, configuration changes and traffic.

"The risk to an unsupported firewall grows every day it stays online," SonicWall said. "One breach reaches everything. A compromised perimeter firewall gives attackers a foothold for credential theft, lateral movement and ransomware deployment."

Cisco Expressway Series Release X15.5.3 and earlier - X15.5.20

IP addresses geolocated: 66.179.31[.]32 and 18.130.47[.]116

The attack has not been attributed to any known threat actor or group. [7] The Hacker News - Critical VMware vCenter Zero-Day Flaw Lets Network Attackers Bypass Authentication
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Thu, 19 Nov 2026 20:41:06 +0530
Link: https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/critical-vmware-vcenter-flaw-cvss-98.html

[TAM METİN - 610 kelime]
A critical flaw in VMware vCenter lets an attacker with network access bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system, Broadcom, which owns VMware, said in an advisory published today.

Fixed versions are out for all supported branches, and the company lists no workaround. vCenter is the central console for managing an organization's ESX hosts and virtual machines.

The vulnerability is tracked as CVE-2026-123890 and is rated 9.8 on the CVSS scoring system. "VMware vCenter contains an authentication bypass vulnerability in the VMware Directory Service," the advisory says.

In an FAQ published with the advisory, the company says the issue "qualifies under ITIL methodologies as an emergency change," and urges organizations to consult their security staff immediately on timing.

The flaw was exploited as a zero-day more than two months before the patch, Google's threat intelligence team said in a technical analysis published November 20. A suspected China-nexus espionage actor tracked as Armory Castle used it in early September to gain administrator access to a vCenter server inside a network the group had already breached. Credit for reporting the bug goes to Google-owned Mandiant.

The bug is present in vCenter 8.0, 9.0, and 9.1, and in the vCenter builds that ship inside VMware Cloud Foundation, vSphere Foundation, and the Telco Cloud Platform and Telco Cloud Infrastructure products. That includes the older Cloud Foundation 5.x line. It is there whether or not Enhanced Linked Mode is in use.

Older versions are not cleared. The company no longer evaluates versions past end of support, and says vSphere 6.5 and 6.7 should be presumed affected. The same goes for vSphere 7.0, which left general support in October 2025, and whose customers can request a patch under an extended support contract.

None of the five flaws in the advisory lets code run on an ESX host from inside a virtual machine, and ESX itself is not affected, the advisory FAQ says.

There is no fallback for systems that cannot be updated yet: asked whether a workaround exists, the FAQ answers "Not as listed by Broadcom," while noting that mitigations may still exist in an organization's own defenses.

The updates are cumulative and cannot be installed through vCenter Quick Patch. Virtual machines continue running while vCenter installs the update, though management access drops briefly, and some encryption operations against a Standard Key Provider become unavailable until vCenter is back online.

One warning applies to upgrades already in progress: installing vCenter 8.0 U3m or 9.0.2.0200 blocks a later upgrade to VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.1, a conflict the FAQ calls a "Back-in-Time" issue. The options are to upgrade vCenter to 9.1.1 first and apply the security update there, or to wait briefly for VCF 9.1.2.

The bypass is the second critical authentication flaw in the VMware Directory Service this year. The earlier vCenter flaws, patched on July 29, included CVE-2026-59309, another 9.8-rated bypass in the same component per the July advisory, alongside a directory-traversal bug, CVE-2026-59310.

Attacks on that traversal flaw began five days after its disclosure, German incident response firm QUIRSO assessed in August, linking them with moderate confidence to a suspected China-nexus actor.

The August attacks compromised an estimated 361 IP addresses in 47 countries and deployed Babuk-derived ransomware on ESXi hosts.

The advisory also fixes four lower-severity flaws, rated 6.7 to 8.1: a SQL injection (CVE-2026-123891) and a command injection (CVE-2026-123892) in SDDC Manager, a privilege escalation to root on the SDDC Manager appliance (CVE-2026-123893), and a SAML token signature bypass in VMware Tools for Windows (CVE-2026-123894), exploitable only where Guest Alias mapping is configured. Each needs an authenticated or already privileged actor, and the last one stays inside the guest virtual machine.

[9] BleepingComputer - Hackers use autonomous AI tool Cairn to find zero-day, take over server
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 12:30:00 -0500
Link: https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-use-autonomous-ai-tool-cairn-to-find-zero-day-take-over-server/

[TAM METİN - 538 kelime]
Hackers used an autonomous AI agent platform called "Cairn" to discover a zero-day vulnerability in a medical imaging application and exploit it to take complete control of a server.

According to Amazon Threat Intelligence, the suspected Chinese-linked attackers simply instructed the AI agents to "obtain shell access," leaving them to independently discover and exploit the flaw.

Amazon Threat Intelligence uncovered the campaign after discovering that the attackers had left their Cairn instance publicly accessible without authentication, exposing their hacking operations.

According to the researchers, the attacks were launched by a Chinese-nexus threat actor between September 8 and 10, 2026, targeting mainly East Asian educational institutions outside China.

Cairn is a legitimate pentesting tool that can be used to coordinate multiple AI agents in cyber-operations, created for research and defense strengthening.

Gambit Security documented cases of Cairn abuse as part of a large-scale credit card stealing operation in September. More recently, Google reported it was deployed in an attack against an aerospace organization in the U.S.

During the campaign investigated by Amazon, the AI agents were not always successful. For example, a 16-hour and 148-action effort to take control of a Redis server failed.

In a separate case targeting a university GPU server, the agents tried over 30,000 credential combinations over six hours but failed to brute-force their way in.

Finding and using a zero-day

According to Amazon, Cairn's AI agents found a path traversal zero-day in MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging application that uses AI to help researchers label medical images.

The flaw enabled the agents to write files to arbitrary locations on the server, and within 11 minutes, they went from mapping the application's API to exploiting the vulnerability.

In a subsequent session, the AI agents used the flaw to write a Python reverse shell to the sitecustomize.py file that automatically loads when Python starts, then triggered an API endpoint to establish root access to the server.

After discovering the zero-day, the operator provided the agents with a proxy into a second university network running the same vulnerable software and directed them to target other machines.

Amazon reported the flaw to MONAI Label maintainers, and they released a security update to address it on November 18.

The researchers attributed the campaign to a Chinese-nexus threat actor with moderate confidence, based on the language of the retrieved prompts, the activity timestamps, and the choice of targets.

Amazon also shared two IP addresses associated with the campaign, observed between September 8 and 10, 2026:

Amazon warned that AI agents can find and exploit vulnerabilities faster than security teams can react, urging organizations to rely more on automated defenses rather than manual investigations.

[10] BleepingComputer - Still tracking company passwords in spreadsheets? You’re flying blind.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 10:00:10 -0500
Link: https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/still-tracking-company-passwords-in-spreadsheets-youre-flying-blind/

[TAM METİN - 1248 kelime]
The password spreadsheet your admins use may look like a complete inventory, but it only reflects some of the credentials employees have reported using. More specifically, that spreadsheet doesn’t show passwords that have been changed, created, or shared since the document was last updated, until someone brings it up to date. That’s assuming someone ever does.

Meanwhile, work passwords can end up in all kinds of places. Someone saves one in their browser.

A teammate sends a shared login in chat to move forward with a project. Another employee decides to put a few passwords in a personal vault because getting access to the company one takes too long.

Unless someone reports these actions, the spreadsheet won’t capture them.

And so, admins may think they have a handle on company credentials when, in fact, their spreadsheet tells only part of the story.

The real reason credentials slip out of admins’ view

The predominant factor is convenience. When the approved process is slow or unclear, employees use what’s at hand: a browser’s built-in password storage, a shared Google document, a Slack message, or one of the sticky notes on their desk.

They may know that that’s against the rules, but in the moment, their priority is getting work done.

That’s why a process that relies on employees to manually report every new password, update, and shared credential is nearly impossible to sustain. If the official route feels like an obstacle rather than the easiest way to access work tools, people are more likely to work around it.

This preference for convenience shows up in people’s password habits, too. Verizon’s 2025 Data Breach Investigations Report found that, in the median case, only 49% of users’ passwords across different services were unique. In other words, more than half of those passwords were reused.

The “TOP 20 Not-So-Secret Business Passwords” report by NordPass has also found “123456” to be the world’s most common password used in a corporate setting. This shows that people generally take the easy route when it comes to passwords.

Without visibility, a company may not even know that one of its most important assets is protected by “123456” or another weak password.

To solve this problem, organizations need an approach that works for both employees and admins. Without one, credentials can remain scattered and difficult to manage, increasing the risk created by those blind spots.

The risks of poor visibility into company credentials

When admins can’t see where work credentials are stored, they also cannot know who uses them, who they’ve been shared with, or whether they’ve changed. They also cannot assess the strength and reuse of the passwords employees rely on every day.

Verizon’s report found that only 3% of compromised passwords in its dataset met basic complexity standards. That finding doesn’t describe every password in an organization, but it shows why teams need a way to identify weak credentials in the systems they manage.

Reuse matters, too: if a password is compromised, reusing it across services can put more than one account at risk.

This leads us to the most important element, which is that credentials still remain one of the main ways attackers gain unauthorized access to company systems and data. The 2026 edition of the Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report identified credential abuse as the initial access vector in 13% of breaches.

It also found that vulnerability exploitation accounted for 31% of breaches, underscoring the need for credential protection as part of a broader security strategy.

Keeping company credentials in a spreadsheet creates another risk. If ransomware attackers gain a foothold in the company network, they may search specifically for files containing passwords.

Ransomware groups such as Pysa have used automated scripts to scan drives for filenames and folders containing terms like “password,” “login,” “pwd,” and “passwd.”

If attackers find a spreadsheet, they may encrypt it and demand a ransom. They could also use the credentials inside to access other accounts and systems, potentially spreading the attack further.

The solution? A structured approach that’s easy for admins to manage and for employees to follow.

To keep company accounts protected, admins should be able to answer a few questions about each company password: Is it strong? Who owns it? Where is it stored? Who has access to it? Is it reused, old, or exposed in a breach?

Each factor matters because any one of them can create risk. A strong password could still be reused across multiple accounts, so if it’s exposed in a breach, attackers may be able to use it to access those other accounts, too.

A recent password change won’t tell you whether the right people still have access, either.

Reviewing factors like these helps admins understand what needs attention. But how can they keep track of all of it?

The right password manager can make this easier by giving your team one place to store and manage work credentials. NordPass, for example, offers organizations a centralized vault protected by XChaCha20 encryption and a zero-knowledge architecture, which means the service provider can’t access what’s stored inside.

NordPass also helps admins check the credentials in the vault. With features like the Data Breach Scanner and Password Health, it can quickly identify weak, reused, old, and exposed passwords.

With NordPass, admins can also set password requirements to make sure all credentials used by employees are strong, while users can share credentials securely over protected channels.

Beyond that, the Sharing Hub feature shows who has access to passwords shared with multiple people or teams, and the activity log records actions related to company passwords.

All of this gives admins a way to spot credential issues early, decide what to address first, and check what changed afterward to make sure company logins are as secure as they can be.

Get a clear view of your company passwords with NordPass

Make sure admins know where business credentials are stored, when they’re changed, and who can access them.

At the same time, give employees quick, easy access to the tools they need without encouraging workarounds.

What a managed vault won’t solve on its own

A password manager can help solve the visibility problem, but it won’t address every aspect of it. Some employees may continue saving passwords in browsers or personal vaults, so adoption depends on making the approved option easy to use and setting clear expectations about how company logins should be handled.

Shared accounts may need clearer ownership, too. Your IT team should decide who is responsible for each login, who needs access, and when that access should be removed.

It’s also important to bear in mind that not every credential is a password. API keys, recovery codes, certificates, and other secrets may need their own storage, access, and ownership rules.

Therefore, a password health report shouldn’t be treated as a complete inventory of every way employees access company resources.

Stronger credential security starts beyond the spreadsheet

A password spreadsheet or any other manually updated document can’t provide a reliable view of your company credentials. But a secure business password manager like NordPass can.

It gives your team a secure place to store work credentials, shows you how healthy the passwords in the vault are, and makes it easier to set password requirements, share credentials securely, and track password-related activity.

So, if you really want to know what’s happening with your company credentials, give NordPass a try, and replace the spreadsheet with a business password manager built for the job.

[13] BleepingComputer - F5 releases emergency patches for critical BIG-IP RCE flaws
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 05:57:43 -0500
Link: https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/f5-releases-emergency-patches-for-critical-big-ip-rce-flaws/

[TAM METİN - 506 kelime]
US cybersecurity company F5 warned customers to patch five BIG-IP vulnerabilities that attackers can exploit to trigger denial-of-service (DoS) or gain remote code execution.

Tracked as CVE-2026-121805, CVE-2026-120292, CVE-2026-120285, CVE-2026-116953, and CVE-2026-123637, these stack-based buffer overflow flaws affect the company's BIG-IP Access Policy Manager (APM) centralized access management proxy solution and the BIG-IP iRules programmable scripting feature.

All five security issues are rated critical severity, and unauthenticated threat actors can exploit them to terminate the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) and execute arbitrary code remotely on systems with vulnerable configurations.

The company also released engineering hotfixes for a high-severity BIG-IP APM SAML vulnerability (CVE-2026-126822) stemming from an integer underflow (wrap or wraparound) weakness that remote, unauthenticated threat actors can abuse in denial-of-service (DoS) attacks.

"Traffic is disrupted while the TMM process restarts. This vulnerability allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to cause a denial-of-service (DoS) on the BIG-IP system and may perform RCE," F5 said. "There is no control plane exposure; this is a data plane issue only."

F5 said it has no mitigation measures for these flaws and advised security teams to install the out-of-band hotfixes released on Wednesday to address them on vulnerable devices.

Internet threat watchdog Shadowserver currently tracks more than 177,000 BIG-IP instances and over 14,600 IP addresses with BIG-IP APM fingerprints exposed online. However, there is no information on how many are honeypots or have already been patched against these vulnerabilities.

Although the company hasn't flagged any of these issues as exploited in attacks, admins should upgrade systems to the latest version as soon as possible, since cybercrime and nation-state threat groups have often abused F5 vulnerabilities in the wild.

Attackers have targeted F5 security flaws to breach corporate networks, map internal servers, hijack devices, deploy data-wiping malware, and steal sensitive files from victims worldwide in recent years.

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has flagged seven F5 vulnerabilities as actively exploited since November 2021, four of them also used by ransomware gangs.

Most recently, in September, F5 also patched a critical BIG-IP APM vulnerability (CVE-2026-94127) that is being actively exploited in zero-day remote code execution attacks.

One year ago, F5 also disclosed that state-backed hackers breached its systems in August 2025 to steal source code and information on undisclosed BIG-IP security vulnerabilities.

F5 is a Fortune 500 tech company that provides cybersecurity, application delivery networking (ADN), and other services to more than 23,000 customers, including 80% of the Fortune Global 500 and 48 of Fortune 50 companies.

[14] BleepingComputer - Windows 11 KB5132057 update released with 28 changes and fixes
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 04:25:35 -0500
Link: https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/microsoft/windows-11-kb5132057-update-released-with-28-changes-and-fixes/

[TAM METİN - 751 kelime]
Microsoft released the KB5132057 November optional cumulative update for Windows 11 versions 25H2 and 26H2, which comes with 28 changes, including improvements to Windows Search, Windows Hello, and the Run dialog.

KB5132057 is a preview update that allows IT administrators to test Windows improvements, bug fixes, and new features before they become generally available in next month's Patch Tuesday release.

However, unlike regular Windows cumulative updates, monthly optional updates don't include security fixes and provide only quality improvements.

The KB5132057 update includes the new Windows Search Box experience that was built on WinUI 3 and removes promotional content from web results for better resource efficiency and a streamlined design.

After installing the November 2026 preview update, users will also get improved Windows Hello facial recognition that lets them sign into their accounts in dark rooms after enabling the "Automatically adjust screen brightness during face recognition" option under Settings > Accounts > Sign-in options > Facial recognition (Windows Hello).

KB5132057 also adds the new Run dialog, unveiled in May with a refreshed design and an almost instant time-to-show of just 94 ms. After installing the update, you can enable it by toggling on "New Run dialog" under Settings > System > Advanced.

You can install KB5132057 by opening Windows Settings, clicking on Windows Update, and then clicking 'Check for Updates.'

​Since KB5132057 is an optional update, click the "Download and install" link if you don't already have the "Get the latest updates as soon as they're available" option enabled, which would prompt the OS to install it automatically.

You can also manually download and install this preview update from the Microsoft Update Catalog.

Windows 11 KB5132057 highlights

Once installed, this optional non-security update will upgrade Windows 11 26H2 and 25H2 devices to builds 26300.10075 and 26200.10075, respectively.

The November 2026 preview update comes with many other changes, some of the most significant ones highlighted below:

Search from This PC in File Explorer is now indexer-based, making it much faster and consistent with search from File Explorer Home.

Inline actions: You can now complete common tasks directly from Windows Search without opening Settings. For example, you can turn on dark mode or Bluetooth, adjust screen brightness, mute your device, or arrange open windows. If you have an Android phone connected through Phone Link, you can also call or text contacts and use phone actions like “Find my phone” and “Do Not Disturb.”

New! If you accidentally trigger the keyboard shortcut for Sticky Keys, Filter Keys, or Toggle Keys, you can now turn it off directly from the prompt that appears. You can still manage notifications and sounds for these features under Settings > Accessibility > Keyboard > Notification preferences.

New! Web sign-in is now supported on Microsoft Entra hybrid-joined devices, in addition to Microsoft Entra-joined devices. At the lock screen, you can sign in without a password by using a FIDO2 security key, a passkey on your phone, or a Temporary Access Pass (TAP). After you sign in, Windows gets a Kerberos ticket, so access to on-premises file shares and internal sites continues to work. For more information, see Web sign-in for Windows.

[File History] This update fixes an issue where the File History restore interface might not find backups when a drive is selected as the backup location.

On Thursday, Microsoft also warned customers that their devices may reboot one more time after deploying the November 2026 optional update and updates rolling out over the next months.

"With recent and upcoming Windows updates over the next few months, a limited number of consumer and business devices might experience one additional restart during installation," Microsoft noted in a message center update. "This one‑time restart occurs after a Secure Boot certificate update is applied as part of the Secure Boot update process."

Microsoft announced this will be the final non-security preview update released this year, as operations wind down for the Western holidays. Normal monthly servicing will resume in January.

[15] Krebs on Security - CTO of ‘RansomwareHelp’ Indicted for Wire Fraud
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 00:36:39 +0000
Link: https://krebsonsecurity.com/2026/11/cto-of-ransomwarehelp-indicted-for-wire-fraud/

[TAM METİN - 1421 kelime]
The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.

A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com.

The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.

“Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the company had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.”

But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the company’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media, but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company].

The indictment says the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim company and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors.

The government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260.

The following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260.

Paul Ihme is co-founder of the security firm Soteria. Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their company and client data.

Ihme said RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.”

A portion of the proposal that RansomwareHelp sent to a victim accounting firm in March 2024. Click to enlarge.

The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.”

“Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed.

Ihme said RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the company could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network.

A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked.

But Ihme said a review of the company’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days.

A screenshot of a 2024 conversation between Lockbit and RansomwareHelp, which was secretly negotiating with the extortion group. Click to enlarge.

“The charitable view would be to say that they were using Anydesk so they could grab the stuff they needed without having to walk the client through downloading and uploading a bunch of stuff,” Ihme said. “A legitimate firm would say, ‘Hey, send us a copy of the ransom note,’ which will have a link or URL to go to and chat with the threat actors. What they were doing is using that access to delete ransomware notes off the systems. The only reason they would do that is to prevent the victim from jumping into that chat itself.”

Indeed, RansomwareHelp pleaded with the Lockbit group throughout the chat not to reveal to the victim that they were negotiating. However, Lockbit quickly grew annoyed with the length of the negotiations, replying that the victims had waited too long and that the ransom demand would increase by $100,000 for every day they dithered further.

The Lockbit representative starts raising the ransom demand after multiple negotiators begin interacting with the threat actors. Click to enlarge.

In the end, the accounting firm took Ihme’s advice and went with a more established security firm that helped them negotiate a payment to Lockbit.

“The victim told us, ‘If we don’t get this data back, our business is over’,” Ihme recalled. “They ended up paying half of what RansomwareHelp was going to charge them.”

The chats show RansomwareHelp kept pestering Lockbit to negotiate a deal even after it was clear a new negotiator was engaging with the ransomware group on the victim’s behalf.

“I tell you something, that person who is negotiating with you for the other chat is damaging the whole process,” RansomwareHelp wrote to Lockbit. “Please do not change the price. I am doing my best to achieve it.”

Ihme said RansomwareHelp primarily targeted small to medium sized businesses that weren’t particularly tech-savvy, noting that many of the technical claims made on the company’s website and in their proposal are patently farcical. For example, the proposal sent to the accounting firm said it could break six types of encryption, and then proceeded to list a number of irrelevant password hashing algorithms like SHA-256.

“If it were really true these guys could decrypt any ransomware out there, this guy would be a billionaire,” Ihme said. “They were going after people who don’t have any technical knowledge, are desperate, and don’t have anyone advising them about how any of this stuff works.”

The case against Palacio marks the latest in a string of recent prosecutions by the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) targeting security firms alleged to have conspired with fraudsters to defraud clients. In early October, the government charged 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky, an executive at the Canadian cybersecurity firm Cybersteward. The government has sealed the case against Dubrovsky, but he is currently facing cyber extortion and conspiracy charges.

Around the same time as Dubrovsky’s arrest, the DoJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DoJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

[16] Security Affairs - CVE-2026-23871: WhatsApp Bug Helped Scammers Make Messages Look Legitimate
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 22:21:12 +0000
Link: https://securityaffairs.com/203622/security/cve-2026-23871-whatsapp-bug-helped-scammers-make-messages-look-legitimate.html

[TAM METİN - 612 kelime]
CVE-2026-23871: WhatsApp Bug Helped Scammers Make Messages Look Legitimate

WhatsApp patched three security flaws, including one exploited in a real scam campaign to make fraudulent messages appear more credible.

WhatsApp’s November security advisory fixes three flaws, including CVE-2026-23871, a vulnerability in Click to WhatsApp ads affecting WhatsApp and WhatsApp Business for Android versions earlier than 2.26.17.4.

“Incomplete validation of external ad-reply URLs in WhatsApp for Android and WhatsApp Business for Android before 2.26.17.4 could have caused a target’s device to reveal its IP information to an attacker if an attacker sent media from an attacker-controlled URL when a crafted Click to WhatsApp ad-reply message was rendered and displayed in a message thread.” reads the advisory. “This issue may have been abused in conjunction with specific spam messages.”

The issue was caused by incomplete checks on external ad-reply URLs. An attacker could use a server under their control to send media through a crafted ad-reply message. When the message appeared in a chat, it could cause the victim’s device to reveal its IP address to the attacker.

SecurityWeek reported that WhatsApp discovered the flaw while investigating a real scam campaign. The company’s security team found that a scammer was exploiting the issue to make fraudulent messages appear more credible.

“Our team found this issue while disrupting a scam campaign, and we believe a scammer was using it to make their scam message seem more credible.” a WhatsApp spokesperson told SecurityWeek.

The second fix is more serious on paper, though WhatsApp has seen no sign it was ever used. CVE-2026-102769 is a SQL injection on WhatsApp for Android before 2.26.35.74, triggered when someone taps a specially crafted “order details” message sent from an unofficial client.

“A SQL injection vulnerability when the recipient tapped on a specially crafted “order details” message from an unofficial client in WhatsApp for Android prior to version 2.26.35.74 could have allowed deletion of locally-stored WhatsApp files and, only if the user is online at time of receipt, leaked one bit of information asked by the attacker about the user’s chat database via an induced-crash delivery receipt timing sidechannel.” continues the report.

The company is not aware of attacks in the wild exploiting this flaw.

The third, CVE-2026-44908, lives deeper in WhatsApp’s infrastructure than in the app itself. It affects the remote-attestation verifier that confirms trust with Meta AI’s confidential computing backend, across WhatsApp and WhatsApp Business on iOS, Android and Mac. Someone positioned inside Meta’s own infrastructure could, in theory, have presented a certificate signed by the wrong key to bypass the hardware root of trust, but such a certificate would first need to appear on a public transparency ledger, and WhatsApp says that ledger shows every published certificate checks out clean.

These issues come after two fixes released in May. One addressed a bug in Instagram Reels message handling that could make another person’s device load media from an attacker-controlled URL. The other fixed a Windows attachment-spoofing trick. By adding a NUL byte to a filename, an attacker could make an executable file look like a normal document. Meta received reports of both flaws through its bug bounty program, and there is no evidence that attackers exploited them.

Of the three new flaws, only one was used in a real-world scam. It also had the lowest technical impact. This shows that scammers don’t always need to exploit serious vulnerabilities or gain access to a device. A convincing message can be enough to deceive a victim. Make sure you update WhatsApp on all your devices. The fixed versions vary across iOS, Android, Mac, Windows and WhatsApp Business.

[17] Security Affairs - JPMorgan, Visa and Mastercard Report Third-Party Data Breaches After N0n Claims
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 14:56:32 +0000
Link: https://securityaffairs.com/203614/data-breach/jpmorgan-visa-and-mastercard-report-third-party-data-breaches-after-n0n-claims.html

[TAM METİN - 673 kelime]
JPMorgan, Visa and Mastercard Report Third-Party Data Breaches After N0n Claims

JPMorgan, Visa and Mastercard disclose third-party data breaches after the N0n extortion group claims to have stolen customer information.

The disclosures involving JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Mastercard highlight a familiar but often underestimated security problem: the risks introduced by third-party service providers. All three companies have confirmed incidents involving external vendors after the N0n extortion group claimed it had stolen customer information and published data allegedly taken from their systems.

The important distinction is that the companies haven’t reported breaches of their own payment infrastructure. Instead, the incidents appear to involve information held by outside providers, showing how a security failure at a supplier can expose data belonging to major financial institutions and their customers.

JPMorgan said the attackers may have accessed marketing information held by its service providers, including customer names and email addresses.

“Based on our ​investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names ‌and email addresses,” a JPMorgan spokesperson told Reuters, adding that the company would be contacting the affected customers directly.

The bank stressed that its services weren’t affected and that the incident had no connection to the technical problems some customers experienced earlier in the week. Where necessary, it plans to contact affected customers and offer free credit monitoring.

Visa confirmed that the incident it was investigating involved a third-party provider in the Asia-Pacific region. The company said its own systems hadn’t been affected and that there was no evidence that payment information, including card numbers, had been exposed.

Mastercard also acknowledged a security incident at an external provider. The company said the exposure involved a limited number of email addresses belonging to a small group of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefits program. It stressed that the information wasn’t related to payments and that its payment network remained fully operational.

The N0n group had listed the three companies on its leak site on November 16, claiming to have obtained customer engagement and marketing data. It subsequently published the allegedly stolen information and marked the companies as having refused to pay. The group’s claims should be distinguished from the information independently confirmed by the companies.

The scale of the alleged exposure is significant. According to Reuters’ review, the JPMorgan-related files contained more than 16,000 customer email addresses, some associated with phone numbers and postal codes. Researchers also identified what appeared to be 124 email addresses belonging to bank employees.

The Visa dataset reportedly contained thousands of customer email addresses, phone numbers and marketing campaign records, mainly relating to Asia-Pacific markets. The available information also suggests that the exposure wasn’t limited to customer contact details, although the authenticity and completeness of the files remain important considerations.

Neither JPMorgan, Visa nor Mastercard has identified the affected service providers or disclosed the total number of customers involved. This leaves important questions unanswered, including how attackers accessed the providers’ systems, how long they maintained access and what security controls failed.

Even when attackers don’t obtain card numbers or account credentials, names, email addresses and phone numbers can be valuable. Criminals can use this information to create convincing phishing messages, impersonate financial institutions and target customers with fraudulent calls or messages. A message that includes a person’s name and references a genuine banking relationship is much more likely to attract attention.

For this reason, third-party risk management needs to go beyond contractual security requirements and periodic questionnaires. Organizations should know what information suppliers can access, limit the data they share, review access privileges and require timely incident reporting. They should also verify that providers apply appropriate security controls and have effective procedures to detect and contain intrusions.

The N0n group emerged in September and has listed roughly 200 alleged victims on its leak site. Its claims against the three financial companies show how cyber extortion can affect organizations through their suppliers, even when their core infrastructure and services remain operational.
