[18] Security Affairs - Hackers Exploit Cisco Expressway Flaw CVE-2026-76466 to Breach Russian Organization
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 12:52:40 +0000
Link: https://securityaffairs.com/203598/hacking/hackers-exploit-cisco-expressway-flaw-cve-2026-76466-to-breach-russian-organization.html

[TAM METİN - 442 kelime]
Hackers Exploit Cisco Expressway Flaw CVE-2026-76466 to Breach Russian Organization

Cisco Expressway flaw CVE-2026-76466 is being exploited to gain root access and move from exposed devices into internal networks.

Attackers have exploited a critical flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-76466 (CVSS score of 9.8) in Cisco Expressway to breach a Russian organization, and they moved fast once a working exploit went public.

“A vulnerability in the database service feature of Cisco Expressway Series could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker with network access to a Cisco Expressway device to execute arbitrary operating system commands as root.” reads the advisory.

An unauthenticated remote attacker can trigger the flaw to run commands as root on an affected device. Cisco shipped a fix on 21 October, so this wasn’t a zero-day by the time it got used.

Russian security firm F6 says this is the first known case of the flaw being exploited in the wild, and it happened on Expressway X15.5.3 devices after a proof-of-concept exploit appeared on GitHub. The attackers started with two internet-facing Expressway boxes.

“The attackers initially compromised two Cisco Expressway internet-facing devices.” reads the advisory by F6. “Through one of them, they gained access to two additional cluster nodes located on the organization’s internal network. After obtaining root access, the attackers began preparing tooling for further lateral movement across the infrastructure.”

The attackers used custom Python scripts to scan networks, find accessible SMB resources, connect to SQL Server and WinRM, and search GitLab repositories. Their goal was to steal credentials and other sensitive information.

F6’s analysts think AI tools helped write those scripts, judging by the comments and fix descriptions left inside them, which is a strange kind of courtesy from an intruder.

F6 published indicators tied to the activity: two IP addresses, a telltale “[email protected]” entry in the Erlang system log on affected devices, and Python scripts staged under a specific disk path.

“One of the key indicators of successful exploitation is the appearance of a nodeup ‘[email protected]’ entry in the Erlang system log (erlang.log) on affected Cisco Expressway devices.” states F6. “Such an entry indicates that a connection was established with an Erlang node whose identifier corresponds to the known exploitation mechanism — CVE-2026-76466. When such events are detected, organizations should review other logs and artifacts to confirm whether compromise has occurred.”

Nobody has linked the attack to a known group yet, so treat this as an active technique without a named author. If you run Expressway, update now, hunt for those indicators, and don’t assume a clean edge device means a clean network behind it.

[19] Security Affairs - Trump’s First Move After the Outages: Fire the Cyber Director

Trump’s First Move After the Outages: Fire the Cyber Director

Trump fired his national cyber director days after outages hit Microsoft, US flights, and the NSA’s classified network. No link to a cyberattack confirmed.

The White House fired national cyber director Sean Cairncross, a person close to the administration told Reuters. It’s the first major personnel move since a string of tech failures hit the country over the past week. Department of Defense Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies will take the role temporarily.

The week brought several major disruptions. A global Microsoft outage affected Outlook and Microsoft 365, disrupting services for hundreds of millions of users. A nationwide ground stop also affected more than 18,000 flights. Then, on November 17, the NSA’s classified internal network, NSANet, also went down. CNN reported that six sources confirmed the outage and that some staff at Fort Meade were told to arrive at different times.

Three separate systems experienced major disruptions in less than two weeks, raising questions about what was happening. A Defense Department official said the NSA outage followed routine maintenance and caused a “temporary degradation.” Sources told CNN there was no evidence of a cyberattack. A former senior NSA official explained that NSANet is made up of several interconnected networks with built-in redundancy, making a complete outage unusual. However, by midweek, the agency had not said when all services would be restored.

“The dismissal of Cairncross is the ​administration’s first major personnel move since the outages. Cairncross oversaw cybersecurity policy and strategy across the federal ​government. Department of Defense Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies will assume the position temporarily, according to the source.” Reuters reports.

“The president fully supported firing Sean Cairncross from his position,” a person, ​who spoke on condition of anonymity, told Reuters.

Cairncross, a former Republican National Committee executive before taking the cyber director job, said in a statement it had been the honor of a lifetime to serve.

It is important to highlight that nobody has linked these outages to each other or to a foreign actor, at least not officially.

“The top US intelligence official ​said on Wednesday the disruptions ​were separate ⁠service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes and not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.” Reuters continues.

Cybersecurity experts told Reuters separately that the outages are more likely linked to companies rushing to patch vulnerabilities that AI tools now surface faster than before.

This is a plausible explanation, even if it is less appealing than blaming a foreign attacker. Finding vulnerabilities faster means companies need to release security updates more quickly. But faster updates also increase the risk of errors that can disrupt services. A series of outages caused by security measures moving too fast may not make dramatic headlines, but it highlights an important lesson: updates must be properly tested before deployment, even when there is pressure to act quickly.

Not everyone in Washington is satisfied with that account. Republican Senator Josh Hawley of Missouri said this week the administration should brief lawmakers on the outages so they can tell the public what’s actually happening.

“His successor will need to be confirmed by the US Senate, which will be controlled by Democrats beginning in January.” Reuters concludes.

[20] Security Affairs - Hunt.io Uncovers Russian-Speaking Credential Theft Operation Targeting US Banks and Government Accounts
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 09:03:11 +0000
Link: https://securityaffairs.com/203554/cyber-crime/hunt-io-uncovers-russian-speaking-credential-theft-operation-targeting-us-banks-and-government-accounts.html

[TAM METİN - 571 kelime]
Hunt.io Uncovers Russian-Speaking Credential Theft Operation Targeting US Banks and Government Accounts

Hunt.io uncovered a credential-stealing operation that compromised 603 PCs and exposed bank, government and password manager accounts.

Hunt.io found an exposed open directory sitting on a Netherlands VPS, and inside it was the live loot store of a credential-theft operation. The report describes decrypted password-manager vaults, cleartext bank logins, and accounts behind the federal identity gateways ID.me and Login.gov. No bank or agency was breached directly; this all happened on the victims’ own Windows PCs.

The attackers used three custom-built tools to manage the operation. HavoX handled communication with infected computers and ran commands, Phantom53 managed victims and tasks, while the Kraken Bridge connected the system to an external control panel.

HavoX used encrypted connections and hidden Python scripts to operate quietly. Phantom53 tracked infected devices, while Kraken Bridge sent commands and delivered tasks through temporary download links that were deleted after use.

The operation affected 603 computers, which had been communicating with three command-and-control systems since October 12. In just three weeks, they generated more than 1.2 million connections. At least 57 victims had US bank or government login details stored on their computers, while 46 had accounts linked to federal benefits or identity services. In one case, the attacker cracked an entire LastPass vault offline, recovering 2,880 logins, including access to a bank account, the IRS and the vault’s own sharing key.

Password managers fared no better. LastPass fell to a custom seven-script pipeline that cracked its AES-CBC storage format and pulled 2,880 logins from one vault alone, plus 17 passkeys and secure notes covering Wi-Fi passwords and security answers. 1Password’s master password was cracked for two victims through a PBKDF2, HKDF, and AES-GCM keyset attack, and a developer’s live KeePass database was lifted straight off a GoLand workstation while the app was still open.

The attackers also targeted more than banks and email accounts. Four PowerShell scripts stole session tokens from 35 AI developer tools, including Claude, Codex and Gemini. They also collected credential files, chat histories and API keys. Three other scripts targeted 44 cryptocurrency platforms and seven browser wallet extensions, stealing 6,570 records from 67 victims.

To maintain access to infected computers, the operator used legitimate remote-access tools, including ConnectWise ScreenConnect and Level.io. The Level.io installer was built into the attack platform, allowing the attackers to keep access even after the original malware was removed.

The operator had developed the platform from the ground, and the custom tooling shows it.

The attribution rests on the operator’s own files. Comments, logs, and docstrings across 249 files are written in Russian, in the kind of casual, private language someone uses when they don’t expect anyone else to read it, from a bridge component’s runtime log to section comments inside a seed-phrase search script.

Hunt.io’s defensive advice centers on treating AI CLI credential files the same as SSH keys, enforcing conditional access tied to device state, and alerting on pythonw.exe spawning from unusual locations. None of the affected institutions were hacked, which is itself the point the researchers want understood.

“None of these institutions is breached. What is exposed is live customer access, which is account-takeover fuel.” concludes the report. “The fix sits on the account side: phishing-resistant authentication, session and device binding, and fast resets for the customers in this loot.”

[21] Security Affairs - Chaotic Eclipse Releases FastUnlock, a New Windows Zero-Day Vulnerability
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Thu, 19 Nov 2026 21:43:09 +0000
Link: https://securityaffairs.com/203537/hacking/chaotic-eclipse-releases-fastunlock-a-new-windows-zero-day-vulnerability.html

[TAM METİN - 867 kelime]
Chaotic Eclipse Releases FastUnlock, a New Windows Zero-Day Vulnerability

The researcher Chaotic Eclipse released FastUnlock, a new Windows zero-day vulnerability exploiting Narrator to bypass the lock screen.

Security researcher Chaotic Eclipse, also known as INFINITE NIGHTMARE, MSNightmare and Nightmare-Eclipse, released a new Windows zero-day vulnerability, dubbed FastUnlock, exploiting Narrator to bypass the lock screen.

According to the researcher, exploiting it can bypass BitLocker encryption and allow code execution under the lock screen’s WsiAccount. He claims he breached a fully encrypted Windows 11 26H2 system in just five minutes, even with the November security updates installed.

“It took a total of 5 minutes from finding this to breaching a fully encrypted bitlocker machine with Windows 11 26H2 November Patch installed, an issue caused by total negligence from Microsoft’s side… The vulnerability seems to be extremely consistent in every machine I tested it in, in other words, if you know how to control narrator in the background properly or just press the correct combination of buttons, you will get code execution in the target machine as well.” reads the advisory published by the researcher.

The attack requires physical access to the computer and at least one user account linked to an online account. The researcher says the flaw undermines BitLocker’s protection, which should prevent access to encrypted data even if an attacker has physical access to the device.

He explains that Microsoft introduced the issue while redesigning Narrator, failing to prevent its new interface from running in the lock screen account context. Unlike earlier lock screen bypass flaws, this one is reportedly easier to exploit. The attack can be triggered through the “I forgot my PIN” or password option.

The researcher explains that the attack starts from the Microsoft account recovery screen. Enabling Narrator causes it to focus on a hidden background window. By navigating its options with the keyboard, an attacker can open Narrator’s settings. From there, the researcher says several paths can lead to code execution under the WsiAccount user, including opening File Explorer through the Bluetooth and Devices and AutoPlay settings.

“Now I didn’t show the full code execution demo because I don’t really have a USB stick but I already did this enough times to know what happens next, your next step is to plugin a USB stick, as soon as you do, narrator will focus on explorer showing your mounted storage content and you can just navigate with the same button combination (CAPS LOCK + Arrow keys/Enter/Space), if you do everything properly the binary in your USB stick will be executed in the context of “WsiAccount”” concludes the report. “I have not checked other windows versions so I am not really sure if this might work on windows 10.”

Chaotic Eclipse is a researcher known for publicly releasing PoC exploits for zero-day vulnerabilities, often after criticizing vendors’ handling of vulnerability reports. His releases have mainly targeted Microsoft products, including Windows and Microsoft Defender, with some later exploited in the wild. Among the most notable are the Undefend and RedSun Defender zero-days.

His work has fueled debate over responsible disclosure and the risks of publishing working exploits.

Recently, Chaotic Eclipse revealed that he is Abdelhamid Naceri, a security researcher. Naceri previously worked with Microsoft in the UK and Germany. In a now-deleted X post, he described his departure from the company, claiming Microsoft terminated his employment without giving him a clear reason. He said Microsoft offered several financial settlements, but he rejected them because he wanted a formal explanation and help staying in Germany.

Naceri also said he challenged the dismissal in a German labor court. According to his account, Microsoft changed its arguments during the case, but the court ultimately upheld the termination. He said the long legal dispute left him with almost no compensation and caused serious financial and emotional problems, including treatment in a psychiatric hospital.

The researcher also admitted that an earlier claim that Microsoft had taken legal action against him was fabricated. The claim came during the controversy over Microsoft’s threats of legal action against security researchers who disclosed zero-day vulnerabilities.

In September, the researcher released a new zero-day exploit targeting Microsoft Defender. He named the exploit BigDiskBuster, it triggers a Denial of Service Vulnerability in Windows Defender Update.

In the same month, Chaotic Eclipse released multiple zero-day exploits targeting Nvidia (GreenSection) and Microsoft Defender (ShieldCrash).

He also released exploits targeting other anti-malware and defense solutions. Chaotic Eclipse released a zero-day exploit targeting Kaspersky Endpoint Security, which he named HardBreacher, that triggers a privilege escalation flaw. The researcher pointed out that the PoC is unstable and may require repeated attempts, but when successful, it creates a DLL in System32 with full user permissions. The researcher also claims that taking control of Kaspersky’s UI process can disrupt the antivirus and interfere with file-access controls, potentially leaving the system in an unstable state.

The researcher also released a zero-day exploit targeting GenDigital Avast Antivirus, named PrettyPrague. The exploit triggers a privilege escalation flaw.

Finally, Chaotic Eclipse released a new zero-day exploit targeting Crowdstrike Falcon cybersecurity platform. The researcher named the exploit FalconFlank, it triggers a privilege escalation flaw.

[22] Graham Cluley - n0n extortion gang leaks data of JPMorgan Chase, Visa, and Mastercard customers
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 18:57:38 +0000
Link: https://www.bitdefender.com/en-us/blog/hotforsecurity/n0n-extortion-leaks-data-jpmorgan-chase-visa-mastercard

[TAM METİN - 545 kelime]
Data belonging to customers of three of the biggest companies in global finance has been leaked online, after hackers breached third-party service providers working for JPMorgan Chase, Visa, and Mastercard.

The finance companies have all acknowledged that security incidents have occurred at unnamed third--party companies, after the n0n extortion gang named all three on its dark web leak site earlier this week.

In JPMorgan Chase's case, it tweeted that although it believed "the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses" there had been "no disruption" to its services.

Mastercard also said that its payment network had not been affected, and that cardholders could continue to use their cards.

According to Visa, the breach occurred at an unnamed third-party provider based in Asia Pacific.

n0n claims to have stolen "hundreds of thousands of campaign interactions" related to JPMorgan Chase. All three of the corporations were given 48 hours to negotiate with the extortion gang, but none of them paid. So, n0n published data on its website exposing the details of thousands of customers.

News of the security breach impacted the share prices of all three companies, after a jittery week of high-profile technology outages in the United States.

According to Reuters, the leaked JPMorgan Chase data included more than 16,000 customer email addresses, and what appeared to be the email addresses of some 124 employees of the bank. Some of the customer information included phone numbers, and post codes.

Clearly scammers and fraudsters could exploit information like that in a variety of ways, including by contacting members of the public claiming to be employees of their bank.

Meanwhile, according to a Cybernews report, the leaked Visa data includes details of over 6000 premium card holders who are signed up to Asia-Pacific dining programmes, including names, phone numbers, the messaging apps they use, and restaurant booking details.

n0n is believed to be a Russia-based extortion gang, and despite only having been operating for a couple of months has already managed to claim the scalps of approximately 200 corporate victims.

Security researchers say n0n has typically broken into organisations using valid login credentials, harvested by info-stealing malware or obtained by credential-stuffing VPNs and poorly secured remote desktop (RDP) services, before using legitimate admin tools to gather data. It is not yet known how the vendors in this case were compromised.

Of course, financial institutions are very experienced at securing their own infrastructure. Where they appear to have fallen down on this occasion is through the use of third-party marketing agencies or loyalty scheme operators who have been less diligent in securing their systems.

You are only as safe as the weakest link in the chain. And customers don't really care whose server it was that leaked their data, when they entrusted it to your care in the first place.

The advice for concerned Chase, Visa or Mastercard customers is simple: be wary of unexpected emails, texts or calls claiming to come from your bank. It would not be a surprise at all if scammers exploit the breach by mentioning it to customers, and offering compensation, or inviting members of the public to "verify" their account.

If you are unsure, contact your bank directly using its published number.

[23] Graham Cluley - Cold Relic: What you need to know
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Thu, 19 Nov 2026 17:10:29 +0000
Link: https://www.fortra.com/blog/cold-relic-what-you-need-know

[TAM METİN - 619 kelime | KAYNAK: proxy okuyucu]
### What Is Cold Relic?

Cold Relic is a Russian state-sponsoredcyber-espionage group. Like many other hacking gangs, it has been given a variety of different names by different security researchers - so you may have heard it described before as "Star Blizzard", "Callisto Group", or "SEABORGIUM."

Google previously tracked the group as "COLDRIVER", but renamed it earlier this year as part of an overhaul of how it names different hacking groups - under which Russian groups now have "RELIC" as part of their name.

### Ok, so the Threat Researchers Have Lots of Fun Coming Up with Names for These Hacking Gangs - but What Does This Group Actually Do?

In this particular case, Cold Relic targets think tanks, NGOs, journalists and academics, defense contractors, government officials - basically anybody who might have information that could be of interest to the Kremlin.

The hacking group has been targeting people of interest for many years. For instance, the UK's NCSC accused it of [targeting British MPs since at least 2015](https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/news/uk-and-allies-expose-cyber-campaign-attempted-political-interference), and in 2023 the US Department of Justice [charged two Russian members of the group](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/two-russian-nationals-working-russias-federal-security-service-charged-global-computer) with launching spear-phishing attacks against targets in the United States and other countries, and stealing information with the intent of manipulating the UK's 2019 election.

### So Is There Anything New that the Group Has Been Up To?

Yes, new research published by Google's threat intelligence team [describes](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/cold-relic-a-case-study-in-impersonation-and-compromise) how the Russian government-backed hackers broke into a US company's Google Workspace admin account. Once there, the hackers stole data, which was then used to impersonate a trusted contact and breach a second US organization via a phishing attack.

### Sounds Nasty. Can You Tell Me More?

In late 2025, Cold Relic managed to obtain the login credentials for a Super Admin account for an unnamed organization's Google Workspace environment. The administrator of the account was then bombarded with multi-factor authentication (MFA) push notifications... until they finally approved one, letting the hackers in.

The hackers then exploited their privileged access to the Workspace, registered a new device and generated MFA backup codes for it, and enrolled rogue passkeys. They were then able to export from the admin console lists of the employees, and domain-wide data, deleting security alerts as they progressed to cover their tracks.

Realizing their mistake in allowing the hackers access to the Google Workspace, the victim ensured that passwords and sessions were reset, but overlooked revoking rogue passkeys - which meant that the Cloud Relic hackers were able to continue to access sensitive information for months.

### Sheesh. And then they exploited their access to attack another firm?

Correct. An employee at a second company, who had links to the first, was approached via an encrypted messaging app. The message pretended to be from a member of staff from the first company, claiming that their servers had been hit by a distributed denial of service (DDoS) attack.

Links shared by the fake worker stole login credentials from the second firm, allowing the hackers to once again enroll their own MFA device and steal data.

### Do We Know What Information Cold Relic Is After?

Aside from email and documents, the hackers appear to be particularly interested in gathering staff lists, contacts, CVs, and the like which can help them craft convincing phishing emails to target other potential victims.

### So What Can an Organization Do About This?

Google's [report](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/cold-relic-a-case-study-in-impersonation-and-compromise) on the incident provides a number of recommendations, including:

*   Replacing push-based MFA with phishing-resistant authentication, such as hardware security keys.
*   Require administrators to approve new MFA devices.
*   Flagging or blocking administrator logins from VPNs and residential proxies.
*   Preventing staff from storing passwords and other secrets in files stores on cloud drives.

[24] Recorded Future - AI Joins the Industrial Attack Workflow
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 00:00:00 GMT
Link: https://www.recordedfuture.com/blog/ai-industrial-attack-workflow

[TAM METİN - 1010 kelime]
AI Joins the Industrial Attack Workflow

On October 11 and 12, 2026, someone changed the defrost settings on refrigeration controllers at more than 700 retail locations in France. This resulted in fires, damaged equipment, and food losses estimated in the tens of millions of euros, highlighting the physical impacts of attacks against operational technology (OT). On November 9, France attributed the attack to Shahid Kaveh, a unit of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Cyber Electronic Command (IRGC-CEC). We track activity that likely belongs to an element of Shahid Kaveh as GreenJuliett.

GreenJuliett (also known as CyberAv3ngers and Bauxite) builds infrastructure aimed at internet-facing PLCs. And while that work continued through at least October 30, despite repeated public reporting on the group, the target set began to widen. Between August and October, we observed GreenJuliett-linked infrastructure scanning, or attempting to exploit, Fortinet FortiGate firewalls, edge devices that protect OT networks, in Bahrain, Israel, Jordan, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, and Qatar. Our network data suggests the group is also working to add internet-of-things (IoT) and CCTV devices to its list.

While we have not independently tied GreenJuliett infrastructure to the refrigeration attacks, over the past three months, we have seen the group continue to target PLCs (programmable logic controllers), which are similar to the internet-exposed controllers the refrigerators in France used. We have also observed that AI is now part of how they work.

From Accounts to Infrastructure

In October 2024, OpenAI banned accounts it assessed as belonging to CyberAv3ngers. The operators had used ChatGPT to research default credentials for PLCs, compile lists of electricity companies and common PLCs in Jordan, and draft scripts against industrial protocols (such as Modbus TCP, a control protocol that allows PLCs to communicate quickly on local networks).

However, in 2026, the picture is different. In October, we found a configuration for LiteLLM (an open-source gateway that puts multiple AI models behind a single interface, suggesting a team-sharing model for access), alongside self-hosted chat applications built for Persian-language users, on infrastructure we assessed as likely used by GreenJuliett-linked operators. We also observed servers in the group's anonymization network communicating with infrastructure that hosts Anthropic's Claude.

While we have not confirmed specific instances of misuse in this research, both OpenAI and Anthropic have reported publicly on detecting and disrupting misuse by Iranian government operators. AI shortens the time it takes to identify vulnerable device types and write targeting scripts, and GreenJuliett has moved it from individual accounts into its operating environment.

GreenJuliett uses AI as an assistant. A separate class of tooling makes AI the operator, and it is already deployed at scale.

For example, ARTEX AI is one of eight offensive AI frameworks we track. Material recovered from exposed ARTEX servers shows how the agent works: Nmap, Masscan, and Nuclei for reconnaissance; Hydra and sqlmap for access; Chisel for tunneling. While the toolkit is familiar, the agent has now become the operator: On one server, archived transcripts show the agent issuing roughly 7,000 shell commands, recording more than 1,000 facts as it worked, and filing 54 findings.

As a result, ARTEX’s footprint roughly doubled in 30 days. We observed 1,506 servers running ARTEX on October 21 and 2,978 on November 19, hosted across 58 countries. (These are observed servers, not attacks or confirmed compromises.)

The steps GreenJuliett uses AI to speed up (finding exposed devices, testing credentials, writing scripts) are the steps these frameworks hand to an agent end-to-end, and the frameworks are openly available. The growing availability of ARTEX and other frameworks lowers the barrier for financially motivated and state actors alike to use AI agents to carry out end-to-end attacks. Agents can probe more environments for weaknesses to exploit, increasing the pace and volume of attempts. While the use of AI does not guarantee a successful attack, the machine-scale volume of attempts makes success somewhere more likely.

Deny Them the Easy Wins

Take controllers off the internet: CERT-FR named Copeland XWEB, Danfoss AK-SC and AK-SM, and Dixell XWEB refrigeration controllers in the French attacks. Use Recorded Future’s Attack Surface Intelligence to inventory which of your devices are exposed, then remove any controller that shouldn’t be publicly reachable.

Lock down edge devices: Since the firewall in front of your OT network is now a target on its own, restrict FortiGate management interfaces to known addresses and keep firmware current.

Hunt based on GreenJuliett indicators: The GreenJuliett infrastructure from this research is available to Recorded Future customers. Search your logs for it, going back to at least August.

Block the framework servers: We track servers running ARTEX AI along with seven other AI automation frameworks every day. Alert on connections from them, and block them whenever there is no authorized testing underway. Most operators will use proxies instead of launching attacks directly from offensive AI framework servers, but blocking is worthwhile even for a small percentage of direct-attack servers.

The List Changes Every Day

While none of these are quick fixes, blocking framework services is harder than it sounds. Only about one in six ARTEX servers we observed was present continuously for 30 days, and roughly 90 new ones appear on a typical day. A blocklist updated by hand each week is stale within days.

This is where defense should mirror the adversary's tactics. Choose one action that is high confidence, low consequence, and reversible (blocking inbound connections from a confirmed framework server qualifies) and let an agent take it without waiting for a person. Measure the results, then widen what the agent is allowed to do. We call this “earned autonomy.”

The adversary is handing its workflow to machines one step at a time. Which of your steps would you hand over first?

Insikt Group adheres to responsible disclosure procedures in conducting its research.

Recorded Future’s Insikt Group, the company’s threat research division, comprises analysts and security researchers with deep government, law enforcement, military, and intelligence agency experience. Its mission is to produce intelligence that reduces risk for customers, enables tangible outcomes, and prevents business disruption.

Explore expert insights, reports, and tools to strengthen your cybersecurity strategy.

Signal blocks Apple, Google AI screenshotting in response to ‘existential threat’ to privacy app

Signal will now block Apple and Google operating systems by default from taking screenshots of user messages in its encrypted messaging app that feed into the companies’ artificial intelligence capabilities, the appmaker’s leadership said Friday.

Signal already had taken similar steps with Microsoft 11 last year to stop Microsoft Recall from capturing and storing messages. It will extend those limitations to Siri AI’s Onscreen Awareness and Gemini Intelligence.

Signal will “restrict agentic systems built into iOS 27 and on Android versions where we can detect an AI assistant attempting to read your Signal screen,” wrote the Signal Foundation’s president, Meredith Whitaker. “Right now, these agentic AI integrations are changing this environment in a way that’s making it increasingly hostile to privacy. This is an existential threat to Signal, and our ability to responsibly uphold our mission.”

“In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents ‘scan’ the information that’s on your screen,” she continued. “In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding.”

The announcement follows reports that Meta’s AI agent Muse was able to access the texts of Signal messages and read them.

Signal took aim at the tech companies that produce the industry-leading operating systems.

“Sadly, OS vendors are integrating agents recklessly, w/o giving Signal and other apps good ways to block AI data access and protect you,” Whitaker wrote on social media.

“We continue to call on the major consumer operating system companies — Apple, Google, and Microsoft — to provide simple technical tools and accurate documentation that give developers like Signal ways to prevent AI agents from accessing sensitive application data,” she said.

Specifically, developers should have a clear way to opt-out of AI data access and processing, and they should come up with better documentation about how AI agents function, Whitaker said.

Apple, Google and Microsoft didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

[26] The Register - PHP 8.6: Things are gonna get a lot more strict around here
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 00:28:47 +0100
Link: https://www.theregister.com/devops/2026/11/20/php-86-things-are-gonna-get-a-lot-more-strict-around-here/5311486

[TAM METİN - 825 kelime]
PHP 8.6: Things are gonna get a lot more strict around here

Like a parent disciplining a misbehaving child, PHP’s annual update clamps down on loose default behaviors to curb malicious hacker horseplay.

Visa, Mastercard theft included info useful for phishing, but not draining bank accounts, say researchers
10 hours ago

Signal slams door on prying AI agents to protect privacy
11 hours ago

China attackers deployed AI agents that autonomously found and exploited a 0-day to take over a university server
14 hours ago

Dutch data watchdog highlights safety issues with AI glasses
15 hours ago

Spy court blasts UK secrecy, forces government to admit Apple ‘backdoor’ demand
19 hours ago

On Thursday,  PHP version 8.6 was released on its usual yearly schedule, popping up as if the web scripting language hadn’t been under intense scrutiny this past month.

For those who missed it: a swarm of unearthed vulnerabilities has plagued PHP since October, allowing unauthenticated attackers to crash PHP workers or execute arbitrary code on the server. Users of every PHP-based application, including WordPress, Laravel, and Symfony, had to scramble to update their PHP instances.

The PHP core development community, along with the PHP Foundation, responded with a coordinated release of patched versions of PHP (8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, 8.2.36 and the new 8.6) that closed seven critical remote code execution (RCE) flaws in one sweep.

In addition to patching specific exploitable holes in the PHP engine, the new version of PHP also tamps down some of PHP’s historically liberal configuration settings.

Lucky for PHP, and for the rest of us, core developer Jörg Sowa called out these lax settings in June, when he posted a proposal to set more security-friendly defaults.

Sowa saw that three configuration settings of PHP’s session extension – Strict Mode, HttpOnly, and SameSite – were designed to boost security but shipped “with defaults that leave applications unnecessarily exposed.”

In a retrospective posted last month, the PHP Foundation admitted that consensus-driven gridlock had stalled complex fixes for months and vowed to get patches out the door sooner, should the vulnerabilities leak ahead of the agreed-upon deadline.

Code-wise, Sowa’s proposal to harden PHP settings was accepted for PHP 8.6. These changes won’t stop the flood of AI-generated CVEs, but at least these holes will be more difficult to exploit.

For Strict Mode, PHP will no longer accept uninitialized session IDs that it didn’t create itself. Before, an attacker could just plant a made-up session ID on the victim to gain entry. “The built-in files handler checks whether a session file for that ID exists on disk; because an attacker-planted ID has no corresponding file, a fresh random ID is generated instead,” Sowa wrote.

Collectively, these changes should thwart session hijacking and cross-site request forgeries. They won’t stop remote code execution hacks, though they will make it a lot more difficult for attackers to gain entry.

The new release brings some other security-minded changes as well.

The PHP engine will be a lot stricter when it encounters strings with null values (“\0”). In many cases, it will now throw an error rather than silently letting it pass. Null values are a favored trick for triggering RCEs. A C function will treat the null value as the end of the string, processing everything before the null byte and ignoring everything after, much to an attacker’s delight.

Continuing in this spirit of “if you see something, say something,” a number of other PHP functions will also no longer remain silent when things go awry. Operations for closing a file or copying data, for instance, will explicitly return a false value when terminating prematurely or failing, an alert developers could use to minimize data integrity bugs.

Beyond security, PHP 8.6 also comes with a number of new goodies.

PHPers are abuzz over Partial Function Application (PFA), which will let them pre-fill some of a function’s arguments to generate a reusable closure on the fly — leapfrogging JavaScript in this ability.

The new edition also gets a native polling API, which will be handy for event-driven networking; a stopwatch-like Duration class that can track elapsed time across more than 250 years; and a clamp() function to ensure a given value stays within an acceptable range.

Another tricky day for PHP devs

For administrators, this PHP update round may be a bit of a shambles.

As backend software engineer Rajekevin Dourepoulle notes in a blog post, these changes will take effect post-installation only if the configurations aren’t specified elsewhere, such as in an application, framework, or even another php.ini file – all of which can override the PHP settings themselves.

“In practice: if your deployment reuses the old php.ini (an Ansible template, a COPY php.ini in a Dockerfile, a file copied from server to server), you move to 8.6 and gain nothing, because the explicit session.use_strict_mode = 0 line overrides the new default,” he wrote.

Despite all these heroic efforts, PHP remains the champion of inscrutability. ®

Signal slams door on prying AI agents to protect privacy
11 hours ago

China attackers deployed AI agents that autonomously found and exploited a 0-day to take over a university server

Visa and Mastercard customer info leaked by the data thieves and extortionists who claim to have stolen it from the financial giants doesn’t include card numbers, passwords, or home addresses.

On Thursday, Visa, Mastercard, and JPMorgan Chase confirmed to The Register that they are investigating third-party breaches that may involve customer information.

Ransomware and extortion crew n0n claimed to be responsible for all three, and on Thursday published samples of the stolen files – data-theft groups typically leak some of the compromised data ahead of the official extortion deadline in an effort to put more pressure on victim companies to pay the ransom demand.

Researchers at SOCRadar, a threat-intelligence firm that has been tracking n0n since it emerged in September, have parsed all 14 files in the n0n’s published Visa and Mastercard archives, and told us that the files don’t contain any financial details belonging to banking customers.

“We found no card numbers, expiry dates, CVVs, passwords, dates of birth, or home addresses in any file,” Ensar Seker, SOCRadar chief information security officer, told The Register. “Visa's statement that no card numbers were affected matches our scan.”

Mastercard previously said that stolen data included a “limited amount of email addresses – non-payments information” from a subset of cardholders in a benefits program.

According to SOCRadar’s analysis, the leaked files do contain mobile numbers, Bank Identification Number (BIN) prefixes, and dated airline, hotel, and restaurant bookings. So while the data doesn’t include card or account numbers that crooks could use to drain customers' bank accounts or rack up massive credit card bills, “that detail is what a fraudster needs to pose as a concierge desk or a bank,” in an email or voice-phishing social engineering attack, Seker said.

It’s also worth noting that the published files only represent about 0.4 percent of the data n0n claims to have hoovered up in the breach: about 4.3 GB and 1.9 million marketing events. “So a further release is possible,” according to Seker.

Plus, both datasets come from the same upstream provider, we’re told. They use the same 27-column booking layout, placeholder text,  and CRM ID format, Seker said, noting that the most recent record in each stops 69 seconds apart on Oct 26.

“This looks like two card programs run on one provider's platform,” he said. “The pattern looks like a batch copy from a marketing and reporting store.”

Customer data has left the building

The security shop hasn’t analyzed the Chase customer data that n0n also claimed to have published.

All three financial firms attributed the compromises to a third-party provider, and while nothing in the stolen files name the vendor, the timing matches up with a Qubole supply-chain campaign disclosed earlier this month by Wiz, working with Google's Mandiant incident responders and AI data security company Sentra.

In that attack, which the threat hunters said began on October 14, cybercrims used compromised identity and access management (IAM) credentials associated with Qubole's AWS account to access dozens of downstream-customers’ environments, stealing secrets and other sensitive data from S3 buckets.

N0n also claimed to have carried out this attack. “The timing fits the Qubole supply-chain campaign,” Seker said, adding that this is his company’s assessment, not a confirmed finding. "If it's right, Qubole would be the access path rather than the holder of the data, and the files point to a concierge-services operator behind the brands.”

Qubole’s parent company Idera did not respond to The Register’s inquiries. The financial institutions declined to answer our questions about which provider(s) was compromised in the breach, and whether Qubole was the access path by which their customers’ data was exposed.®

[28] The Register - Signal slams door on prying AI agents to protect privacy
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 21:42:04 +0100
Link: https://www.theregister.com/security/2026/11/20/signal-slams-door-on-prying-ai-agents-to-protect-privacy/5311466

[TAM METİN - 942 kelime]
Signal slams door on prying AI agents to protect privacy

Apple, Google, and Microsoft called out for failing to provide developers with adequate AI agent controls

Support tech fixed malware by charging client less for their services
1 day ago

Google continues model chemistry experiment with Neon
1 day ago

Daily disruptive outages that ground planes and halt work – welcome to the new normal
3 days ago

Opting out of Gemini tracking? Google will still hold your data 20x longer
3 days ago

California sues OpenAI for misleading public about AI safety
4 days ago

Signal, the encrypted messaging app, has barred Google Gemini, Apple Siri, and other AI agents from accessing messages unless the user has explicitly granted permission, based on privacy concerns.

Citing the screenshot blocking implemented last year to defend against Microsoft Recall, Signal CEO Meredith Whittaker said similar measures have become necessary to prevent agentic software available in iOS and Android from gaining access to communication that's intended to be private.

"Google and Apple are integrating agentic capabilities like Gemini Intelligence with Google Gemini and Onscreen Awareness with Siri AI deep into their operating systems," wrote Whittaker in a blog post.

"In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents 'scan' the information that’s on your screen. In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding."

The result is that private messages ingested by these agentic systems may end up on someone else's server where they're no longer private.

Updates to Signal's iOS and Android apps now include controls that by default block Siri on iOS and Gemini and other agents on Android from taking screenshots, which AI agents process using optical character recognition to extract text.

Whittaker says that those who wish to take screenshots of their messages can disable this protection via Signal's settings menu, but warns doing so risks exposing your Signal content (and that sent by your contacts) to AI agents.

Screenshot blocking, Whittaker concedes, is only a partial solution since AI agents may have other ways to access application data through the device file system.

"We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy," she said.

"Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are currently unable to implement these protections on macOS."

Apple is taking some action to implement protection from AI agents on macOS, though it appears to be doing so largely to defend against third-party access to data rather than to limit its own Siri service. Siri can be turned off separately.

With macOS 27.3, currently in public beta testing, Apple's desktop operating system will get more granular controls on two APIs: Device Control and Data Access, and Full Disk Access. The result will be more permission prompts for users of macOS apps that seek access to user data, and the inconvenience of applying for an entitlement from Apple to obtain Full Disk Access for backup software and assistive technologies that use Accessibility APIs.

"As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially," Apple said when it introduced the Full Disk Access change. "We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy."

Apple is also reportedly working on its own AI agent in a bid to compete with Anthropic and OpenAI. It remains to be seen whether Apple will use its operating system ownership as competitive leverage against AI firms that threaten its gatekeeping power, as it has done with web browsers.

First the flood, then the dams

While Apple casts itself as an ally that's helping to defend device customers against prying AI agents, Signal's decision to block Siri shows that AI agents have complicated trust decisions and the competitive landscape. AI agents are supposed to serve the user but when they spirit data away to the cloud and come between customers and merchants, they wear out their welcome.

AI agents also threaten the business relationship between consumers and merchants.

Amazon has blocked shopping agents like Meta Muse from its e-commerce site (though not AWS Marketplace) while Walmart has invited third-party agents to interact through its AI Gateway. Anthropic has blocked subscription customers from using third-party harnesses. United Airlines has banned transactions from unauthorized AI bots. Similar barriers or limitations related to third-party AI agents have been erected by Target, Home Depot, Etsy, eBay, JPMorgan Chase, Charles Schwab, Citigroup, and Wells Fargo, among others.

Meanwhile, there's a burgeoning industry in bot detection and mitigation, led by the likes of Cloudflare, Akamai, and DataDome, to name a few.

The web browser is sometimes referred to as a user agent, based on the idealistic notion that it serves its user. That vision has been muddied by online advertising and data collection, and default settings that often serve the interests of browser makers instead of promoting privacy.

Now AI agents face the same scrutiny as people wonder whether their agents really serve them or someone else. After a year or two of agent vendors arguing for access to all digital data for the sake of personalization and context, the backlash has arrived. ®

[29] The Register - China attackers deployed AI agents that autonomously found and exploited a 0-day to take over a university server
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 18:30:00 +0100
Link: https://www.theregister.com/security/2026/11/20/china-attackers-deployed-ai-agents-that-autonomously-found-and-exploited-a-0-day-to-take-over-a-university-server/5311382

[TAM METİN - 677 kelime]
China attackers deployed AI agents that autonomously found and exploited a 0-day to take over a university server

'Agents kept adapting for nearly a full day without human direction,' Amazon CISO said

Amazon's split personality: AWS embraces bot commerce while main site enforces bans
8 hours ago

Dutch data watchdog highlights safety issues with AI glasses
15 hours ago

AI boom threatens circuit board crunch to rival pandemic-era chip shortage
15 hours ago

AI could open wallets where ERP upgrade pitches can't, says PwC
19 hours ago

US let Nvidia and AMD sell bucketloads of chips to military-linked Chinese companies
1 day ago

Suspected Chinese spies deployed AI agents which worked autonomously to find a zero-day in an open source application and then abuse the flaw to break into university networks, gaining full control of a server, according to Amazon CISO CJ Moses.

The China-linked attacker used Cairn, an open source, penetration-testing framework that has become increasingly popular with cybercriminals who use the AI tool to carry out multi-stage intrusions with no human assistance.

In this case, the agents found and exploited a zero-day MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging AI application. Amazon notified the project's maintainers of the vulnerability, and they released a fix and a security advisory.

On September 10, Amazon's Threat Intelligence Team found a server with a publicly hosted instance of Cairn that provided visibility into the campaign targeting universities in East Asia, outside Mainland China, Moses said in a Friday report shared with The Register.

The campaign occurred over a period of 48 hours beginning on September 8, and the prompts were written in Simplified Chinese, with timestamps in executed scripts configured to China Standard Time.

Before the AI agents found and exploited the zero day, however, they tried to break into another university’s Redis server over about 16 hours and 148 sequential actions, including abusing Redis's replication feature to load unauthorized code, escaping its scripting sandbox, writing to its configuration files, and corrupting its memory.

None of these were successful, and when those actions failed, the agents also attempted a Log4Shell injection against a different service, a server-side request forgery (SSRF) attack against a vulnerability in a co-located Qdrant instance, and several credential sprays against PostgreSQL, SSH, and other tools.

Meanwhile, a separate operation running for more than 6 hours targeted a university GPU server with another credential-spray attack, compiling a list of 80 real user names found across the school’s public websites, academic papers and other documents.

"Neither operation succeeded, yet together they show that the agents kept adapting for nearly a full day without human direction," Moses wrote.

Then the AI agents found the zero-day path traversal vulnerability in MONAI Label, and this time they were able to gain access to the server.

"The agents identified the application's framework, mapped its API endpoints, and found an upload endpoint with a filename parameter," Moses wrote. They tested that parameter for path traversal, and the parameter was vulnerable. In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server."

Later, the agents abused the same flaw to execute a Python reverse shell running as root.

In another session, after the agents discovered the zero-day, the human operator provided them with a proxy that tunneled into a second university network, and connected to a server running the same vulnerable code.

Amazon's discovery follows an earlier report by Gambit Security's threat intelligence team that also documented a Chinese operator using Cairn to carry out at least 105 attacks, and managing to compromise, "to varying degrees," at least 27 companies.

This campaign also occurred in September. In addition to Cairn, the attacker used two other open source AI harnesses to steal credit card records and other sensitive data from a Fortune 500 hospitality company, a major US airline, a large private US industrial supplies distributor, and a US online fashion retailer, and other companies.

"Together, these cases show that this autonomous AI agent framework is being adopted in both espionage and criminal operations," Moses wrote. ®

[30] The Register - Dutch data watchdog highlights safety issues with AI glasses
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 17:44:00 +0100
Link: https://www.theregister.com/security/2026/11/20/dutch-data-watchdog-highlights-safety-issues-with-ai-glasses/5311345

[TAM METİN - 1133 kelime]
Dutch data watchdog highlights safety issues with AI glasses

Devices found to misinterpret medication instructions and other scenarios impacting human safety

Amazon's split personality: AWS embraces bot commerce while main site enforces bans
8 hours ago

China attackers deployed AI agents that autonomously found and exploited a 0-day to take over a university server
14 hours ago

AI boom threatens circuit board crunch to rival pandemic-era chip shortage
15 hours ago

AI could open wallets where ERP upgrade pitches can't, says PwC
19 hours ago

US let Nvidia and AMD sell bucketloads of chips to military-linked Chinese companies
1 day ago

The Dutch Data Protection Authority (AP) has officially advised consumers against buying AI-powered smart glasses after safety tests revealed concerning behaviors beyond their controversial recording capabilities.

The AP recently tested six different models of smart glasses and found glaring issues, including a willingness to display dating advice to an adult glasses-wearer who expressed an interest in a minor.

In another case involving a cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) simulation, testers noted that one pair of glasses informed the wearer that emergency services had been called and were scheduled to arrive at the scene, despite no one having made the call.

Some glasses did not properly process safety warnings on children’s toys, others made mistakes when reading medication leaflets, and some misinterpreted warnings for extreme weather events.

The AP did not specify the models it tested, saying only that they tested six models ranging from under €100 ($110) to over €500 ($550), including two that "were extensively tested in simulated real-life situations where human safety played a key role."

A spokesperson also declined to match any specific behavior to a model by price point (minor dating advice linked to a €354 pair of glasses, for example), adding that the research was intended to highlight the risks of AI glasses in a broader sense.

"Glasses that film you unnoticed are already concerning. Glasses that also give you incorrect advice when someone's life is at stake go a step too far," said Monique Verdier, vice chair at the AP.

"AI offers many opportunities, but we must be able to trust that technology. With the camera glasses examined, that trust cannot currently be justified."

The warning issued this week follows the regulator's previous work on smart glasses. The AP reminded the public in September that everyone has the right to privacy and encouraged organizations to ban them where necessary.

The same warning mentioned the potential risks regarding data processing under the GDPR, as well as those related to the training of AI.

The AP doubled down on these earlier criticisms, saying the latest tests showed that the AI functions rely on processing data using servers mostly located outside of the European Union. Relatedly, it found that users were not given sufficient information about how the AI was processing the data they captured.

On a cybersecurity note, the tests threw up a range of issues, including the ability for people nearby the glasses-wearer to connect to the device without permission, view recordings, and in some cases operate the camera.

Further, the regulator echoed the pre-existing concerns about smart specs - those that helped give them their colloquial name “pervert glasses.”

Its tests found that with "virtually all of the camera glasses examined," the recording lights that are supposed to clearly show when a user is recording were dim and easily coverable.

The AP said that models could also be wangled into recording even when that light indicator was covered, which goes against what manufacturers so often claim.

"As a result, bystanders can barely see whether they are being filmed," it said.

The technology has a number of beneficial use cases, such as assisting the visually impaired, those with lower literacy levels, or for any number of other scenarios where people need help understanding the world around them

However, the watchdog's official stance on the technology, as it is today, deems smart glasses "unsafe… due to the risks to users and bystanders."

Verdier said politicians in the Netherlands and across Europe should take note of the results when developing AI policy.

"It is important that we, as a society, learn to deal with these types of high-risk AI products," she said.

"Simply banning everything provides some leeway in the beginning, but we cannot sustain that indefinitely. It is important that we collectively work on awareness, resilience, and ethical conscience."

Smart specs can't shake the hate

When DEF CON announced a no pervert glasses policy ahead of its event in August, the move was broadly welcomed by attendees.

"Love to see a ‘no pervert glasses’ policy at DEF CON," said Eva Galperin, EFF director of cybersecurity, at the time.

Several other organizations have implemented similar restrictions, including Monopoly Events, which manages UK Comic Cons, national treasure pub chain Wetherspoons, and even Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Most members of the general public will have at least come to terms with the fact that the smartphone generation, and their willingness to snap shots anywhere and everywhere, means there is no enshrined human right to privacy in public spaces.

Public video recording once carried an air of expectation or consideration for bystanders’ personal privacy, although smartphone users have slowly eradicated that over time.

Like it or not, it's generally understood that a smartphone is usually recording something - or someone - at any given time, especially in urban areas.

On paper, the fact that smart glasses can record in public spaces isn’t wildly different from what’s already come to be expected from smartphones.

However, given how similar they appear to analog glasses and the ability to cover the recording light, it makes the act of public recording via glasses far more surreptitious, and thus concerning.

With smartphones, it's easy to see from the user's body language - holding the phone out in front of them - that they are recording. There are no overt signals displayed by wearers of smart glasses during image or video capture, which fuels a sense of unease about the technology in general.

A quick search online for "smart glasses privacy violation" yields a slew of complaints about the technology, often regarding behavior toward women and children.

There are also worries about how easily the devices can get past security checks, potentially providing opportunities to those who wish to cause greater harm than a mere blight on personal privacy.

A joint investigation by The Observer and BBC Radio 4 recently revealed how AI-enabled glasses went undetected through the airport-style security scanners used in the UK parliament.

The two news outlets found that a £60 ($78) pair of Chinese-made glasses bypassed the scanners and could be used to read upside-down documents on MPs' desks, recording data such as phone numbers and addresses to be accessed at a later point. ®

[31] The Register - Spy court blasts UK secrecy, forces government to admit Apple ‘backdoor’ demand
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 13:18:19 +0100
Link: https://www.theregister.com/security/2026/11/20/spy-court-blasts-uk-secrecy-forces-government-to-admit-apple-backdoor-demand/5311292

[TAM METİN - 896 kelime]
Spy court blasts UK secrecy, forces government to admit Apple ‘backdoor’ demand

Notice's existence can be acknowledged without harming national security, but its precise demands remain under wraps

NASA Mars rover and orbiter suffer glitches
now

Amazon's split personality: AWS embraces bot commerce while main site enforces bans
8 hours ago

PHP 8.6: Things are gonna get a lot more strict around here
8 hours ago

Visa, Mastercard theft included info useful for phishing, but not draining bank accounts, say researchers
10 hours ago

Signal slams door on prying AI agents to protect privacy
11 hours ago

The Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT) has confirmed that the UK government served Apple with a secret Technical Capability Notice (TCN), rejecting the Home Office's argument that acknowledging its existence would damage national security.

The order has been widely reported as demanding access to end-to-end encrypted iCloud data.

The three judges pointed to extensive public reporting, statements by US officials, and media briefings they concluded had been authorized by the UK government.

The Home Office had previously adopted its "neither confirm nor deny" (NCND) policy, as is standard when discussing national security matters.

The story broke in February 2025, when The Washington Post reported that the Home Office had demanded an iCloud backdoor the previous month.

A TCN is a notice issued under the Investigatory Powers Act 2016, which compels recipients, such as tech companies, to implement technical changes that facilitate the UK government's legal surveillance powers.

For Apple, a company that has long made privacy central to its marketing, and famously rejected an FBI order to break open an iPhone to assist a terror probe, being served the TCN meant it either had to somehow defy a legal order issued by the UK, or undermine the encryption technology that customers expected.

UK Home Office silent on alleged Apple backdoor order

While it remained officially unconfirmed at the time, Apple's decision to revoke Advanced Data Protection (ADP) for UK users in February 2025 was widely interpreted as indirect confirmation of the demand.

At the same time, US policymakers urged then-director of national intelligence Tulsi Gabbard to oppose the UK's demands under the assumption that they also sought to backdoor Apple's data in a way that would affect US citizens.

In August 2025, Gabbard announced that the UK had agreed to drop its demand for access to Americans' encrypted data. ADP is still available to users in the US.

Apple's ADP extends end-to-end encryption to additional categories of iCloud data, including backups, photos, and notes. Only trusted devices retain access to the relevant encryption keys, leaving Apple unable to decrypt that protected content for investigators.

Without ADP, those additional categories revert to standard protection: the data remains encrypted, but Apple holds the keys and can disclose content in response to valid legal demands. Some categories remain end-to-end encrypted regardless.

Apple has an explainer on what data types remain end-to-end encrypted, even without ADP enabled, and those that are not.

What the judgment does not confirm

While the IPT's judgment confirms that the Home Office served Apple with a TCN, judges have yet to decide whether key details about the case can be made public.

"Although there has been extensive media coverage and public statements about the existence of a technical capability notice, there has been no publication of its precise content," the judgment stated. "All parties recognize that there may be matters of detail that must be kept secret in order to preserve national security and the public interest.

"We agree that it would be damaging to national security if all of the material (including the content of the technical capability evidence, and the evidence of Apple and the respondent) were publicly disclosed.

"That does not mean every detail must be kept secret in order to preserve national security. There may be some information that could be disclosed publicly without damaging national security. It is not, however, practical to determine the precise boundaries now."

The parties are working toward a substantive hearing in the first half of 2027. Apple's first challenge was dismissed following a "change in circumstances," and it filed a second claim in July 2026.

The Financial Times reported in October 2025 that the UK had replaced its original notice with a new order focused on British users.

The proceedings also include a separate challenge to the TCN regime brought by Liberty, Privacy International, and two individuals.

A government spokesperson said: "Terrorists, child abusers and organized crime groups cannot be allowed to operate beyond the reach of the law. The right to privacy is crucial but it should not come at the expense of the safety of the British public.

"A judge can authorize access to a criminal's home, a parcel they've sent, or a car they drive. The online world is no different. These powers are subject to strict safeguards and the government never has direct access to a company's communications systems or data.

"Apple has been helping the police and intelligence agencies pursue criminals and bring them to justice for several years, in accordance with the law. This Technical Capability Notice simply requires that they maintain the ability to do so.

"Decisions affecting the safety of the British public must be made by democratically elected governments and independent judges, not in the boardrooms of technology companies."

Apple did not immediately respond to our request for comment. ®

A Windows 11 passkey bug can leave Android phones announcing that authentication failed even when it succeeded. Microsoft has now released a fix for versions 25H2 and 26H2.

The problem occurs when users sign in on a Windows 11 PC using a passkey stored on an Android phone. Scan the QR code, and the Android device might display the message: "Something went wrong. Restart the process on your other device and try again."

Except it might not have gone wrong at all. Microsoft's guidance explains: "In cases where authentication completes successfully on the Windows device, the error message on the Android device is not supposed to appear and can be safely ignored."

Cross-device authentication lets users sign in on one device using a passkey held on another, without typing a password or copying a verification code. Microsoft says the issue affects operations using Microsoft Authenticator and Google Password Manager, and can occur in Edge or Chrome – not just when signing in through Microsoft Entra ID.

Cross-device passkey operations with an iPhone aren't affected.

An authentication system that cries failure after a successful sign-in isn't doing much for user confidence. Nor will it endear itself to support teams fielding the resulting tickets.

Microsoft has included a fix in KB5132057, the optional non-security preview update released on November 19 for Windows 11 25H2 and 26H2. Until affected devices are patched, users can ignore the Android error if authentication has completed successfully on the PC. ®

[33] TechCrunch Security - Experts warn: Nearly everyone in AI is susceptible to a honey-trap scheme right now
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 20:58:29 +0000
Link: https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/20/experts-warn-nearly-everyone-in-ai-is-susceptible-to-a-honey-trap-scheme-right-now/

[TAM METİN - 1092 kelime]
Even as the fall-out for Nvidia over Jensen Huang’s alleged honey-trap scandal is still unfolding, Silicon Valley has yet to reckon with a new reality: many more people among them are at risk.

“Nobody briefs founders on counterintelligence,” Aaron Brown, a former senior CIA officer and current founder of the software company Lumbra, told TechCrunch.

That’s because historically honey traps have been associated with politicians, the military, and national intelligence — the people “behind clearances and a workforce trained to expect an approach,” from spies and other attackers.

But now many of the most valuable secrets “sit inside companies building chips, models, and infrastructure,” Brown says, adding that a spy “wants what the CEO can touch. The roadmap, the export decisions, the customer list, who gets the technology. The CEO is the shortest path to all of it.”

Huang has been accused of falling for just such a honey trap by having an affair with Alice Huang. She’s a former executive of a Singapore neocloud who’s been accused of being a Chinese spy and of smuggling billions of dollars’ worth of restricted Nvidia chips into China.

After the Huang allegations broke, jokes flooded the internet about which tech CEO will be next, but it’s not just CEOs and founders who are at risk. The WSJ reported that OpenAI started warning its employees about outsiders trying to cozy up to them in search of company secrets. Anyone with access to sensitive information — from board members to executive assistants — can be the target of a honey trap.

And typically, the attackers aren’t lovers. Friendship is actually the oldest honey-trap scheme around, Brown said.

Honey traps gain access to their targets as investors, customers, recruiters, and consultancies. Their requests look legitimate on paper and don’t need their targets to fall in love. “They need you to feel comfortable talking,” Brown said. “They last longer because nobody’s looking.”

What’s interesting, too, is the irony. So many tech founders are moving to automate and digitize so much of human life and yet remain vulnerable to the oldest bug around, a person who preys on the human need to be understood by others.

“Why fight through a firewall when you can get close to the person who can open doors, influence decisions, or make requests nobody wants to question?” Perry Carpenter, a criminologist and chief deception strategist at KnowBe4, told TechCrunch.

Once targets realize they have been compromised, the threat can escalate: attackers now have a means of blackmail.

Another irony: AI has made honey-trapping much easier and cheaper. Planning a scheme used to take months or years of research, crafting a persona, knowing the target, and executing a plan. These days, it’s easy to use AI to research a target, generate fake social profiles, fake backgrounds, even fake voice calls.

“AI can help sustain an entire fictional backstory,” Carpenter said. “The technology helps set the stage, but the deception ultimately plays out through human relationships.”

The AI industry “became a national security industry faster than its culture caught up,” Brown said.

“Part of being honey-trapped is not knowing,” he added. “It doesn’t feel like manipulation. It feels genuine, even lucky.”

Carpenter said a good first step is looking for unusual patterns. Note, for instance, “coincidental encounters that happen a little too often,” he said. There are also obvious signs, like persistent curiosity about work and colleagues, or requesting secrecy about meeting up, and pressing for introductions or information.

Bigger red flags include if someone’s requests are getting bigger, pushing the boundaries of what you usually would be uncomfortable doing. “A simple gut check,” Brown said. “Would this person still be around if you lost your job tomorrow?”

It also helps to try and understand when emotions might be influencing a decision. Carpenter suggests putting up a clear boundary between one’s personal and professional life. Within companies, it also helps to “eliminate executive exceptionalism,” he said, the idea that the rules don’t apply to people in power at the company.

Brown added that company culture plays another role, too: Are employees comfortable with raising concerns, challenging unusual requests, and escalating possible threats? “One of the most dangerous security cultures is one where nobody feels comfortable questioning the CEO,” Carpenter said.

“Founders need to take risks, and they need to explore business opportunities,” Brown said. “Paranoia doesn’t help. Recognizing you’re a target does.”
