[34] TechCrunch Security - A transcription firm used by police, prosecutors, and tech giants exposed customer data online
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 15:46:07 +0000
Link: https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/20/a-transcription-firm-used-by-police-prosecutors-and-tech-giants-exposed-customer-data-online/

[TAM METİN - 1036 kelime]
A transcription company that caters to law enforcement, government departments, and Silicon Valley tech giants has resolved a security lapse after leaving a large amount of internal data, including customer transcriptions and their source materials, exposed to the web.

The data security lapse at San Francisco-based Tigerfish exposed transcriptions of police interviews, body-cam footage, and customers’ raw audio and video footage. The exposed data also included invoices of the company’s customers, which include police departments and prosecutors’ offices.

According to Anurag Sen, a good faith security researcher who found the data, the files were located on an Amazon-hosted (S3) cloud server that was openly listed and accessible to anyone via an easy-to-guess web address — no passwords needed.

The security lapse underscores how simple flaws or misconfigurations can result in sensitive information getting exposed online, especially as AI makes it easier to uncover weaknesses that can put companies and their data at risk.

Sen discovered the exposed data online in October and alerted the company to the issue, but did not hear back. Sen later provided details to TechCrunch in an effort to flag the incident with the company for resolution.

Sen, 30, is no stranger to TechCrunch. For the past decade, he has searched for sensitive datasets exposed online with the goal of notifying the companies and organizations that their information is open to the internet. Like many security researchers, much of his efforts are driven by a duty to secure the internet, and he describes his work as an “unpaid air-traffic controller.”

From his island home in Indonesia, Sen has uncovered sensitive U.S. military emails spilling from a compartmentalized Department of Defense cloud server; databases exposing reams of customer records; the inner workings of a country’s national license plate surveillance system; and public systems that inadvertently sent out streams of SMS codes used by people around the world to log into their online accounts.

Given Sen’s propensity for finding often highly confidential information online, we verified the source of the leak and the data, and contacted Tigerfish.

Soon after making contact, Tigerfish secured its exposed S3 cloud bucket.

“We’ve blocked all public access to the bucket you identified, including directory listings and individual files,” Tigerfish president, Adam Goldberg, said in an email. “We’ve also verified that all of our other S3 buckets are blocked to public access.”

“We’re continuing to review and strengthen our storage security more broadly,” added Goldberg.

The company said that Sen’s email disclosing the data leak was caught in its spam filter.

It’s unclear if the company has notified its customers. Tigerfish did not respond to a follow-up email.

Discoveries of exposed datasets have consumed a large part of Sen’s early cybersecurity career so far. He scours the web daily using automated scanners and specialist search engines to identify databases, cloud storage, or other sensitive information that likely shouldn’t be left unprotected online.

The modern web runs on absolute trust, he said, and operates under the notion that the world’s data is kept secure. But he described how his findings reveal the reality of how “fragile” the internet is behind the scenes.

Despite the recent focus on how AI is accelerating people’s ability to discover vulnerabilities, Sen said that many of the data leaks and exposures that he finds come down to basic human errors.

“An engineer spinning up a test cloud database on a Friday, disabling authentication to test an API, and forgetting to shut the door before heading into the weekend,” was just one example, he recounted.

Sen’s findings over the years highlight the ongoing problems caused by such security mistakes, just as the new wave of vibe-coding and AI-generated development is creating new security problems due to insecure and unchecked code deployed to the web.

Similar to Amazon’s recent efforts to make it difficult to make S3 buckets public without going through clear multistep warnings, newer vibe-coding platforms like Lovable and Supabase have also made changes to their platforms to prevent user mistakes.

“Everyone often fears shadowy hackers,” Sen said. But he argues that the real crisis is leaving sensitive systems and databases “wide open to the public internet without a password.”

[35] CSO Online - PHP2Shell aftershock: 18 more PHP flaws put enterprise web admins on alert
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 00:39:17 +0000
Link: https://www.csoonline.com/article/4251713/php2shell-aftershock-18-more-php-flaws-put-enterprise-web-admins-on-alert.html

[TAM METİN - 1071 kelime]
The PHP team has patched several vulnerabilities, including a 9.2-rated request-smuggling flaw. The risk depends on server configuration, reinforcing the need to inventory PHP across enterprise environments.

PHP continues to root out flaws in its architecture, this week releasing fixes for a slew of additional security issues in the wake of PHP2Shell.

The patches address 18 vulnerabilities, including a critical request smuggling flaw that could allow unauthenticated attackers to remotely execute code on vulnerable servers. Other vulnerabilities affect PHP’s core engine, session handling, process manager, and Common Gateway Interface (CGI) protocol, which bridges web servers with external application programs.

The updates were released for all supported PHP versions, with PHP 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, and 8.2.36 containing the fixes.

The disclosure comes as enterprises continue to grapple with the full impact of PHP2Shell, a pair of 9.2-severity-rated vulnerabilities disclosed in October. The flaws prompted the outright shutdown of some government websites, and, by some estimates, have borne the brunt of millions of exploit attempts.

“Enterprises should read this release as PHP2Shell’s aftershock: Smaller, but it shakes the same walls,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research.

Flaws enabling RCE, DoS, memory corruption

One of the most serious flaws disclosed this week, CVE-2026-129289, is rated a critical 9.2 on the Common Vulnerabilities Scoring System (CVSS). The request smuggling vulnerability impacts PHP-FPM, a background service that executes code for high-volume websites and apps.

If exploited, the flaw could allow unauthenticated actors to execute PHP code remotely on vulnerable servers that reuse connections to PHP-FPM under certain conditions. It impacts specific nginx, Apache, HAProxy, and LSAPI configurations that reuse backend connections to PHP-FPM.

When paired with a code execution bug, it can “carry an attacker from the web worker toward the whole server,” Dickson explained.

Several of the other patches also address vulnerabilities that could allow remote code execution (RCE). Still others address issues including information disclosure, memory corruption, denial-of-service (DoS) interruptions, potentially unsafe handling of HTTPS and FTPS URLs, and cross-site scripting.

While there may be heavy focus on the 9.2-rated CVE-2026-129289, the lesser flaws still matter, Dickson said. For instance, in one case, one capital letter turned off encryption; a URL written as HTTPS:// or FTPS:// with an uppercase S could send passwords, tokens, form data, and files in plaintext, even through a redirect, to anyone watching the network.

Not quite PHP2Shell level, but still high priority

An attacker who exploits a PHP code-execution flaw gains access to whatever the PHP worker can touch, “which is just about everything,” Dickson said. Successful exploitation executes code with the privileges of the PHP worker, which holds the database password, API keys, cloud credentials, and session data.

For example, he described what he called an “ugly” attack path:

The threat actor gets in through the web application.

Reads the configuration file;

Dumps the customer database;

Plants a web shell to come back later.

He pointed out that PHP warned that PHP2Shell puts every installation serving web requests at risk, with no login required. “This release returns to the same neighborhood: session upload progress, fatal error backtraces, and how PHP behaves when it runs out of memory,” he said.

Fritz Jean-Louis, principal cybersecurity advisor at Infotech, agreed that this is a high-priority patching event, if not a PHP2Shell-level emergency. Although several of the critical vulnerabilities require specific configurations or uncommon deployment scenarios, “they still affect one of the most widely deployed web runtimes in the world,” he noted.

RCE is the most concerning outcome, as it can give an attacker control over the application server. From there, they may be able to access sensitive business data, steal credentials or session tokens, deploy persistent backdoors, modify application behavior, or use the compromised system as a foothold for deeper intrusion.

“Even vulnerabilities that appear less severe, such as information disclosure or memory corruption, can become highly impactful when chained together by a determined attacker,” Jean-Louis said.

What enterprises should do now

Dickson emphasized the a PHP version number alone will not tell security teams whether they are exposed. Checking the version number is the easy part, but Linux distributions often backport fixes without changing the version string, so the package changelog tells more than the version number does.

The hard part is finding every copy: Web servers, containers, hosting control panels, and appliances can all quietly bundle PHP, Dickson said. Then check the settings that matter:

Is session upload progress on?

Do PHP 8.5 workers include arguments in error backtraces?

Does php-cgi face the internet?

Is the PHP-FPM status page reachable from outside?

He advised security teams to start with internet-facing PHP 8.5 servers, anything with session upload progress enabled, and any setup where several applications share one session store. PHP 8.5 should be first because it is the only branch exposed to the new backtrace flaw, and fatal error backtraces are on by default there, he explained.

“Then patch everything else on a normal fast cycle,” Dickson said.

He pointed out that PHP 8.2 has just six weeks to live; it will receive no security fixes after December 31, 2026. That means this release may be one of the last it receives. Running 8.2 into January is a risk decision; PHP 8.1 and older, meanwhile, receive no fixes from the PHP project.

Interestingly, PHP’s advisory for the new PHP 8.5 backtrace flaw says a change in 8.5.12, the PHP2Shell release, is what made the new attack path reachable. “Emergency fixes are built fast, and fast work sometimes creates a new vulnerability,” Dickson noted.

In light of this, his advice is to preserve the PHP inventory built for PHP2Shell, “and keep it current,” because no one ever said during an incident, “We knew about too many of our PHP servers.”

Understanding everywhere PHP runs

Jean-Louis agreed that security teams should immediately inventory all PHP deployments, including those embedded in vendor products and appliances. They should also prioritize internet-facing systems, verify PHP-FPM and session management configurations, and deploy the latest supported PHP versions “as quickly as operationally feasible.”

Organizations should view this as a continuation of the lesson learned from PHP2Shell, he said: Runtime vulnerabilities deserve the same attention as application vulnerabilities. While PHP2Shell was more “immediately exploitable” and quickly attracted real-world attacks, this release reinforces the need for strong asset inventory, rapid patch deployment, and visibility into underlying software components.

“The biggest question for CISOs is not whether they run PHP; it’s whether they know everywhere it runs,” Jean-Louis said.

[36] CSO Online - F5 scrambles to fix more critical BIG-IP security flaws
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 00:16:44 +0000
Link: https://www.csoonline.com/article/4251711/f5-scrambles-to-fix-more-critical-big-ip-security-flaws-2.html

[TAM METİN - 408 kelime]
Just two months after it fixed a critical RCE bug, F5 has released out of band patches for five more critical vulnerabilities in its Access Policy Manager.

F5 has released a batch of out of band patches for BIG-IP Access Policy Manager (APM) and BIG-IP iRule programmable scripting, five of which are rated 9.8 (Critical) in severity. BIG-IP Access Policy Manager (APM) is the vendor’s application access management and security product while BIG-IP iRules lets network administrators customize how BIG-IP handles application traffic.

All five of the patches are stack-based buffer overflows that could let an unauthenticated threat actor terminate the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) and execute code remotely on vulnerable systems.

F5 described them as follows:

CVE-2026-120292: When an HTTP profile and an iRule using the MR:message route command are configured on a virtual server, undisclosed requests can cause the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) to terminate and may lead to remote code execution (RCE);

CVE-2026-120285: When an HTTP profile and an iRule containing the PSC:ip_address command are configured on a virtual server, undisclosed requests can cause the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) to terminate and may lead to remote code execution (RCE);

CVE-2026-116953: When an iRule that processes client traffic using the GENERICMESSAGE:route command is configured on a virtual server, undisclosed requests can cause the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) to terminate and may lead to remote code execution (RCE);

CVE-2026-123637: When BIG-IP APM is provisioned and a per-request policy that includes the Client Information agent and Endpoint Security agents is applied to a virtual server, undisclosed requests can cause the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) to terminate and may lead to remote code execution (RCE).

The company said there are no mitigations for the flaws and advised customers to install the hotfixes on vulnerable devices, and to upgrade vulnerable versions without a listed fix to a patched version.

In the same batch of out of band patches, F5 also addressed CVE-2026-126822, a high severity integer underflow vulnerability in BIG-IP APM SAML that could also crash TMM and lead to denial of service.

This is the second critical issue in two months for APM; September’s zero-day bug was already being exploited when it was patched. F5 did not indicate that any of the current batch is as yet being exploited but given the growing trend of attacks on edge devices by criminals and nation-state threat actors, admins should update systems as soon as possible.

This article originally appeared on NetworkWorld.

# In Security, Words Matter as Much as Tools, Maybe More

From talking cloud security to using AI, cyber leaders are finding that clear, disciplined communication is now a front-line defense capability across the enterprise.

[![Image 5: Picture of Becky Bracken](https://eu-images.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt6d90778a997de1cd/blt07f8ecb5868dd4fd/6750aa66113e14656849e053/becky_mug_2024.jpg?width=100&auto=webp&quality=80&disable=upscale)](https://www.darkreading.com/author/becky-bracken)

[Becky Bracken,](https://www.darkreading.com/author/becky-bracken)Media & Projects Director,Dark Reading
November 20, 2026

3 Min Read

![Image 6: Two professionals talking in an office](https://eu-images.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt6d90778a997de1cd/blt36f1afcfa92ff2c5/6af766db3c02eaba0a4aae0d/cyber_talk_ATHVisions_Getty.jpg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=80&disable=upscale)

OPINION

The best tool cyber teams can wield to defend their organizations has nothing to do with tech; it's how they talk. Whether the audience is the C-suite, the development team, or the sheepish user who just fell for a phish, communications savvy is increasingly mission-critical.

During a [Dark Reading Virtual Event](https://www.darkreading.com/events) panel I recently put together to talk tech, tools, integration, and frameworks, called "Key Tools & Technologies for Locking Down Your Cloud," SANS instructor Ahmed AbuGharbia urged cybersecurity teams to "learn the language of the cloud" to build credibility with IT, and to do the same for developers. We discussed technology and products, too, but I was surprised at the amount of time that was spent on stressing the importance of communication and language when it comes to having effective conversations with vendors, executives, and users.

My other panelist, Theresa Lanowitz, a principal analyst at Omdia, detailed the distinction between security "of" the cloud and security "in" the cloud, noting that under existing shared responsibility models, cloud service providers assume responsibility "of" the cloud itself, rather than what organizations decide to put "in" the cloud.

Related:[Why Holiday Security Can't Wait for Black Friday](https://www.darkreading.com/cybersecurity-operations/why-holiday-security-cant-wait-black-friday)

This wasn't the first time I had noticed a shift in the way security practitioners focus on a commitment to using effective language.

A couple of weeks ago I sat in several sessions at the [ISC2 Strategic Conference](https://www.darkreading.com/cyber-risk/people-are-getting-weird-about-ai) in Denver that spent a remarkable amount of time on strategies for clearly communicating risk and documenting those exchanges in much the same way as they would any other log, piece of evidence, or asset. In the past, these conversations would have been more focused on [translating tech talk into corporate speak](https://www.darkreading.com/cybersecurity-operations/how-cisos-communicate-boards-effectively). CISOs have worked for a long time on [how to talk to leadership](https://www.darkreading.com/cybersecurity-operations/bridging-gap-between-ciso-board) about risk and budget; it's been an ongoing conversation for several years. However, emphasis on how cyber teams can learn to ask the right questions not just of leadership, but pertinent people both inside and outside the business, feels like a fresh effort. Using precise language and presenting strategic (not just technical and tactical) concepts effectively is no longer being discussed as a nice thing for security pros to be able to do, but critical to fundamental enterprise defense.

For example, CISO and expert Laura Vaughn has cleverly broken down threat modeling into [4 Simple Questions on a White Board](https://www.darkreading.com/cyber-risk/threat-modeling-4-simple-questions). Her strategy distills years of experience and technical expertise into plain language anyone can understand, like, "What [cyber incident] would hurt most on Monday morning?" That honed language helps get teams to the heart of the threats, and helps them understand the work that needs to happen next. That all saves time and money, and eliminates the scariest risks first. Other deceptively simple questions she suggests asking include, "Who hacks organizations like ours and how?" And, "What is the cheapest control?" Smart comms informs and focuses the technical work.

# L o a d i n g...

Related:[As Test Takers Turn to AI, Exam Security Plays Catch-Up](https://www.darkreading.com/cybersecurity-operations/test-takers-ai-exam-security-catch-up)

Likewise, technologist and attorney Daniel B. Garrie, CEO of Law and Forensics, [presents language as a frontline defense,](https://www.darkreading.com/cyber-risk/3-frameworks-cisos-ai-liability) and coaches CISOs and cyber leaders on the finer points of contract negotiations. He advocates rigorous documentation of communications on risk and defense decisions, so those [decisions would be defensible later](https://www.darkreading.com/cyberattacks-data-breaches/sec-charges-against-solarwinds-ciso-send-shockwaves-through-security-ranks), and so that transparency can help drive cybersecurity across the organization.

The introduction of AI is also requiring cybersecurity teams to [pick their words carefully](https://www.darkreading.com/remote-workforce/isc2-orgs-increasingly-leaning-ai). AI has put a language interface between the user and compute operations that benefits those who can ask the best questions. Likewise, experts across the cyber sector urge caution around using [humanizing language to describe AI agents](https://www.darkreading.com/insider-threats/blame-rogue-ai-security-failures) or attribute human motivation to their actions.

Related:[Attackers in Binance Breach Targeted Known Weakness, Missing Controls](https://www.darkreading.com/cybersecurity-operations/attackers-binance-breach-targeted-weakness-missing-controls)

Being an expert communicator is no longer a skill that's nice to have in cybersecurity; it's fundamental to enterprise defense. Be precise in the words you choose, and meet your audiences where they are. You might be surprised to find it's becoming the most powerful tool you or your organization could ever deploy against the next threat.

[TAM METİN - 2480 kelime | KAYNAK: proxy okuyucu]
AI companies are high-value targets for nation-state actors and cyber-espionage groups, but the recent Nvidia scandal shows the threats extend beyond the cyber realm.

As discussed in [a previous "What We Missed" episode](https://www.darkreading.com/cyber-risk/what-we-missed-knicks-phishing-test-out-of-bounds), an explosive report by [The New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/29/us/politics/nvidia-china-jensen-huang-trump.html) last month claimed Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a close relationship with a tech executive, Alice Huang, suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset. While Nvidia initially denied any impropriety, [Huang resigned](https://www.techtarget.com/news/jensen-huangs-scandal-fueled-ouster-exposes-enterprise-doubts-about-ai/874471/) last week and admitted to extramarital affairs, with one such affair involving Alice Huang.

According to reports, US officials suspected Alice Huang to be working on behalf of China's Ministry of State Security, which had targeted Jensen Huang with a "honey trap" — a type of social engineering scheme that uses romantic relationships to manipulate individuals and gather sensitive information. The scandal, which shook the US technology industry and affected Nvidia's stock price, illustrates the severe risks — both cyber and physical — facing AI companies these days.

Related:[9 Cyber Awareness Tips That Actually Match Today's Maze of Threats](https://www.darkreading.com/cyber-risk/9-cyber-awareness-tips-todays-maze-threats)

Dark Reading senior writer [Alex Culafi](https://www.darkreading.com/author/alexander-culafi) and senior news director [Rob Wright](https://www.darkreading.com/author/robert-wright) discuss the situation on this episode. Also on tap: Last week's [Microsoft 365 outage](https://www.cfodive.com/news/microsoft-outage-enterprise-resiliancy/874892/) sparks concerns about the downstream effects of patching a growing number of vulnerabilities; and the Indian technology firm [eMudhra](https://www.darkreading.com/cyber-risk/tech-giants-emudhra-certificates-compromised-keys) lands in hot water again after more of its intermediate certificates are revoked.

[39] Dark Reading - Qwen Incidents Show Self-Hosted AI Models Need Stronger Steering
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Thu, 19 Nov 2026 22:40:03 GMT
Link: https://www.darkreading.com/cyber-risk/qwen-incidents-self-hosted-ai-models-stronger-steering

[TAM METİN - 998 kelime | KAYNAK: proxy okuyucu]
4 Min Read

![Image 1: Steering wheel on an old sailing ship.](https://eu-images.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt6d90778a997de1cd/bltdca0689384b67fb8/6aff731dfef3359545395d0a/old-ship-steering-wheel-DmitriiElj-shutterstock.jpg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=80&disable=upscale)

Source: DmitriiElj via Shutterstock

When researchers at AI firm Cohere asked their open-weight model to write a defensive detection rule, the model didn't do as it was asked.

Instead, the AI model — the next-generation Qwen3.8-Flash-Next from Chinese search engine giant Alibaba — fingerprinted the system and tried to upload the data to an Alibaba Cloud storage bucket, Cohere's research team stated in an Oct. 26 analysis. While the group's [sandbox system](https://www.darkreading.com/application-security/ai-agents-escape-sandboxes-old-security-rules-apply) blocked communication to the Internet, the incident raised questions about why a model, which had been instructed not to use tools, attempted to do so.

"We cannot answer whether this is deliberate or a leftover glitch from training, but defenders and policymakers face the same reality: a weight file you can't trust is still a black box, and running it yourself just moves the black box inside your firewall," [the researchers stated](https://cohere.com/blog/concerning-behaviour-popular-open-weight-ai-model).

Christofer Hoff, a well-known cybersecurity professional, ran into similar issues when running OpenMuse as an agentic-framework front end and a local Qwen model. He also saw it reach out to Alibaba, which became apparent because he was [testing OpenMuse in an OpenShell sandbox instance](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/choff_model-weights-open-or-closed-can-exhibit-share-7526838434045526016-N3_t/) with deny-all as the default. As a part of his framework to keep control of the agents, Hoff has created a dashboard interface, which made it readily apparent the agents attempted to call to external sites.

Related:[What We Missed: Nvidia CEO Scandal Rocks AI Industry](https://www.darkreading.com/cyber-risk/what-we-missed-nvidia-ceo-scandal-rocks-ai-industry)

"The way I accidentally found this was just staring at a GUI — it just came back and said in the interface, 'Hey, I can't get to this thing in China,'" says Hoff. "And I'm like, 'What the f--- are you talking about?'"

Within a 24-hour period, the anomalous communication happened a handful of times, he says.

## Learned Behavior, Not Malicious Behavior

The incidents come as organizations look for ways to enforce controls on the operation of AI agents. In July, a frontier model being tested by OpenAI [escaped containment and compromised Hugging Face](https://www.darkreading.com/application-security/openai-rogue-model-claims-more-victims-beyond-hugging-face), a provider of AI-model hosting. Soon after, multiple AI companies acknowledged that [rogue behavior is not all that uncommon](https://www.darkreading.com/cyber-risk/insurers-search-answers-rogue-ai): Meta's Muse Spark and Anthropic's Claude [both logged incidents](https://www.darkreading.com/cyber-risk/rogue-incidents-debate-ai-safety-gets-real).

Anomalous AI behavior has shown up when companies assign AI agents a task, only to find it exceeding its authorization — [deleting production databases](https://www.darkreading.com/cloud-security/ais-so-smart-keep-deleting-production-databases), for example.

Other firms have confirmed and explored Cohere's findings.

Independent AI evaluator Vals [validated the issue on Oct. 27](https://www.vals.ai/blogs/qwen-alibaba-requests), theorizing that the illicit communication could be leftover artifacts from reinforcement training of Qwen3.8, since the issue does not appear to happen in Qwen3.7. Cybersecurity firm Check Point Software found that 64 different trials ended up [producing 52 distinct hostnames](https://research.checkpoint.com/2026/coheres-qwen-story-looks-more-like-model-jaggedness/), only six of which pointed to Alibaba Cloud, while other names such as localhost and domains leading to Amazon AWS were more common.

Related:[Strike Graph Launches Integration AI to Automate Continuous Compliance Evidence Using Any Existing Tool](https://www.darkreading.com/cyber-risk/strike-graph-launches-integration-ai-to-automate-continuous-compliance-evidence-using-any-existing-tool)

![Image 2: Vertical bar chart showing relative frequency of generated domains.](https://eu-images.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt6d90778a997de1cd/blt594d09708871625a/6aff7290fb9d50736e19f804/chart-addresses-generated-by-qwen3-8-check_point.jpg?width=1400&auto=webp&quality=80&disable=upscale)

Sixty-four tests resulted in 52 different hostnames being generated, with most not going to China. Source: Check Point Research

The research shows that the odd behavior is not a backdoor, but the model's attempt to do something — complete an upload address, for example — likely resulted from something it learned during training, says Steve Giguere, principal for AI security strategy at Check Point.

"Agents very often will try to travel as the crow flies," he says. "They don't necessarily know that what they're doing is wrong, but they understand that if the urgency to complete a goal reaches a certain perceived level within the agent, they will justify their actions."

## Companies Should Monitor and Steer, Not Kill

Such behavior has lent volume to calls for [the creation of a kill switch](https://www.darkreading.com/cybersecurity-operations/defining-ai-kill-switch-hard-but-necessary) as a feature to control agentic AI. But companies should start with defense-in-depth strategies, improving the security of the environments on which agentic frameworks are operating, Check Point's Giguere says. They should follow that with controls and runtime monitoring to detect unauthorized agentic activity.

Additionally, cybersecurity leaders should lean toward "steering" agentic systems — correcting them and reinforcing their legitimate objectives — rather than outright blocking the agent or using a kill switch, he says.

Related:[Optimizely Malware Attacks Highlight Third-Party Vendor Risks](https://www.darkreading.com/cyber-risk/optimizely-malware-attacks-third-party-vendor-risks)

"If you steer an agent away from something it's not meant to do, it will very happily not do that in most cases," Giguere says. "Whereas if you prevent an agent from doing something with no explanation, it will actually potentially get worse or try something even more obscure."

If an actual attacker is behind the behavior, then [using a kill switch is appropriate](https://blog.checkpoint.com/ai-security/ai-agent-kill-switch-agentic-steering/), he says.

At a minimum, companies should proxy all traffic leaving their network and monitor for anomalous communications, says Hoff.

"There should be nothing that leaves your network that's not proxied," he says. "And by proxying, I mean you must have the ability to inspect its content — both the request as well as the response."

In the end, the Qwen behavior is likely not malicious, but for companies deploying AI agents, it should be disturbing all the same.

[40] Dark Reading - Second Norwegian Energy Company Breached in 2 Days
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Thu, 19 Nov 2026 20:14:15 GMT
Link: https://www.darkreading.com/cyberattacks-data-breaches/second-norwegian-energy-company-breached

[TAM METİN - 1056 kelime | KAYNAK: proxy okuyucu]
4 Min Read

![Image 1: Equinor's headquarters in Oslo.](https://eu-images.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt6d90778a997de1cd/blte4910babc7878a94/6aff5ad57ab982a4c314744c/Equinor-makasana-Getty.jpg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=80&disable=upscale)

Source: makasana via Getty Images

Two Norwegian energy companies announced that they'd been breached on two consecutive days this week.

On the evening of Nov. 17, Equinor — one of the world's most economically and geopolitically significant oil and gas companies — announced that it had [suffered a cyberattack](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/energy-equinor-investigates-cyberattack/875035/). Hardly a day later, another billion-dollar Norwegian energy company called Skagerak Energi admitted to the same. The two companies' breach disclosures read remarkably similarly, though there is no evidence yet that the two attacks are connected.

Equinor did not respond to a request for comment on this story. Skagerak Energi declined to comment on specifics of the company's incident.

## What We Know About the Equinor Cyberattack

Equinor first publicly [reported](https://www.equinor.com/news/20261711-equinor-detected-cyber-attack) its cyberattack on the evening of Nov. 17, Central European Time (CET). Its initial investigation suggested that no data had been stolen, and that operations and production would remain uninterrupted. The issue seemed to be limited to internal IT systems. For instance, one employee told [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/technology/equinor-detects-ongoing-cyberattack-output-unaffected-2026-11-17/) that the company's email system was down.

Related:[Philippine Migrant Worker Data Likely Leaked in 69GB Government Breach](https://www.darkreading.com/cyberattacks-data-breaches/philippine-migrant-worker-data-69gb-government-breach)

The next morning, the company reported having gained "a clearer understanding of how the attack was carried out and which systems have been affected." Without sharing much, it alluded to the attack not being viral in nature, so there was "no risk" of it spreading. Besides that, it said there was no evidence employees, partners, or suppliers were impacted.

Despite all of the good signs in its first two updates, Equinor reported on the morning of Nov. 19 that it was still dealing with the attack, with no timetable for when the situation might resolve itself.

"This is yet another high-stakes cyberattack in what seems like weeks of [relentless firefighting throughout Europe](https://www.darkreading.com/ics-ot-security/eu-grocers-unpatched-fridge-firmware)," says Anders Storbråten, cybersecurity expert at IDEX Biometrics. "Equinor says there is no indication that data has been stolen, but I wouldn't breathe a sigh of relief just yet. They wouldn't be the first company to offer early reassurances, only to have to backtrack once details become clearer."

Even if the breach does turn out to have been limited, he adds, "Energy companies depend on business systems to organize staff, maintenance and supplies. If those stay unavailable, keeping operations running safely gets harder. Production is unaffected, but nobody should need to see the gas stop flowing before taking this seriously."

## A Wider Threat to Norway's Energy Sector

Also in its most recent update, Equinor noted that its attack "does not appear to be specifically targeting Equinor." This was especially notable seeing as, between its Wednesday and Thursday updates, nearby Skagerak Energi disclosed that it too had fallen victim to a cyberattack.

Related:[State Bank of India Suffers a Customer PII Data Leak](https://www.darkreading.com/cyberattacks-data-breaches/state-bank-india-customer-pii-data-leak)

In many ways, the Eastern Norwegian renewable energy and [power utility company's](https://www.darkreading.com/cybersecurity-operations/physical-convergence-electrical-grid-cybersecurity) press releases mirrored Equinor's. First, on Nov. 18, it [reported](https://www.skagerakenergi.no/presse/pressemeldinger/skagerak-energi-utsatt-for-forsok-pa-cyberangrep) an attack affecting its IT systems, which didn't impact operations or production. It added that there was no indication that any data had been lost. The next day it [reported](https://www.skagerakenergi.no/presse/pressemeldinger/oppdatering-pa-forsok-pa-cyberangrep) having obtained a better view of the situation, but provided no additional details.

Though the two companies' breaches remain separate incidents based on public reporting, other Norwegian energy sector companies have been put on high alert. A representative of oil and gas giant Aker BP told the press on Wednesday that it has mobilized its emergency preparedness and strengthened its monitoring, and the hydropower company Statkraft said it's also closely [monitoring](https://www.aftenposten.no/norge/i/GPG6VQ/kraftselskap-paa-oestlandet-rammet-av-dataangrep) the situation.

"Every other energy company should be asking: Are we exposed to the same thing?" Storbråten advises. "The danger is treating this as Equinor’s problem until it becomes your own."

## Norwegian Government Agencies Sound the Alarm

Three weeks before these incidents became public, Norway's National Security Authority (NSM) published an unprecedented [warning](https://nsm.no/aktuelt/nsm-hever-det-nasjonale-cyberrisikonivaet-til-hoyt). For the first time in its history, it declassified its national cyber-risk assessment, warning that Norway faced a "high" cybersecurity risk to businesses. NSM's director stated that it was time to finally share its assessment with the public, "because it is absolutely necessary to strengthen both resilience and the ability to handle cyber operations in Norwegian companies."

Related:[Russian Influence Operation Widely Targets Latin America](https://www.darkreading.com/cyberattacks-data-breaches/russian-influence-operation-targeting-latin-america)

Storbråten says that since the warning, "NSM and DSB [The Norwegian Directorate for Civil Protection] have urged households to prepare for power, water, and communications outages, and, earlier this month, the government called for every municipality to [stress-test](https://www.techtarget.com/news/What-is-penetration-testing/836584/) its security. But people still remain paralyzed and unsure what to do. The guidance is just that: guidance. It's not clear instruction, and thus businesses and civilians alike are in a sort of limbo."

Amid all this, less than one week before the incidents became public, Norway's Police Security Service (PST) published its own [warning](https://www.pst.no/sabotasjetrusselen-i-norge-er-skjerpet/) regarding the threat of cyber sabotage in Norway. Besides the defense industry and its suppliers, the press release highlighted that "Critical infrastructure can also be affected, for example, objects within the energy sector."

The country's energy sector has been trying to match its government's action. Earlier this autumn, representatives of Equinor and Aker BP, among other organizations, took part in "Grey Dawn Petroleum" — an oil and gas-themed [tabletop exercise](https://www.havtil.no/en/explore-technical-subjects2/technical-competence/features/2026/exercise-in-uncertainty/) jointly arranged by the Norwegian Ocean Industry Authority (Havtil) and KraftCERT, a sector-specific combination Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT), Information Sharing and Analysis Center (ISAC), and Incident Response Team (IRT).

Per Atle Vagle, Equinor's head of cyber defense, characterized the exercise as "good training," which provided him with "new perspectives that we can bring back to our own business."

[41] Dark Reading - Critical PHP Flaws Allow Code Execution, but Don't Panic 'PHP2Shell'-Style
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Thu, 19 Nov 2026 19:57:31 GMT
Link: https://www.darkreading.com/application-security/critical-php-flaws-code-execution-panic-php2shell

[TAM METİN - 1135 kelime | KAYNAK: proxy okuyucu]
5 Min Read

![Image 1: Abstract source code against a black background](https://eu-images.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt6d90778a997de1cd/blt63f30aa2e4f7a5b8/6aff560d615b4f7719adda8c/source_code_background-scanrail-GettyImages-832282452.jpg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=80&disable=upscale)

Source: scanrail via Getty Images

The PHP team has released a new security update that fixes a wide swath of vulnerabilities and issues, but compared with last month's PHP2Shell chaos, it's harder to pin down how much these bugs will appeal to attackers.

That's because, [according to](https://www.php.net/archive/2026.php#2026-11-18-1) PHP's maintainers, the seven issues rated "critical" in the latest monthly security update "require either non-default configuration or uncommon setups." The update, published Nov. 19, affects all supported versions of PHP, and maintainers strongly encourage users to upgrade promptly.

This latest update comes on the heels of [threat actors targeting PHP2Shell](https://www.darkreading.com/application-security/php2shell-bugs-red-alert-security-industry) — a pair of vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) capable of remote code execution (RCE) in PHP — en masse. PHP is an open source scripting language common in Web development and present in much of the server infrastructure keeping the Internet afloat. Given PHP's ubiquity, [the rush to patch](https://www.darkreading.com/cyberattacks-data-breaches/no-safe-exploit-you-can-still-validate-php2shell)[created a fervor across the security industry](https://www.darkreading.com/vulnerabilities-threats/navigating-vulnerability-hysteria-ai-era) hardly seen since [Log4Shell in 2021](https://www.techtarget.com/news/Log4Shell-Experts-warn-of-bugs-severity-reach/838654/).

Related:[Cursor Traces Malicious Claude Code Extensions to Third-Party Breach](https://www.darkreading.com/application-security/cursor-malicious-claude-code-extension-third-party-breach)

PHP versions 8.2 through 8.5 now have patches available through [the project's downloads page](https://www.php.net/downloads.php), in the form of 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, and 8.5.13. 8.6.0; the latest major release of PHP also launched today with fixes included.

Of the dozens of issues accounted for in [the changelog](https://www.php.net/ChangeLog-8.php#8.5.13), the seven marked critical (CVSS 9.2) on GitHub were: session serializer mismatch RCE flaw [CVE-2026-115560](https://github.com/php/php-src/security/advisories/GHSA-658j-r8rw-q6mx); use-after-free via repopulation of last_fatal_error_backtrace global after shutdown flaw [CVE-2026-129182](https://github.com/php/php-src/security/advisories/GHSA-2fjv-p558-g82m); time zone cache use-after-free RCE vulnerability [CVE-2026-129496](https://github.com/php/php-src/security/advisories/GHSA-gr4f-wgx5-jpfv); use-after-free after interrupted session shutdown bug [CVE-2026-129481](https://github.com/php/php-src/security/advisories/GHSA-g3vh-838c-65v7); use-after-free in magic method backtraces RCE bug [CVE-2026-129474](https://github.com/php/php-src/security/advisories/GHSA-8mjj-2r7p-4hg2); PHP-FPM request smuggling through an unread HTTP request body bug [CVE-2026-129289](https://github.com/php/php-src/security/advisories/GHSA-qc49-hpvq-g2w6); and PHP file-based session handler RCE vulnerability [CVE-2026-126714](https://github.com/php/php-src/security/advisories/GHSA-fm2m-fjf5-v3cp).

While maintainers included workarounds in most critical advisories (barring CVE-2026-115560), they're considered temporary mitigations, and users should upgrade as soon as they can.

Justin Moore, director of adversary operations at Arctic Wolf, tells Dark Reading that two challenges organizations will run into when patching these issues are business continuity for servers running critical functions and visibility.

"A lot of organizations don’t have a complete inventory of where PHP is running, especially with legacy applications, internally developed Web services, managed hosting environments, or third-party software. It's baked into CMS platforms, hosting control panels, vendor appliances, and old internal apps," he says. "When a vulnerability is disclosed, the primary challenge is identifying every aspect of the business that is affected. The reality is that Internet-facing PHP systems should move toward the front of the patch queue because attackers have repeatedly demonstrated an interest in rapidly exploiting PHP vulnerabilities when a path to code execution exists."

Related:[Grok Bots Attempt to Access Corporate Data Without User Approval](https://www.darkreading.com/application-security/grok-bots-corporate-data-without-user-approval)

## PHP Bugs to Prioritize Patching

Among the critical flaws, there are some that experts recommend focusing on first. According to Upwind, which published [an analysis](https://www.upwind.io/blog/php-critical-vulnerabilities-affected-versions-and-mitigations) of the security release, PHP-FPM bug CVE-2026-129289 is the one to close first, because it "gives an unauthenticated attacker PHP code execution with a single request," with no memory corruption, gadget chain, or race required to exploit. Although Upwind assesses it's the most direct route to code execution, "It does need a front end that reuses FastCGI connections and an application path that opens php://input without reading it to the end."

Upwind also noted that three of the vulnerabilities address gaps introduced by the PHP2Shell fixes last month. "PHP ties CVE-2026-129481 and CVE-2026-129182 to cases the October fix for CVE-2026-109619 did not cover," according to the analysis. "A third, CVE-2026-129474, became remotely reachable through a change introduced in 8.5.12."

Related:[F-Secure Identifies 26 Ways AI Can Harm Consumers, and Where to Stop Them](https://www.darkreading.com/application-security/f-secure-26-ways-ai-harm-consumers-where-to-stop-them)

All three depend on specific configurations and versions. CVE-2026-129474 and CVE-2026-129182 are only applicable to PHP 8.5, while CVE-2026-129481 excludes PHP 8.2. CVE-2026-129474 and CVE-2026-129182 both rely on PHP 8.5's fatal error backtrace engine feature, which was introduced with that version; for CVE-2026-129481, the session cleanup behavior it exploits was introduced in PHP 8.3.

Finally, among the other recommendations the analysis makes, one broader tip may ring true for a wide range of PHP-using organizations: "Don't forget container images and appliances that bundle their own PHP build. They need a rebuild or a vendor update."

Meanwhile, WatchTowr's Jake Knott tells Dark Reading that CVE-2026-115560, CVE-2026-126714, and CVE-2026-129289 are the ones the firm expects attackers to go after first.

In any case, while not the same level of emergency as seen last month, users should absolutely apply this latest update as soon as they can.

## Everyone's PHP Priorities Will Be Different

Just because a vulnerability is rated critical does not necessarily mean it applies to all organizations equally or that threat actors will target each issue like the PHP2Shell bugs last month.

Knott, who is WatchTowr's head of threat intelligence, says organizations must consider factors such as how a vulnerability is exploited and how likely real-world exploitation is. And more specifically, whether that organization uses the affected configurations or meets the prerequisites for exploitation. Only then can one determine where attackers have a viable path and how defenders can prioritize securing their environments.

He says the best place to start is with three questions. First, how is PHP being run (be it PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php, php-cgi, or something else)? Second, how are sessions configured, and is session upload progress enabled? And third, what settings is PHP running with, and where are errors being logged?

"Organizations should absolutely take these vulnerabilities seriously, and many of the other critical and high-rated vulnerabilities from this week," Knott says. "There is a stark difference in business-as-usual accelerated patching in response to a critical vulnerability, and panic driven by trivially exploitable default configuration vulnerabilities that typically carry the [product2shell](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/php2shell-exploited-chained-attacks-check-point/874751/) monikers, which these aren't."

He adds, "Answers to these questions will quickly rule out many of these vulnerabilities and let organizations patch prioritized sets of assets from a position of understanding and actual risk."

[42] Dark Reading - Navigating Vulnerability Hysteria in the AI Era
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Thu, 19 Nov 2026 19:46:44 GMT
Link: https://www.darkreading.com/vulnerabilities-threats/navigating-vulnerability-hysteria-ai-era

[TAM METİN - 3000 kelime | KAYNAK: proxy okuyucu]
The pressure on cybersecurity teams to patch critical vulnerabilities is reaching a boiling point, exacerbated by incessant coverage and rapid-fire disclosures of AI-discovered bugs. Last month, it was PHP2Shell. This week, it's [Java4Shell](https://www.darkreading.com/vulnerabilities-threats/java4shell-flaw-threatens-global-java-application-ecosystem) ([CVE-2026-114938](https://censys.com/advisory/cve-2026-114938/)), a 9.2 CVSS flaw in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder unearthed in just one hour using OpenAI's Codex by [Calif Research](https://calif.io/java4shell), and NGINX2Root ([CVE-2026-123007](https://censys.com/advisory/nginx2root/)), a 9.2 CVSS critical integer underflow vulnerability affecting nginx HTTP/2 discovered by [Rapid7 MDR](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/ve-cve-2026-123007-critical-nginx-http-2-integer-underflow-leads-to-rce-fixed/).

In the latest installment of the monthly Reporters' Notebook video series, TechTarget Cybersecurity's [Alissa Irei,](https://www.techtarget.com/editors/airei/) Cybersecurity Dive's [David Jones](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/editors/djones/), and Dark Reading's [Fahmida Y. Rashid](https://www.darkreading.com/author/fahmida-y-rashid) discuss [last month's PHP2Shell vulnerability](https://www.darkreading.com/application-security/php2shell-bugs-red-alert-security-industry) and examine whether the industry is falling victim to communal panic.

PHP2Shell refers to two critical PHP vulnerabilities — CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 — discovered by Calif (the same company that found Java4Shell) and rated 9.2 on the CVSS scale. Caused by out-of-memory corruption and stale global state errors, the flaws enable unauthenticated remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on Web servers without requiring credentials or prior access. Following a rocky, coordinated disclosure process marked by accidental leaks on X, many organizations preemptively pulled websites and critical services offline, fearing that threat actors leveraging AI would rapidly launch automated attacks before Web servers and applications could be patched.

Related:[NIST Enrichment Reductions Impact CVE Coverage, Accuracy](https://www.darkreading.com/vulnerabilities-threats/nist-enrichment-reductions-cve-coverage-accuracy)

However, the anticipated wave of machine-speed exploits failed to immediately materialize during "Black October," raising questions about whether extreme preemptive shutdowns do more harm than good. While AI accelerates vulnerability discovery, complex exploit paths, hardware dependencies, and flawed proof-of-concept code mean that severe flaws do not automatically lead to immediate compromises, even when attackers use AI. Constantly shuttering operations or broadcasting catastrophes can create early-warning fatigue, akin to ignored national weather alerts, leaving organizations numb when a genuine emergency strikes.

A similar wave of urgency currently surrounds Java4Shell, where researchers demonstrated unauthenticated remote code execution in widely deployed enterprise tools like Keycloak and Jenkins, prompting CISA to call for immediate patching. However, Java4Shell does not have a universal exploit, meaning attackers must consider each application's memory layout and timing, how Base64 is used, and take application-dependent steps to exploit it.

Related:[Java4Shell Flaw Threatens Global Enterprises, Java Application Ecosystem](https://www.darkreading.com/vulnerabilities-threats/java4shell-flaw-threatens-global-java-application-ecosystem)

A CISO's primary responsibility is not to unilaterally order costly operational shutdowns or carry sole accountability for business risk, but to clearly communicate technical an,,,m d operational risks to executive leadership equipped to weigh security threats against business continuity. Staying calm, focusing on risk-based prioritization, and adhering to core security fundamentals remain the most effective defenses against modern threats.

Learn more in the video, and also check out other Reporters' Notebook episodes, [available here](https://www.darkreading.com/series/reporters-notebook), for insights and coverage from across Informa TechTarget's network of cybersecurity sister sites.

[43] Dark Reading - Why Holiday Security Can't Wait for Black Friday
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Thu, 19 Nov 2026 14:00:00 GMT
Link: https://www.darkreading.com/cybersecurity-operations/why-holiday-security-cant-wait-black-friday

[TAM METİN - 1047 kelime | KAYNAK: proxy okuyucu]
4 Min Read

![Image 1: A shopper checking out with a retail clerk using tap to pay.](https://eu-images.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt6d90778a997de1cd/blt3a97d098a9dd9e12/6afe0f2eb91ada7c366c492c/Holiday_shopping_tap_to_pay-Nastasic-GettyImages-2235710285.jpg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=80&disable=upscale)

Source: Nastasic via Getty Images

Cyber experts have long drawn connections between [the accelerated volumes of holiday shopping and threat actors looking for opportunities to take advantage](https://www.darkreading.com/cyberattacks-data-breaches/the-ransomware-holiday-bind-burnout-or-be-vulnerable), but as the festive season kicks off, it's important to remember that security posture during this time period is a marathon — not a sprint.

Verizon today published survey results for its [holiday](https://www.darkreading.com/cyberattacks-data-breaches/europol-holiday-ddos-attacks) trends report, tracking the insights of 600 small business owners and decision-makers in the US. Of those [surveyed](https://www.verizon.com/about/news/verizon-survey-small-businesses-social-media-ai-holidays), 11% said they have dealt with a cyberattack or data-security incident during the holidays, and a third expect to increase cybersecurity investments this holiday season compared with last year.

Meanwhile, managed security services firm [VikingCloud this week published a report](https://go.vikingcloud.com/l/1000211/2026-11-13/5b8r8/1000211/1794582259VUWVlzPW/_Report__2026_Retail_Cyber_Resilience_Nov26.pdf) surveying security and IT leaders which made even steeper claims: a full 86% of respondents said their business has faced at least one successful cyberattack in the past 12 months, and a whopping 98% said at least one came during the 2025 holiday season. And the Retail & Hospitality Information Sharing and Analysis Center (RH-ISAC) [last year said](https://rhisac.org/press-release/holiday-threats-2025/) the holiday season continues to be the most active fraud environment from a defender standpoint.

Related:[In Security, Words Matter as Much as Tools, Maybe More](https://www.darkreading.com/cybersecurity-operations/security-words-matter)

Some reasons behind the prominence of cyberattacks during this time period are straightforward: Many cybersecurity teams [experience lighter staffing during holiday periods and weekends](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa21-243a) (leaving the door open for easier [ransomware](https://www.techtarget.com/news/ai-labs-and-ransomware-whos-responsible-for-catching-misuse/874962/) attacks). The chaos of the holiday season also means online services and retailers are inundated with activity, giving threat actors cover. And on the social engineering front, the holidays give plenty of pretext for threat actors conducting [phishing](https://www.darkreading.com/perimeter/themailer-phishing-kit-ai-drivers-seat) campaigns (fake emails promising unbelievable Black Friday deals, [charity scams](https://www.darkreading.com/cyberattacks-data-breaches/israeli-hamas-conflict-spells-opportunity-for-online-scammers), and so on).

Some teams may take this as a cue to prepare for a few select days or weeks of this last part of the year, such as Black Friday or the week leading up to Christmas. But new research around one narrow corner of the threat landscape suggests that may not be wise.

## Happy Holidays! It's Your Own Box of Bots!

One of the less-discussed types of threat activity retailers face each season is an influx of malicious bots.

[F5 today published](https://www.f5.com/labs/articles/2026-black-friday-bot-report) a study dedicated to automated threat activity leading up to Black Friday. The report analyzed bot and automation traffic across three Black Friday shopping seasons (2023 to 2025) using data from F5 Distributed Cloud Bot Defense. It covers retailers in three retail sub-industries: fashion, e-commerce, and quick-service restaurants (QSR). The report's authors observed that overall automation rose across the three seasons, from 17.4% of transactions in 2023 to 18.5% in 2024, and then 28.6% in 2025.

Related:[As Test Takers Turn to AI, Exam Security Plays Catch-Up](https://www.darkreading.com/cybersecurity-operations/test-takers-ai-exam-security-catch-up)

The types of activity differ across industries, but F5 observed bots being used for product scraping and inventory hoarding, credential stuffing and account takeover, fake account creation (to claim new user offers), and gift card cracking (inserting gift card numbers into balance checkers to test for valid accounts).

In terms of trends overall, cyberattackers are increasingly leaning toward Web stores over mobile APIs, and a broad rise in bot sophistication over time. But one of the most notable conclusions that F5 researchers made is that there's no single best date to defend. Attackers start their bot onslaught weeks before Black Friday, and continue it well into the weeks after.

As Sean Murphy, F5's field chief information security officer (CISO) for North America, tells Dark Reading, "The data shows that automated activity can be elevated well before the shopping weekend, and the busiest day for automation varied dramatically from year to year."

## Holiday Defense Requires Weeks, Not Days, of Effort

[Bot traffic](https://www.darkreading.com/vulnerabilities-threats/ai-bad-bots-are-taking-over-web) does not necessarily reflect all threat activity, but there may be a broader lesson here: that steeling your security hygiene for the holiday season is not a few single days or weekends to prepare for but a broader stretch of time that spans from early November to the end of the year. Murphy says security teams "should have monitoring and protections in place throughout the shopping season rather than scaling them up only for Thanksgiving week."

Related:[Attackers in Binance Breach Targeted Known Weakness, Missing Controls](https://www.darkreading.com/cybersecurity-operations/attackers-binance-breach-targeted-weakness-missing-controls)

For those in ecommerce dealing with Web and mobile APIs, he urges ensuring protection isn't substantially weaker on one than the other.

"Web traffic had much higher automation rates among the retailers studied, but the report specifically cautions against interpreting that as evidence that APIs are inherently safer. Where API protection is weaker, attackers can shift toward that channel," he says. "And because the dataset contains both simple scripts and automation designed to imitate legitimate users, defenses need to account for a spectrum of bot sophistication rather than relying on a single detection technique."

Finally, he recommends organizations prioritize targeted employee security awareness and training, particularly for those teams handling customer accounts, payments, and other sensitive information. "Many attacks still begin with [social engineering](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/threat-groups-social-engineering-attacks-healthcare/831383/) and credential theft, so employees need to know how to recognize suspicious requests and protect account access."

Chris Flood, senior vice president and CRO of Verizon Business, tells Dark Reading that small businesses can reduce their risk with four fairly simple steps: require multifactor authentication, train employees how to spot scams, keep guest Wi-Fi separate from payment systems, and keep software and devices updated.

[44] SecurityWeek - WhatsApp Fixes Flaw Uncovered While Disrupting Scam Campaign
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 16:01:02 +0000
Link: https://www.securityweek.com/whatsapp-fixes-flaw-uncovered-while-disrupting-scam-campaign/

[TAM METİN - 3519 kelime]
WhatsApp Fixes Flaw Uncovered While Disrupting Scam Campaign

Tracked as CVE-2026-23871, the vulnerability was found by WhatsApp’s security team, and it may have been used to make scam messages more credible.

Flipboard





Reddit





Whatsapp





Whatsapp





Email

WhatsApp has patched a low-impact vulnerability in its Android apps that it believes a scammer may have exploited to make scam messages seem more credible.
Tracked as CVE-2026-23871, WhatsApp’s security team found the flaw. It’s tied to Click to WhatsApp ads and affects both WhatsApp and WhatsApp Business for Android.



“Incomplete validation of external ad-reply URLs in WhatsApp for Android and WhatsApp Business for Android before 2.26.17.4 could have caused a target’s device to reveal its IP information to an attacker if an attacker sent media from an attacker-controlled URL when a crafted Click to WhatsApp ad-reply message was rendered and displayed in a message thread,” WhatsApp explained in its advisory.



The advisory also says the vulnerability “may have been abused in conjunction with specific spam messages.”



Asked by SecurityWeek about the exploitation, a WhatsApp spokesperson said, “Our team found this issue while disrupting a scam campaign, and we believe a scammer was using it to make their scam message seem more credible.”



WhatsApp also published advisories for two medium-impact vulnerabilities, saying it has seen no evidence that either was exploited.Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.


One of them, CVE-2026-102769, is an SQL injection bug affecting WhatsApp for Android versions prior to 2.26.35.74. Tapping a maliciously crafted “order details” message sent from an unofficial client could lead to the deletion of WhatsApp files stored on the device.



If the recipient was online when the message arrived, an attacker could also have learned one bit of information about their chat database. An external researcher reported the issue through Meta’s bug bounty program.



The second, CVE-2026-44908, was discovered by Meta’s own researchers. It affects the remote-attestation verifier that WhatsApp apps use to confirm they can trust Meta AI’s confidential computing backend.



Someone “positioned within Meta infrastructure” could have bypassed the hardware root of trust using a certificate not signed by the hardware manufacturer’s key.



The bug impacted certain versions of WhatsApp and WhatsApp Business for iOS and Android, as well as WhatsApp for Mac.



WhatsApp noted that such a certificate could not have been used without first being published to a third-party binary transparency ledger that WhatsApp Private Processing relies on.



“The ledger shows that every published VCEK certificate chains to the hardware root of trust, confirming no exploitation,” the company said.

One of them, CVE-2026-102769, is an SQL injection bug affecting WhatsApp for Android versions prior to 2.26.35.74. Tapping a maliciously crafted “order details” message sent from an unofficial client could lead to the deletion of WhatsApp files stored on the device.



If the recipient was online when the message arrived, an attacker could also have learned one bit of information about their chat database. An external researcher reported the issue through Meta’s bug bounty program.



The second, CVE-2026-44908, was discovered by Meta’s own researchers. It affects the remote-attestation verifier that WhatsApp apps use to confirm they can trust Meta AI’s confidential computing backend.



Someone “positioned within Meta infrastructure” could have bypassed the hardware root of trust using a certificate not signed by the hardware manufacturer’s key.



The bug impacted certain versions of WhatsApp and WhatsApp Business for iOS and Android, as well as WhatsApp for Mac.



WhatsApp noted that such a certificate could not have been used without first being published to a third-party binary transparency ledger that WhatsApp Private Processing relies on.



“The ledger shows that every published VCEK certificate chains to the hardware root of trust, confirming no exploitation,” the company said.



Related: WhatsApp Adds Multiple Passkeys and Stronger 2SV in Account Security Update
Related: WhatsApp Unveils New Scam Alert Feature
Related: WhatsApp Rolling Out Username Feature to Bolster Phone Number Privacy

“Incomplete validation of external ad-reply URLs in WhatsApp for Android and WhatsApp Business for Android before 2.26.17.4 could have caused a target’s device to reveal its IP information to an attacker if an attacker sent media from an attacker-controlled URL when a crafted Click to WhatsApp ad-reply message was rendered and displayed in a message thread,” WhatsApp explained in its advisory.



The advisory also says the vulnerability “may have been abused in conjunction with specific spam messages.”

In Other News: Norwegian Energy Firm Cyberattacks, Supercomputer Hack, New Nightmare Eclipse Exploit

Noteworthy stories that might have slipped under the radar:  EU adds NoName057(16) to cyber sanctions list, malware targets CACs left in personal computers, Gemini agents targeted Epoch AI.

Reddit





Whatsapp





Whatsapp





Email

SecurityWeek’s weekly cybersecurity news roundup offers a concise overview of important developments that may not receive full standalone coverage yet remain relevant to the broader threat landscape.
This curated summary highlights key stories across vulnerability disclosures, emerging attack methods, policy updates, industry reports, and other noteworthy events to help readers stay well-informed about the evolving cybersecurity environment.



Here are this week’s highlights: 
Gemini agents targeted Epoch AI
AI evaluation firm Trajectory Labs says Gemini 4 Argon agents it stress-tested in October, with Gemini’s API safeguards turned on, tried to hack Epoch AI’s live website while hunting for answers to non-existent FrontierMath problems, attempting SQL injection and impersonating Epoch staff. Trajectory has paused all misalignment testing. Epoch says no private information was accessed.



Google brings Gemini 4 Neon to defenders Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.


Google has released Gemini 4 Neon, a faster, lower-cost model for coding and enterprise work, and says a cyber-focused version will reach eligible members of its Fairwind Program for trusted defenders in the coming days. Google claims the model performs at frontier level across finding, validating and patching vulnerabilities. It also says Neon keeps Carbon-level safeguards against cyber and biosecurity misuse while turning down far fewer legitimate requests in those areas.



Compromised migration vendor opens door to Infoblox data theft
Networking and security company Infoblox has confirmed that hackers accessed certain company information through a compromised third-party data migration vendor, which TechCrunch’s sources say handled SharePoint migration. The Register has since reported that the stolen files included NIOS configuration snapshots for some customers and personal details of employees and their dependents. Infoblox says it has no indication that its products, cloud services, software updates or build-and-release processes were involved.



EU adds NoName057(16) to cyber sanctions list
The Council of the EU has sanctioned 30 individuals and two entities over Russian information manipulation and cyber activity, including the Moscow-based Social Design Agency, 24 of its employees, and several pro-Kremlin propagandists. Under its cyber sanctions regime, the Council also listed NoName057(16), the pro-Russian group that has claimed attacks on government bodies, critical infrastructure and companies in Ukraine, the US and EU member states. 



Japanese supercomputer offline after intrusion
Japan’s Riken research institute has suspended operations of the Fugaku supercomputer and cut off external access after detecting suspicious traffic on its user authentication system. In a November 17 notice, Riken said an outside party used a public dashboard showing Fugaku’s operational status to break into the system’s internal operations network and tamper with multiple servers. Names, email addresses and user IDs of up to 4,597 Fugaku and RIKYU users may have been exposed.



Ukraine arrests ransomware suspects, 8-Digits member extradited to US
Ukrainian police, working with the FBI, have arrested four alleged key members of a ransomware gang that posed as IT support in calls powered by an AI voice platform to obtain credentials or get remote access software installed. Separately, Kazakh national Roman Khlynovskiy has appeared in US court after being extradited from Italy over his alleged role in the 8-Digits Team, an INC and Lynx ransomware affiliate accused of stealing data from US hospitals, healthcare entities and schools and making over $500 million in ransom demands. In Florida, five people were arrested in a nationwide crackdown on account-takeover fraud schemes linked to more than $54 million in losses at over 65 US financial institutions.



Test environment intrusion exposes Rakuten Securities customer data
Japanese online brokerage Rakuten Securities says login IDs and branch codes for up to 11.25 million accounts, and personal and financial information for up to 4.47 million accounts, may have been exposed after attackers accessed a test environment system on November 11. The exposed details include names, dates of birth, addresses, employers, withdrawal bank account numbers, and declared annual income and financial assets.



Equinor stops cyberattack as Skagerak Energi reports attempted intrusion
Norwegian energy giant Equinor says it has stopped a cyberattack against some of its IT systems that it detected on November 17, adding that production was not affected and there is no sign that data was stolen or altered. The company said the attack was not a virus attack and did not appear to be specifically targeting it. A day after Equinor’s disclosure, Norwegian power company Skagerak Energi reported activity that may have been an attempted cyberattack on some of its IT systems, saying operations and production were not affected and there is no sign that information was leaked.



Nightmare Eclipse drops unpatched Windows lock screen escape
Researcher Nightmare Eclipse has published FastUnlock, an unpatched Windows 11 zero-day that abuses the Narrator screen reader to get past the lock screen and run code as the lock screen account. The attack requires physical access and at least one account linked to an online Microsoft account.



Malware targets CACs left in personal computers
The NSA says threat actors are using malware against the personal computers that Department of War (DoW) employees use with Common Access Card (CAC) readers. Once the malware has recorded the card’s PIN, it can use the CAC’s credentials to sign into federal and DoW websites for as long as the card stays in the reader. That often gives attackers access to anything the cardholder can normally reach.

Norwegian energy giant Equinor says it has stopped a cyberattack against some of its IT systems that it detected on November 17, adding that production was not affected and there is no sign that data was stolen or altered. The company said the attack was not a virus attack and did not appear to be specifically targeting it. A day after Equinor’s disclosure, Norwegian power company Skagerak Energi reported activity that may have been an attempted cyberattack on some of its IT systems, saying operations and production were not affected and there is no sign that information was leaked.



Nightmare Eclipse drops unpatched Windows lock screen escape
Researcher Nightmare Eclipse has published FastUnlock, an unpatched Windows 11 zero-day that abuses the Narrator screen reader to get past the lock screen and run code as the lock screen account. The attack requires physical access and at least one account linked to an online Microsoft account.



Malware targets CACs left in personal computers
The NSA says threat actors are using malware against the personal computers that Department of War (DoW) employees use with Common Access Card (CAC) readers. Once the malware has recorded the card’s PIN, it can use the CAC’s credentials to sign into federal and DoW websites for as long as the card stays in the reader. That often gives attackers access to anything the cardholder can normally reach.

Gemini agents targeted Epoch AI
AI evaluation firm Trajectory Labs says Gemini 4 Argon agents it stress-tested in October, with Gemini’s API safeguards turned on, tried to hack Epoch AI’s live website while hunting for answers to non-existent FrontierMath problems, attempting SQL injection and impersonating Epoch staff. Trajectory has paused all misalignment testing. Epoch says no private information was accessed.



Google brings Gemini 4 Neon to defenders Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.


Google has released Gemini 4 Neon, a faster, lower-cost model for coding and enterprise work, and says a cyber-focused version will reach eligible members of its Fairwind Program for trusted defenders in the coming days. Google claims the model performs at frontier level across finding, validating and patching vulnerabilities. It also says Neon keeps Carbon-level safeguards against cyber and biosecurity misuse while turning down far fewer legitimate requests in those areas.



Compromised migration vendor opens door to Infoblox data theft
Networking and security company Infoblox has confirmed that hackers accessed certain company information through a compromised third-party data migration vendor, which TechCrunch’s sources say handled SharePoint migration. The Register has since reported that the stolen files included NIOS configuration snapshots for some customers and personal details of employees and their dependents. Infoblox says it has no indication that its products, cloud services, software updates or build-and-release processes were involved.



EU adds NoName057(16) to cyber sanctions list
The Council of the EU has sanctioned 30 individuals and two entities over Russian information manipulation and cyber activity, including the Moscow-based Social Design Agency, 24 of its employees, and several pro-Kremlin propagandists. Under its cyber sanctions regime, the Council also listed NoName057(16), the pro-Russian group that has claimed attacks on government bodies, critical infrastructure and companies in Ukraine, the US and EU member states. 



Japanese supercomputer offline after intrusion
Japan’s Riken research institute has suspended operations of the Fugaku supercomputer and cut off external access after detecting suspicious traffic on its user authentication system. In a November 17 notice, Riken said an outside party used a public dashboard showing Fugaku’s operational status to break into the system’s internal operations network and tamper with multiple servers. Names, email addresses and user IDs of up to 4,597 Fugaku and RIKYU users may have been exposed.



Ukraine arrests ransomware suspects, 8-Digits member extradited to US
Ukrainian police, working with the FBI, have arrested four alleged key members of a ransomware gang that posed as IT support in calls powered by an AI voice platform to obtain credentials or get remote access software installed. Separately, Kazakh national Roman Khlynovskiy has appeared in US court after being extradited from Italy over his alleged role in the 8-Digits Team, an INC and Lynx ransomware affiliate accused of stealing data from US hospitals, healthcare entities and schools and making over $500 million in ransom demands. In Florida, five people were arrested in a nationwide crackdown on account-takeover fraud schemes linked to more than $54 million in losses at over 65 US financial institutions.

Japanese online brokerage Rakuten Securities says login IDs and branch codes for up to 11.25 million accounts, and personal and financial information for up to 4.47 million accounts, may have been exposed after attackers accessed a test environment system on November 11.
