Again, taking banks as an example, can customers sign in, see a balance, and complete a payment? Give the incident lead the authority to pause a rollout when those checks fail and rehearse how to restore service while keeping the vulnerable component isolated. Second, look across accounts for signs of coordination. One new account, one login, or one small transfer can look perfectly ordinary. When dozens of apparently unrelated accounts start moving money in the same sequence toward the same destinations, the pattern tells a different story.”



Chris Hughes, Vice President of Security Strategy, Noma Security:



“Artificial Intelligence (AI) has industrialized vulnerability discovery, organizations are racing to fix what’s being found, and the patching itself can disrupt operations. That’s the availability piece of the CIA triad. We’ve seen industrialized vulnerability discovery all year, in programs like Patch the Planet and Project Glasswing and in a steady stream of findings from frontier labs and researchers. Vulnerability trackers reported the 2026 CVE count passing 100,000 earlier this month, more than double last year and a record. That volume is outpacing the ability to patch and test safely, and when teams compress testing windows to keep up, they raise the risk of exactly these kinds of outages. The work that matters is risk-based prioritization around exploitability, known exploited vulnerabilities, and reachability, along with better testing, rollback plans, and resilience.



So, what technical indicators would support an AI-driven, coordinated attack as an explanation for these incidents? You’d want indicators that actually tie the incidents together: shared tooling or TTPs, artifacts consistent with autonomous offensive frameworks, and timing or targeting that can’t be explained by a common vendor, a maintenance window, or a shared patch cycle. Based on what’s public, we can’t say that’s what happened, and many of these disruptions have been described as planned maintenance or the result of accelerated patching. The coincidences are hard to ignore, which is why the speculation has taken off, but the better-supported story right now is accumulated technical debt and rushed remediation under the pressure of industrialized discovery. Organizations should still prepare for agentic offensive frameworks, even if this cluster isn’t ultimately attributed to them.”



Alex Orleans, Head of Threat Intelligence, Sublime Security:



“What I feel AI is more likely contributing to these outages is not patching speed or the discovery of vulnerabilities but code of dubious quality. As more and more development and engineering is devolved to vibe-coding, the internals of the resultant code are less and less understood by both the organizations deploying it and the engineers who maintain it. This makes crashes and outages more likely. 



I would also say that across the outages we’ve seen, there hasn’t been a firmly identified shared type of cause (AI related or otherwise). Each outage should be taken on its own technical merits, not viewed as if there is some sort of unidentified overlap based on coincidental timing.”



Gerasimos Marketos, Chief Product Officer, Hack The Box:



“These incidents make security teams realize that attackers may use the same AI (used to discover the vulnerability x) to turn a published patch into a working exploit within hours. The answer is to give defenders and red teamers the same advantage. 



A red team working with AI can show within hours which of a thousand flaws are actually exploitable in your environment, so only those few get the emergency treatment. A SOC working with AI can put detection and containment around a new flaw the same day, which buys the time to roll the patch out safely.”




Patrick Quirk, President, Opengear: 



“We don’t have specifics on these incidents, and outages have many causes, so I’ll speak to the pattern. AI is accelerating how quickly vulnerabilities are found, which means patches are arriving faster, and that speed is an advantage only when every rollout is tested in a staging environment first. Skip that step or miss a key dependency and the fix becomes the failure.



Speed doesn’t change the question that matters on the day something breaks: can your team get back into the affected systems and start recovery? That’s where many organizations fall short. They manage and troubleshoot their infrastructure over the same production network that just went down, so when it fails, IT and security lose access to the very systems they need to restore. In a cyberattack that dependency is dangerous, because visibility and control are what contain the threat.



Design your infrastructure assuming it will fail and build an independent management path that stays reachable when the primary network does not. That gives your team a way to diagnose the problem, isolate affected systems, and begin recovery without relying on the infrastructure that failed.”



Crystal Morin, Senior Cybersecurity Strategist, Sysdig:



“We swung the pendulum too far one way. For years, the security mantra was “patch faster.” Don’t get me wrong, that’s still the right approach. But many orgs have taken it to an extreme where the answer to every finding is “ship the fix, now, everywhere.” Pair that with a software delivery culture that already moves at breakneck speed, plus an AI-driven firehose of findings, and you get change volume that surpasses their ability (or desire?) to test and stage before deploying.



System fragility is the ultimate issue here. Systems are toppling over when you try to fix them because they were already broken. It’s like pulling the final brick in Jenga. These are architecture and infrastructure debts coming back to haunt us. AI-speed vulnerability discovery just delivered the bill to our doorstep.



Patching is prevention, and prevention is necessary, but it has a limit. What we’re seeing is what happens when you blow past that limit. So to bridge that gap while you fix your architecture, you need to turn to detection, which doesn’t have those limits.”

The preparation for failures and cyberattacks is largely the same. An adversary can deliberately create these same disruptions, coordinate them across multiple locations and interfere with recovery. If a system can’t survive an accident, it won’t survive an adversary.”



Benny Czarny, CEO and Founder, OPSWAT:



“Faster patching can actually contribute to outages when testing and recovery cannot keep up. AI is increasing the pressure to fix vulnerabilities quickly, but you can’t attribute anything to AI without evidence from the investigation.



Failures this week have resulted from cloning systems and their weaknesses along with them. When a primary system and its backup run the same software, receive the same update, and depend on the same network, then they really aren’t that independent.



From a cybersecurity standpoint, critical infrastructure needs the same design mindset as an airplane cockpit, where primary and secondary systems use different hardware and software to reduce the chance that one defect disables every way of performing a critical function.”



Bryson Byrd, Cybersecurity Advisor, Huntress:



“Right now, there is no definitive link between these outages, and we should be careful about rushing to conclusions that AI or cyberattacks are responsible without having all the facts. What we do know is that there is a significant AI race going on between defenders and threat actors. As AI accelerates vulnerability discovery, defenders are under increasing pressure to engineer, test and push patches quickly to stay one step ahead. When companies are focused on speed of development, mistakes can happen. In the age of rapid patching, testing and verifying updates is arguably more important than ever.



My concern is that these outages will cause organizations to start dialing back patches out of fear of being the next Microsoft or FAA. We cannot afford to go back to a time when system administrators could wait several days before deploying critical security updates. The window between vulnerability discovery and potential exploitation is shrinking, and slowing down patches could leave organizations exposed to threats they already know about. So we cannot stop updates or sacrifice testing for speed. We need to double down on resilience and make sure organizations are prepared when an update doesn’t go as planned.



When it comes to critical patches and updates, there should always be a fallback plan in place, whether that’s a known, good backup or the last working code push that teams can quickly return to. We often see security teams with these plans documented, but the mechanisms haven’t actually been tested and verified to work. As infrastructure continues to evolve, these plans need to be tested regularly. Otherwise, when a bad update happens, organizations may not be prepared to respond, and a relatively contained issue can quickly grow into a much larger disruption.”



Grayson North, Principal Threat Intelligence Consultant, GuidePoint Security:



“This situation is a combination of increased media attention and a flurry of technical changes caused by AI’s rapid acceleration of vulnerability discovery. Outages are fairly common, but a few hours of downtime on a highly-visible system draws heightened attention. It can be compared to the DCA airline crash last year in a sense. After that incident, every near miss got national attention rather than being the usual footnote. 



We are also clearly in a period of flux in regards to vulnerability discovery/patch management. AI has made discovery of vulnerabilities trivial for those willing to spend tokens. As such the pure number of vulnerabilities being reported is through the roof (thus the “Vulnpocalypse” that some have dubbed the moment). Some of these discoveries lead to big, scary cyberattacks, yes, but all of them lead to patches to fix the problem. Every time you make a change to a production system, you risk causing an unforeseen issue. This risk scales exponentially with the number of patches and number of underlying systems. There are questions of whether or not holiday code freezes are forcing organizations to hurry up and implement more changes than usual this time of year. Every organization handles its change windows differently but this could certainly be exacerbating the issue.



Optimistically I believe that the number of vulnerabilities that exist and are waiting to be discovered is finite, so (hopefully) we just have to wait for all the major organizations to shake out a few years of technical debt and we will return to relative normalcy. The “Patchpocalypse” to address the “Vulnpocalypse,” if you will.”



Patrick Harr, Chief Executive Officer, DataVisor:



“What stands out to me with these outages is the breadth. Banks, major technology companies, and government systems all experienced disruptions. Separate organizations can face the same pressure at the same time. When AI uncovers vulnerabilities faster than teams can test the fixes, systems that run reliably on an ordinary day can struggle with the pace of change. That’s a form of fragility we need to take seriously. 



AI can find a flaw in minutes. It can take much longer to understand what happens to every service that depends on the software you’re about to change. Imagine a bank patches its sign-in system. The fix can close the security hole and pass its own tests, yet customers could still lose access if the mobile app can no longer authenticate them. That’s why I’d prioritize testing the whole customer journey and rolling the fix out in stages. Whether a particular organization missed a test is a question for its incident review.



Security teams need to change their monitoring, incident response and recovery plans. First, monitor what customers can actually do. Again, taking banks as an example, can customers sign in, see a balance, and complete a payment? Give the incident lead the authority to pause a rollout when those checks fail and rehearse how to restore service while keeping the vulnerable component isolated. Second, look across accounts for signs of coordination. One new account, one login, or one small transfer can look perfectly ordinary. When dozens of apparently unrelated accounts start moving money in the same sequence toward the same destinations, the pattern tells a different story.”

“These incidents make security teams realize that attackers may use the same AI (used to discover the vulnerability x) to turn a published patch into a working exploit within hours. The answer is to give defenders and red teamers the same advantage. 



A red team working with AI can show within hours which of a thousand flaws are actually exploitable in your environment, so only those few get the emergency treatment. A SOC working with AI can put detection and containment around a new flaw the same day, which buys the time to roll the patch out safely.”




Patrick Quirk, President, Opengear: 



“We don’t have specifics on these incidents, and outages have many causes, so I’ll speak to the pattern. AI is accelerating how quickly vulnerabilities are found, which means patches are arriving faster, and that speed is an advantage only when every rollout is tested in a staging environment first. Skip that step or miss a key dependency and the fix becomes the failure.



Speed doesn’t change the question that matters on the day something breaks: can your team get back into the affected systems and start recovery? That’s where many organizations fall short. They manage and troubleshoot their infrastructure over the same production network that just went down, so when it fails, IT and security lose access to the very systems they need to restore. In a cyberattack that dependency is dangerous, because visibility and control are what contain the threat.



Design your infrastructure assuming it will fail and build an independent management path that stays reachable when the primary network does not. That gives your team a way to diagnose the problem, isolate affected systems, and begin recovery without relying on the infrastructure that failed.”



Crystal Morin, Senior Cybersecurity Strategist, Sysdig:



“We swung the pendulum too far one way. For years, the security mantra was “patch faster.” Don’t get me wrong, that’s still the right approach. But many orgs have taken it to an extreme where the answer to every finding is “ship the fix, now, everywhere.” Pair that with a software delivery culture that already moves at breakneck speed, plus an AI-driven firehose of findings, and you get change volume that surpasses their ability (or desire?) to test and stage before deploying.



System fragility is the ultimate issue here. Systems are toppling over when you try to fix them because they were already broken. It’s like pulling the final brick in Jenga. These are architecture and infrastructure debts coming back to haunt us. AI-speed vulnerability discovery just delivered the bill to our doorstep.



Patching is prevention, and prevention is necessary, but it has a limit. What we’re seeing is what happens when you blow past that limit. So to bridge that gap while you fix your architecture, you need to turn to detection, which doesn’t have those limits.”

Failures this week have resulted from cloning systems and their weaknesses along with them. When a primary system and its backup run the same software, receive the same update, and depend on the same network, then they really aren’t that independent.



From a cybersecurity standpoint, critical infrastructure needs the same design mindset as an airplane cockpit, where primary and secondary systems use different hardware and software to reduce the chance that one defect disables every way of performing a critical function.”



Bryson Byrd, Cybersecurity Advisor, Huntress:



“Right now, there is no definitive link between these outages, and we should be careful about rushing to conclusions that AI or cyberattacks are responsible without having all the facts. What we do know is that there is a significant AI race going on between defenders and threat actors. As AI accelerates vulnerability discovery, defenders are under increasing pressure to engineer, test and push patches quickly to stay one step ahead. When companies are focused on speed of development, mistakes can happen. In the age of rapid patching, testing and verifying updates is arguably more important than ever.



My concern is that these outages will cause organizations to start dialing back patches out of fear of being the next Microsoft or FAA. We cannot afford to go back to a time when system administrators could wait several days before deploying critical security updates. The window between vulnerability discovery and potential exploitation is shrinking, and slowing down patches could leave organizations exposed to threats they already know about. So we cannot stop updates or sacrifice testing for speed. We need to double down on resilience and make sure organizations are prepared when an update doesn’t go as planned.



When it comes to critical patches and updates, there should always be a fallback plan in place, whether that’s a known, good backup or the last working code push that teams can quickly return to. We often see security teams with these plans documented, but the mechanisms haven’t actually been tested and verified to work. As infrastructure continues to evolve, these plans need to be tested regularly. Otherwise, when a bad update happens, organizations may not be prepared to respond, and a relatively contained issue can quickly grow into a much larger disruption.”



Grayson North, Principal Threat Intelligence Consultant, GuidePoint Security:



“This situation is a combination of increased media attention and a flurry of technical changes caused by AI’s rapid acceleration of vulnerability discovery. Outages are fairly common, but a few hours of downtime on a highly-visible system draws heightened attention. It can be compared to the DCA airline crash last year in a sense. After that incident, every near miss got national attention rather than being the usual footnote. 



We are also clearly in a period of flux in regards to vulnerability discovery/patch management. AI has made discovery of vulnerabilities trivial for those willing to spend tokens. As such the pure number of vulnerabilities being reported is through the roof (thus the “Vulnpocalypse” that some have dubbed the moment). Some of these discoveries lead to big, scary cyberattacks, yes, but all of them lead to patches to fix the problem. Every time you make a change to a production system, you risk causing an unforeseen issue. This risk scales exponentially with the number of patches and number of underlying systems. There are questions of whether or not holiday code freezes are forcing organizations to hurry up and implement more changes than usual this time of year. Every organization handles its change windows differently but this could certainly be exacerbating the issue.



Optimistically I believe that the number of vulnerabilities that exist and are waiting to be discovered is finite, so (hopefully) we just have to wait for all the major organizations to shake out a few years of technical debt and we will return to relative normalcy. The “Patchpocalypse” to address the “Vulnpocalypse,” if you will.”



Patrick Harr, Chief Executive Officer, DataVisor:



“What stands out to me with these outages is the breadth. Banks, major technology companies, and government systems all experienced disruptions. Separate organizations can face the same pressure at the same time. When AI uncovers vulnerabilities faster than teams can test the fixes, systems that run reliably on an ordinary day can struggle with the pace of change. That’s a form of fragility we need to take seriously. 



AI can find a flaw in minutes. It can take much longer to understand what happens to every service that depends on the software you’re about to change. Imagine a bank patches its sign-in system. The fix can close the security hole and pass its own tests, yet customers could still lose access if the mobile app can no longer authenticate them. That’s why I’d prioritize testing the whole customer journey and rolling the fix out in stages. Whether a particular organization missed a test is a question for its incident review.



Security teams need to change their monitoring, incident response and recovery plans. First, monitor what customers can actually do. Again, taking banks as an example, can customers sign in, see a balance, and complete a payment? Give the incident lead the authority to pause a rollout when those checks fail and rehearse how to restore service while keeping the vulnerable component isolated. Second, look across accounts for signs of coordination. One new account, one login, or one small transfer can look perfectly ordinary. When dozens of apparently unrelated accounts start moving money in the same sequence toward the same destinations, the pattern tells a different story.”



Chris Hughes, Vice President of Security Strategy, Noma Security:



“Artificial Intelligence (AI) has industrialized vulnerability discovery, organizations are racing to fix what’s being found, and the patching itself can disrupt operations. That’s the availability piece of the CIA triad. We’ve seen industrialized vulnerability discovery all year, in programs like Patch the Planet and Project Glasswing and in a steady stream of findings from frontier labs and researchers. Vulnerability trackers reported the 2026 CVE count passing 100,000 earlier this month, more than double last year and a record. That volume is outpacing the ability to patch and test safely, and when teams compress testing windows to keep up, they raise the risk of exactly these kinds of outages. The work that matters is risk-based prioritization around exploitability, known exploited vulnerabilities, and reachability, along with better testing, rollback plans, and resilience.



So, what technical indicators would support an AI-driven, coordinated attack as an explanation for these incidents? You’d want indicators that actually tie the incidents together: shared tooling or TTPs, artifacts consistent with autonomous offensive frameworks, and timing or targeting that can’t be explained by a common vendor, a maintenance window, or a shared patch cycle. Based on what’s public, we can’t say that’s what happened, and many of these disruptions have been described as planned maintenance or the result of accelerated patching. The coincidences are hard to ignore, which is why the speculation has taken off, but the better-supported story right now is accumulated technical debt and rushed remediation under the pressure of industrialized discovery. Organizations should still prepare for agentic offensive frameworks, even if this cluster isn’t ultimately attributed to them.”



Alex Orleans, Head of Threat Intelligence, Sublime Security:



“What I feel AI is more likely contributing to these outages is not patching speed or the discovery of vulnerabilities but code of dubious quality. As more and more development and engineering is devolved to vibe-coding, the internals of the resultant code are less and less understood by both the organizations deploying it and the engineers who maintain it. This makes crashes and outages more likely. 



I would also say that across the outages we’ve seen, there hasn’t been a firmly identified shared type of cause (AI related or otherwise). Each outage should be taken on its own technical merits, not viewed as if there is some sort of unidentified overlap based on coincidental timing.”



Gerasimos Marketos, Chief Product Officer, Hack The Box:



“These incidents make security teams realize that attackers may use the same AI (used to discover the vulnerability x) to turn a published patch into a working exploit within hours. The answer is to give defenders and red teamers the same advantage. 



A red team working with AI can show within hours which of a thousand flaws are actually exploitable in your environment, so only those few get the emergency treatment. A SOC working with AI can put detection and containment around a new flaw the same day, which buys the time to roll the patch out safely.”

We are also clearly in a period of flux in regards to vulnerability discovery/patch management. AI has made discovery of vulnerabilities trivial for those willing to spend tokens. As such the pure number of vulnerabilities being reported is through the roof (thus the “Vulnpocalypse” that some have dubbed the moment). Some of these discoveries lead to big, scary cyberattacks, yes, but all of them lead to patches to fix the problem. Every time you make a change to a production system, you risk causing an unforeseen issue. This risk scales exponentially with the number of patches and number of underlying systems. There are questions of whether or not holiday code freezes are forcing organizations to hurry up and implement more changes than usual this time of year. Every organization handles its change windows differently but this could certainly be exacerbating the issue.



Optimistically I believe that the number of vulnerabilities that exist and are waiting to be discovered is finite, so (hopefully) we just have to wait for all the major organizations to shake out a few years of technical debt and we will return to relative normalcy. The “Patchpocalypse” to address the “Vulnpocalypse,” if you will.”



Patrick Harr, Chief Executive Officer, DataVisor:



“What stands out to me with these outages is the breadth. Banks, major technology companies, and government systems all experienced disruptions. Separate organizations can face the same pressure at the same time. When AI uncovers vulnerabilities faster than teams can test the fixes, systems that run reliably on an ordinary day can struggle with the pace of change. That’s a form of fragility we need to take seriously. 



AI can find a flaw in minutes. It can take much longer to understand what happens to every service that depends on the software you’re about to change. Imagine a bank patches its sign-in system. The fix can close the security hole and pass its own tests, yet customers could still lose access if the mobile app can no longer authenticate them. That’s why I’d prioritize testing the whole customer journey and rolling the fix out in stages. Whether a particular organization missed a test is a question for its incident review.



Security teams need to change their monitoring, incident response and recovery plans. First, monitor what customers can actually do. Again, taking banks as an example, can customers sign in, see a balance, and complete a payment? Give the incident lead the authority to pause a rollout when those checks fail and rehearse how to restore service while keeping the vulnerable component isolated. Second, look across accounts for signs of coordination. One new account, one login, or one small transfer can look perfectly ordinary. When dozens of apparently unrelated accounts start moving money in the same sequence toward the same destinations, the pattern tells a different story.”



Chris Hughes, Vice President of Security Strategy, Noma Security:



“Artificial Intelligence (AI) has industrialized vulnerability discovery, organizations are racing to fix what’s being found, and the patching itself can disrupt operations. That’s the availability piece of the CIA triad. We’ve seen industrialized vulnerability discovery all year, in programs like Patch the Planet and Project Glasswing and in a steady stream of findings from frontier labs and researchers. Vulnerability trackers reported the 2026 CVE count passing 100,000 earlier this month, more than double last year and a record. That volume is outpacing the ability to patch and test safely, and when teams compress testing windows to keep up, they raise the risk of exactly these kinds of outages. The work that matters is risk-based prioritization around exploitability, known exploited vulnerabilities, and reachability, along with better testing, rollback plans, and resilience.



So, what technical indicators would support an AI-driven, coordinated attack as an explanation for these incidents? You’d want indicators that actually tie the incidents together: shared tooling or TTPs, artifacts consistent with autonomous offensive frameworks, and timing or targeting that can’t be explained by a common vendor, a maintenance window, or a shared patch cycle. Based on what’s public, we can’t say that’s what happened, and many of these disruptions have been described as planned maintenance or the result of accelerated patching. The coincidences are hard to ignore, which is why the speculation has taken off, but the better-supported story right now is accumulated technical debt and rushed remediation under the pressure of industrialized discovery. Organizations should still prepare for agentic offensive frameworks, even if this cluster isn’t ultimately attributed to them.”



Alex Orleans, Head of Threat Intelligence, Sublime Security:



“What I feel AI is more likely contributing to these outages is not patching speed or the discovery of vulnerabilities but code of dubious quality. As more and more development and engineering is devolved to vibe-coding, the internals of the resultant code are less and less understood by both the organizations deploying it and the engineers who maintain it. This makes crashes and outages more likely. 



I would also say that across the outages we’ve seen, there hasn’t been a firmly identified shared type of cause (AI related or otherwise). Each outage should be taken on its own technical merits, not viewed as if there is some sort of unidentified overlap based on coincidental timing.”



Gerasimos Marketos, Chief Product Officer, Hack The Box:



“These incidents make security teams realize that attackers may use the same AI (used to discover the vulnerability x) to turn a published patch into a working exploit within hours. The answer is to give defenders and red teamers the same advantage. 



A red team working with AI can show within hours which of a thousand flaws are actually exploitable in your environment, so only those few get the emergency treatment. A SOC working with AI can put detection and containment around a new flaw the same day, which buys the time to roll the patch out safely.”




Patrick Quirk, President, Opengear: 



“We don’t have specifics on these incidents, and outages have many causes, so I’ll speak to the pattern. AI is accelerating how quickly vulnerabilities are found, which means patches are arriving faster, and that speed is an advantage only when every rollout is tested in a staging environment first. Skip that step or miss a key dependency and the fix becomes the failure.



Speed doesn’t change the question that matters on the day something breaks: can your team get back into the affected systems and start recovery? That’s where many organizations fall short. They manage and troubleshoot their infrastructure over the same production network that just went down, so when it fails, IT and security lose access to the very systems they need to restore. In a cyberattack that dependency is dangerous, because visibility and control are what contain the threat.



Design your infrastructure assuming it will fail and build an independent management path that stays reachable when the primary network does not. That gives your team a way to diagnose the problem, isolate affected systems, and begin recovery without relying on the infrastructure that failed.”



Crystal Morin, Senior Cybersecurity Strategist, Sysdig:



“We swung the pendulum too far one way. For years, the security mantra was “patch faster.” Don’t get me wrong, that’s still the right approach. But many orgs have taken it to an extreme where the answer to every finding is “ship the fix, now, everywhere.” Pair that with a software delivery culture that already moves at breakneck speed, plus an AI-driven firehose of findings, and you get change volume that surpasses their ability (or desire?) to test and stage before deploying.



System fragility is the ultimate issue here. Systems are toppling over when you try to fix them because they were already broken. It’s like pulling the final brick in Jenga. These are architecture and infrastructure debts coming back to haunt us. AI-speed vulnerability discovery just delivered the bill to our doorstep.



Patching is prevention, and prevention is necessary, but it has a limit. What we’re seeing is what happens when you blow past that limit. So to bridge that gap while you fix your architecture, you need to turn to detection, which doesn’t have those limits.”

My concern is that these outages will cause organizations to start dialing back patches out of fear of being the next Microsoft or FAA. We cannot afford to go back to a time when system administrators could wait several days before deploying critical security updates. The window between vulnerability discovery and potential exploitation is shrinking, and slowing down patches could leave organizations exposed to threats they already know about. So we cannot stop updates or sacrifice testing for speed. We need to double down on resilience and make sure organizations are prepared when an update doesn’t go as planned.



When it comes to critical patches and updates, there should always be a fallback plan in place, whether that’s a known, good backup or the last working code push that teams can quickly return to. We often see security teams with these plans documented, but the mechanisms haven’t actually been tested and verified to work. As infrastructure continues to evolve, these plans need to be tested regularly. Otherwise, when a bad update happens, organizations may not be prepared to respond, and a relatively contained issue can quickly grow into a much larger disruption.”



Grayson North, Principal Threat Intelligence Consultant, GuidePoint Security:



“This situation is a combination of increased media attention and a flurry of technical changes caused by AI’s rapid acceleration of vulnerability discovery. Outages are fairly common, but a few hours of downtime on a highly-visible system draws heightened attention. It can be compared to the DCA airline crash last year in a sense. After that incident, every near miss got national attention rather than being the usual footnote. 



We are also clearly in a period of flux in regards to vulnerability discovery/patch management. AI has made discovery of vulnerabilities trivial for those willing to spend tokens. As such the pure number of vulnerabilities being reported is through the roof (thus the “Vulnpocalypse” that some have dubbed the moment). The “Patchpocalypse” to address the “Vulnpocalypse,” if you will.”

Optimistically I believe that the number of vulnerabilities that exist and are waiting to be discovered is finite, so (hopefully) we just have to wait for all the major organizations to shake out a few years of technical debt and we will return to relative normalcy. The “Patchpocalypse” to address the “Vulnpocalypse,” if you will.”



Patrick Harr, Chief Executive Officer, DataVisor:



“What stands out to me with these outages is the breadth. Banks, major technology companies, and government systems all experienced disruptions. Separate organizations can face the same pressure at the same time. When AI uncovers vulnerabilities faster than teams can test the fixes, systems that run reliably on an ordinary day can struggle with the pace of change. That’s a form of fragility we need to take seriously. 



AI can find a flaw in minutes. It can take much longer to understand what happens to every service that depends on the software you’re about to change. Imagine a bank patches its sign-in system. The fix can close the security hole and pass its own tests, yet customers could still lose access if the mobile app can no longer authenticate them. That’s why I’d prioritize testing the whole customer journey and rolling the fix out in stages. Whether a particular organization missed a test is a question for its incident review.



Security teams need to change their monitoring, incident response and recovery plans. First, monitor what customers can actually do. Again, taking banks as an example, can customers sign in, see a balance, and complete a payment? Give the incident lead the authority to pause a rollout when those checks fail and rehearse how to restore service while keeping the vulnerable component isolated. Second, look across accounts for signs of coordination. One new account, one login, or one small transfer can look perfectly ordinary. When dozens of apparently unrelated accounts start moving money in the same sequence toward the same destinations, the pattern tells a different story.”



Chris Hughes, Vice President of Security Strategy, Noma Security:



“Artificial Intelligence (AI) has industrialized vulnerability discovery, organizations are racing to fix what’s being found, and the patching itself can disrupt operations. That’s the availability piece of the CIA triad. We’ve seen industrialized vulnerability discovery all year, in programs like Patch the Planet and Project Glasswing and in a steady stream of findings from frontier labs and researchers. Vulnerability trackers reported the 2026 CVE count passing 100,000 earlier this month, more than double last year and a record. That volume is outpacing the ability to patch and test safely, and when teams compress testing windows to keep up, they raise the risk of exactly these kinds of outages. The work that matters is risk-based prioritization around exploitability, known exploited vulnerabilities, and reachability, along with better testing, rollback plans, and resilience.



So, what technical indicators would support an AI-driven, coordinated attack as an explanation for these incidents? You’d want indicators that actually tie the incidents together: shared tooling or TTPs, artifacts consistent with autonomous offensive frameworks, and timing or targeting that can’t be explained by a common vendor, a maintenance window, or a shared patch cycle. Based on what’s public, we can’t say that’s what happened, and many of these disruptions have been described as planned maintenance or the result of accelerated patching. The coincidences are hard to ignore, which is why the speculation has taken off, but the better-supported story right now is accumulated technical debt and rushed remediation under the pressure of industrialized discovery. Organizations should still prepare for agentic offensive frameworks, even if this cluster isn’t ultimately attributed to them.”



Alex Orleans, Head of Threat Intelligence, Sublime Security:



“What I feel AI is more likely contributing to these outages is not patching speed or the discovery of vulnerabilities but code of dubious quality. As more and more development and engineering is devolved to vibe-coding, the internals of the resultant code are less and less understood by both the organizations deploying it and the engineers who maintain it. This makes crashes and outages more likely. 



I would also say that across the outages we’ve seen, there hasn’t been a firmly identified shared type of cause (AI related or otherwise). Each outage should be taken on its own technical merits, not viewed as if there is some sort of unidentified overlap based on coincidental timing.”



Gerasimos Marketos, Chief Product Officer, Hack The Box:



“These incidents make security teams realize that attackers may use the same AI (used to discover the vulnerability x) to turn a published patch into a working exploit within hours. The answer is to give defenders and red teamers the same advantage. 



A red team working with AI can show within hours which of a thousand flaws are actually exploitable in your environment, so only those few get the emergency treatment. A SOC working with AI can put detection and containment around a new flaw the same day, which buys the time to roll the patch out safely.”




Patrick Quirk, President, Opengear: 



“We don’t have specifics on these incidents, and outages have many causes, so I’ll speak to the pattern. AI is accelerating how quickly vulnerabilities are found, which means patches are arriving faster, and that speed is an advantage only when every rollout is tested in a staging environment first. Skip that step or miss a key dependency and the fix becomes the failure.



Speed doesn’t change the question that matters on the day something breaks: can your team get back into the affected systems and start recovery? That’s where many organizations fall short. They manage and troubleshoot their infrastructure over the same production network that just went down, so when it fails, IT and security lose access to the very systems they need to restore. In a cyberattack that dependency is dangerous, because visibility and control are what contain the threat.



Design your infrastructure assuming it will fail and build an independent management path that stays reachable when the primary network does not. That gives your team a way to diagnose the problem, isolate affected systems, and begin recovery without relying on the infrastructure that failed.”



Crystal Morin, Senior Cybersecurity Strategist, Sysdig:



“We swung the pendulum too far one way. For years, the security mantra was “patch faster.” Don’t get me wrong, that’s still the right approach. But many orgs have taken it to an extreme where the answer to every finding is “ship the fix, now, everywhere.” Pair that with a software delivery culture that already moves at breakneck speed, plus an AI-driven firehose of findings, and you get change volume that surpasses their ability (or desire?) to test and stage before deploying.



System fragility is the ultimate issue here. Systems are toppling over when you try to fix them because they were already broken. It’s like pulling the final brick in Jenga. These are architecture and infrastructure debts coming back to haunt us. AI-speed vulnerability discovery just delivered the bill to our doorstep.



Patching is prevention, and prevention is necessary, but it has a limit. What we’re seeing is what happens when you blow past that limit. So to bridge that gap while you fix your architecture, you need to turn to detection, which doesn’t have those limits.”

We are also clearly in a period of flux in regards to vulnerability discovery/patch management. AI has made discovery of vulnerabilities trivial for those willing to spend tokens. As such the pure number of vulnerabilities being reported is through the roof (thus the “Vulnpocalypse” that some have dubbed the moment). Some of these discoveries lead to big, scary cyberattacks, yes, but all of them lead to patches to fix the problem. Every time you make a change to a production system, you risk causing an unforeseen issue. This risk scales exponentially with the number of patches and number of underlying systems. There are questions of whether or not holiday code freezes are forcing organizations to hurry up and implement more changes than usual this time of year. Every organization handles its change windows differently but this could certainly be exacerbating the issue.



Optimistically I believe that the number of vulnerabilities that exist and are waiting to be discovered is finite, so (hopefully) we just have to wait for all the major organizations to shake out a few years of technical debt and we will return to relative normalcy. The “Patchpocalypse” to address the “Vulnpocalypse,” if you will.”

Patching is prevention, and prevention is necessary, but it has a limit. What we’re seeing is what happens when you blow past that limit. So to bridge that gap while you fix your architecture, you need to turn to detection, which doesn’t have those limits.”

AI can find a flaw in minutes. It can take much longer to understand what happens to every service that depends on the software you’re about to change. Imagine a bank patches its sign-in system. The fix can close the security hole and pass its own tests, yet customers could still lose access if the mobile app can no longer authenticate them. That’s why I’d prioritize testing the whole customer journey and rolling the fix out in stages. Whether a particular organization missed a test is a question for its incident review.



Security teams need to change their monitoring, incident response and recovery plans. First, monitor what customers can actually do. Again, taking banks as an example, can customers sign in, see a balance, and complete a payment? Give the incident lead the authority to pause a rollout when those checks fail and rehearse how to restore service while keeping the vulnerable component isolated. Second, look across accounts for signs of coordination. One new account, one login, or one small transfer can look perfectly ordinary. When dozens of apparently unrelated accounts start moving money in the same sequence toward the same destinations, the pattern tells a different story.”



Chris Hughes, Vice President of Security Strategy, Noma Security:



“Artificial Intelligence (AI) has industrialized vulnerability discovery, organizations are racing to fix what’s being found, and the patching itself can disrupt operations. That’s the availability piece of the CIA triad. We’ve seen industrialized vulnerability discovery all year, in programs like Patch the Planet and Project Glasswing and in a steady stream of findings from frontier labs and researchers. Vulnerability trackers reported the 2026 CVE count passing 100,000 earlier this month, more than double last year and a record. That volume is outpacing the ability to patch and test safely, and when teams compress testing windows to keep up, they raise the risk of exactly these kinds of outages. The work that matters is risk-based prioritization around exploitability, known exploited vulnerabilities, and reachability, along with better testing, rollback plans, and resilience.



So, what technical indicators would support an AI-driven, coordinated attack as an explanation for these incidents? You’d want indicators that actually tie the incidents together: shared tooling or TTPs, artifacts consistent with autonomous offensive frameworks, and timing or targeting that can’t be explained by a common vendor, a maintenance window, or a shared patch cycle. Based on what’s public, we can’t say that’s what happened, and many of these disruptions have been described as planned maintenance or the result of accelerated patching. The coincidences are hard to ignore, which is why the speculation has taken off, but the better-supported story right now is accumulated technical debt and rushed remediation under the pressure of industrialized discovery. Organizations should still prepare for agentic offensive frameworks, even if this cluster isn’t ultimately attributed to them.”



Alex Orleans, Head of Threat Intelligence, Sublime Security:



“What I feel AI is more likely contributing to these outages is not patching speed or the discovery of vulnerabilities but code of dubious quality. As more and more development and engineering is devolved to vibe-coding, the internals of the resultant code are less and less understood by both the organizations deploying it and the engineers who maintain it. This makes crashes and outages more likely. 



I would also say that across the outages we’ve seen, there hasn’t been a firmly identified shared type of cause (AI related or otherwise). Each outage should be taken on its own technical merits, not viewed as if there is some sort of unidentified overlap based on coincidental timing.”



Gerasimos Marketos, Chief Product Officer, Hack The Box:



“These incidents make security teams realize that attackers may use the same AI (used to discover the vulnerability x) to turn a published patch into a working exploit within hours. The answer is to give defenders and red teamers the same advantage. 



A red team working with AI can show within hours which of a thousand flaws are actually exploitable in your environment, so only those few get the emergency treatment. A SOC working with AI can put detection and containment around a new flaw the same day, which buys the time to roll the patch out safely.”




Patrick Quirk, President, Opengear: 



“We don’t have specifics on these incidents, and outages have many causes, so I’ll speak to the pattern. AI is accelerating how quickly vulnerabilities are found, which means patches are arriving faster, and that speed is an advantage only when every rollout is tested in a staging environment first. Skip that step or miss a key dependency and the fix becomes the failure.



Speed doesn’t change the question that matters on the day something breaks: can your team get back into the affected systems and start recovery? That’s where many organizations fall short. They manage and troubleshoot their infrastructure over the same production network that just went down, so when it fails, IT and security lose access to the very systems they need to restore. In a cyberattack that dependency is dangerous, because visibility and control are what contain the threat.



Design your infrastructure assuming it will fail and build an independent management path that stays reachable when the primary network does not. That gives your team a way to diagnose the problem, isolate affected systems, and begin recovery without relying on the infrastructure that failed.”



Crystal Morin, Senior Cybersecurity Strategist, Sysdig:



“We swung the pendulum too far one way. For years, the security mantra was “patch faster.” Don’t get me wrong, that’s still the right approach. But many orgs have taken it to an extreme where the answer to every finding is “ship the fix, now, everywhere.” Pair that with a software delivery culture that already moves at breakneck speed, plus an AI-driven firehose of findings, and you get change volume that surpasses their ability (or desire?) to test and stage before deploying.



System fragility is the ultimate issue here. Systems are toppling over when you try to fix them because they were already broken. It’s like pulling the final brick in Jenga. They manage and troubleshoot their infrastructure over the same production network that just went down, so when it fails, IT and security lose access to the very systems they need to restore. In a cyberattack that dependency is dangerous, because visibility and control are what contain the threat.



Design your infrastructure assuming it will fail and build an independent management path that stays reachable when the primary network does not. That gives your team a way to diagnose the problem, isolate affected systems, and begin recovery without relying on the infrastructure that failed.”



Crystal Morin, Senior Cybersecurity Strategist, Sysdig:



“We swung the pendulum too far one way. For years, the security mantra was “patch faster.” Don’t get me wrong, that’s still the right approach. But many orgs have taken it to an extreme where the answer to every finding is “ship the fix, now, everywhere.” Pair that with a software delivery culture that already moves at breakneck speed, plus an AI-driven firehose of findings, and you get change volume that surpasses their ability (or desire?) to test and stage before deploying.



System fragility is the ultimate issue here. Systems are toppling over when you try to fix them because they were already broken. It’s like pulling the final brick in Jenga. These are architecture and infrastructure debts coming back to haunt us. AI-speed vulnerability discovery just delivered the bill to our doorstep.



Patching is prevention, and prevention is necessary, but it has a limit. What we’re seeing is what happens when you blow past that limit. So to bridge that gap while you fix your architecture, you need to turn to detection, which doesn’t have those limits.”

Gerasimos Marketos, Chief Product Officer, Hack The Box:



“These incidents make security teams realize that attackers may use the same AI (used to discover the vulnerability x) to turn a published patch into a working exploit within hours. The answer is to give defenders and red teamers the same advantage. 



A red team working with AI can show within hours which of a thousand flaws are actually exploitable in your environment, so only those few get the emergency treatment. A SOC working with AI can put detection and containment around a new flaw the same day, which buys the time to roll the patch out safely.”




Patrick Quirk, President, Opengear: 



“We don’t have specifics on these incidents, and outages have many causes, so I’ll speak to the pattern. [47] SecurityWeek - SBC Medical Group Data Breach Impacts Over 2 Million
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 11:36:51 +0000
Link: https://www.securityweek.com/sbc-medical-group-data-breach-impacts-over-2-million/

[TAM METİN - 4830 kelime]
SBC Medical Group Data Breach Impacts Over 2 Million

Threat actors accessed databases containing customer information associated with clinics in Japan.

Flipboard





Reddit





Whatsapp





Whatsapp





Email

California-based SBC Medical Group Holdings Incorporated (NASDAQ: SBC) has disclosed a data breach impacting over 2 million individuals in Japan.
The medical services organization provides consulting, management, and operational support to medical corporations and clinics.



Hackers accessed an online platform SBC Medical Group manages and compromised databases containing customer information associated with certain clinics in Japan, the company said in a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).



SBC Medical Group continues to investigate the attack but has confirmed that personal and medical information was likely compromised.



The hackers stole the basic information of 1,624,000 individuals, including names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, dates of birth, gender, patient card numbers, member IDs, and survey responses.



They also compromised the reservation-request information of 255,416 people, as well as the content entered in web inquiry forms by 217,769 individuals.Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.


According to the filing, 4,513 people also had their treatment descriptions and stored image file names stolen, while 15,007 had the basic information, treatment names, and review text exfiltrated. For 14 individuals, credit card information was also compromised.



“The Company has confirmed that all of these credit cards were in a state in which additional payments could not be processed, such as having expired,” SBC Medical Group said.



Additionally, the hackers stole customer passwords, along with 20,000 records containing employee names, IDs, and passwords.



“For 459 employees, information provided at the time of employment, including bank account and pension-related information, withholding tax certificates and dependent exemption declarations, was also affected,” the company said.



In a separate incident involving the third-party reservation service Tribeau, hackers accessed administrator accounts and accessed the information of approximately 19,000 individuals.



For 12,641 of them, the threat actors compromised Kana names, phone numbers, age, and requested treatments. For three people, the hackers also accessed message contents, dates of birth, and gender, and for 6,804 they compromised reservation information and treatment details.



“The operator confirmed that the obtained information was not linked to case or review information, including photographs, on Tribeau. Email addresses, residential addresses, credit card information, passwords, and electronic medical records were not included in that platform incident. The company and the provider continue to investigate the access and its cause,” the company said.



SBC Medical Group said both incidents have been remediated. It isolated the affected server and evicted the hackers, and rotated the passwords for all the clinics to which it provides management services on Tribeau.



“The company is continuing to assess the potential impact of the incidents on its business, financial condition and results of operations,” SBC Medical Group said.

SBC Medical Group continues to investigate the attack but has confirmed that personal and medical information was likely compromised.



The hackers stole the basic information of 1,624,000 individuals, including names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, dates of birth, gender, patient card numbers, member IDs, and survey responses.



They also compromised the reservation-request information of 255,416 people, as well as the content entered in web inquiry forms by 217,769 individuals.Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.


According to the filing, 4,513 people also had their treatment descriptions and stored image file names stolen, while 15,007 had the basic information, treatment names, and review text exfiltrated. For 14 individuals, credit card information was also compromised.



“The Company has confirmed that all of these credit cards were in a state in which additional payments could not be processed, such as having expired,” SBC Medical Group said.



Additionally, the hackers stole customer passwords, along with 20,000 records containing employee names, IDs, and passwords.



“For 459 employees, information provided at the time of employment, including bank account and pension-related information, withholding tax certificates and dependent exemption declarations, was also affected,” the company said.



In a separate incident involving the third-party reservation service Tribeau, hackers accessed administrator accounts and accessed the information of approximately 19,000 individuals.



For 12,641 of them, the threat actors compromised Kana names, phone numbers, age, and requested treatments. For three people, the hackers also accessed message contents, dates of birth, and gender, and for 6,804 they compromised reservation information and treatment details.



“The operator confirmed that the obtained information was not linked to case or review information, including photographs, on Tribeau. Email addresses, residential addresses, credit card information, passwords, and electronic medical records were not included in that platform incident. The company and the provider continue to investigate the access and its cause,” the company said.



SBC Medical Group said both incidents have been remediated. It isolated the affected server and evicted the hackers, and rotated the passwords for all the clinics to which it provides management services on Tribeau.



“The company is continuing to assess the potential impact of the incidents on its business, financial condition and results of operations,” SBC Medical Group said.

[48] SecurityWeek - Ruby Patches Ruby2Shell Vulnerability That Could Lead to RCE
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 10:34:10 +0000
Link: https://www.securityweek.com/ruby-patches-ruby2shell-vulnerability-that-could-lead-to-rce/

[TAM METİN - 4129 kelime]
Ruby Patches Ruby2Shell Vulnerability That Could Lead to RCE

Tracked as CVE-2026-132825, the bug is a heap-based buffer overflow that could lead to remote code execution (RCE).

Flipboard





Reddit





Whatsapp





Whatsapp





Email

Fresh security updates for the Ruby programming language resolve seven vulnerabilities in its regular expression engine and in the case conversion of strings. Proof-of-concept (PoC) code demonstrating remote code execution (RCE) exists for five of them.
At the top of the list sits CVE-2026-132825 (CVSS score of 7.4), described as a heap-based buffer overflow in the case conversion of strings that could potentially lead to RCE in certain scenarios.



Dubbed Ruby2Shell, the flaw impacts character case-conversion operations. In some single-byte encodings, including ISO-8859-1 and Windows-1252, when changing the case of a string, Ruby may end up writing one byte past the output buffer.



“For example, converting the German character ß to uppercase produces SS. In affected code, Ruby checks that sufficient space exists for one byte but writes two, potentially corrupting adjacent heap memory,” Previdian explains.



Veria Labs reports that, in default Ruby configurations, unauthenticated attackers could trigger the security defect from Rails, classic-style Sinatra, and potentially other frameworks.



According to preemptive exposure management firm WatchTowr, “any Ruby application that changes the case of external text in a single-byte encoding” is affected by the vulnerability.Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.


According to Veria Labs, which plans to release a PoC after major vendors have rolled out patches, GitHub Enterprise Server is affected. Chatwoot, GitLab, Mastodon, OpenProject, and the Discourse base image have patched the bug.



Successful exploitation of Ruby2Shell in production environments is likely to be challenging, WatchTowr principal threat intelligence specialist Yordan Ganchev told SecurityWeek.



According to him, correctly laying out memory is difficult, and “attackers would also need the right non-glibc memory allocator, runtime configuration, and application logic preconditions, making exploitation even more challenging.”



“And if that weren’t enough, they’d need to contend with anyone else hammering the system on the internet and, in the end, defeat Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), making the whole journey a complete odyssey,” Ganchev noted.



Most likely, malformed requests could lead to denial-of-service (DoS) and service disruption, he said.



The other four vulnerabilities with a PoC demonstrating RCE include a double free, two integer overflows, and a heap-based buffer overflow. CVE identifiers for these issues have been requested but not assigned yet. PoC code also exists for an out-of-bounds read, demonstrating memory corruption.



Ruby also resolved an out-of-bounds read in its regular expression engine that could lead to memory leaks and process crashes.



Patches for all seven vulnerabilities were included in Ruby versions 4.0.10, 3.4.13, or 3.3.14. Users are advised to apply the fixes as soon as possible.

Related: Hackers Exploit Cisco Expressway Vulnerability Soon After PoC Release
Related: Critical Apache Roller, Axis Vulnerabilities Exploited in Attacks
Related: F5 Patches Critical NGINX2Root Flaws as PoC Exploits Go Public

Veria Labs reports that, in default Ruby configurations, unauthenticated attackers could trigger the security defect from Rails, classic-style Sinatra, and potentially other frameworks.



According to preemptive exposure management firm WatchTowr, “any Ruby application that changes the case of external text in a single-byte encoding” is affected by the vulnerability.Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.


According to Veria Labs, which plans to release a PoC after major vendors have rolled out patches, GitHub Enterprise Server is affected. Chatwoot, GitLab, Mastodon, OpenProject, and the Discourse base image have patched the bug.



Successful exploitation of Ruby2Shell in production environments is likely to be challenging, WatchTowr principal threat intelligence specialist Yordan Ganchev told SecurityWeek.



According to him, correctly laying out memory is difficult, and “attackers would also need the right non-glibc memory allocator, runtime configuration, and application logic preconditions, making exploitation even more challenging.”



“And if that weren’t enough, they’d need to contend with anyone else hammering the system on the internet and, in the end, defeat Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), making the whole journey a complete odyssey,” Ganchev noted.



Most likely, malformed requests could lead to denial-of-service (DoS) and service disruption, he said.



The other four vulnerabilities with a PoC demonstrating RCE include a double free, two integer overflows, and a heap-based buffer overflow. CVE identifiers for these issues have been requested but not assigned yet. PoC code also exists for an out-of-bounds read, demonstrating memory corruption.



Ruby also resolved an out-of-bounds read in its regular expression engine that could lead to memory leaks and process crashes.



Patches for all seven vulnerabilities were included in Ruby versions 4.0.10, 3.4.13, or 3.3.14. Users are advised to apply the fixes as soon as possible.

[49] SecurityWeek - N-able Blames Service Disruption on Cyberattack
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 09:08:35 +0000

N-able Blames Service Disruption on Cyberattack

The incident affected Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud and could have led to credential theft.

Flipboard





Reddit





Whatsapp





Whatsapp





Email

N-able Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud services experienced a days-long disruption across all regions after hackers compromised one of the company’s servers.
The disruption began on November 16, and N-able initially blamed it on “a combination of platform configuration and service dependencies”.



Mail flow and filtering were not affected, but related services, such as logging, mailbox synchronization, the management portal, and quarantine, were taken offline.



On November 18, the company confirmed that a cyberattack was behind the disruption, noting that it found no evidence that customer data was compromised.



“Our investigation determined that the incident was isolated to a single web server, where an unauthorized party may have been able to access certain credentials stored on the platform,” the company told SecurityWeek.



N-able says its restoration and remediation efforts continue. While inbound and outbound filtering are operating, access to its portal and API remains disabled.Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.


“We took immediate action to contain the incident, including taking the affected server offline, rotating internal platform credentials, revoking existing customer API tokens, invalidating OAuth tokens, and proactively resetting passwords for local users,” N-able said.



The company says its investigation into the incident remains ongoing while it scrambles to securely restore its dashboard and API access.



“We have provided customers with specific guidance based on how they access and configure Mail Assure or SpamExperts Hosted Cloud and will continue to provide updates,” N-able said.



According to the company, the cyberattack is unrelated to the recent N-central incident, in which it took the RMM and UEM platform offline to develop and roll out patches for dozens of zero-days a researcher dropped on GitHub.

West Virginia Legislature hit with cyber incident affecting IT systems

West Virginia’s state legislature is responding to a cyberattack that has taken down its website and impacted IT systems.

Ann Ali, deputy chief of staff for the House of Delegates, told Recorded Future News that the attack started on Thursday and has continued through Friday.

“Upon discovery, the relevant teams immediately took steps to contain the incident and began an investigation with the help of outside cybersecurity specialists,” Ali said.

“In connection with the investigation, access to certain Legislature IT systems has been temporarily disabled. However, based on what we know so far, the incident appears to be limited to the Legislature’s computer systems.”

She added that no other state agencies or offices are impacted by the cyberattack. An investigation into the incident is ongoing but Ali did not respond to follow-up questions about whether it was a ransomware attack.

No hacking groups have taken credit as of Friday.

The West Virginia legislature is split between two bodies, a Senate and a House of Delegates with 134 total members representing the state’s 1.7 million residents. Multiple municipalities in the state have dealt with ransomware attacks in recent years, including the cities of Beckley and Westmoreland.

Security research firm Comparitech tracked 132 ransomware attacks on government bodies across the U.S. in the third quarter — a 91% increase compared to Q3 last year. At least 41 of the attacks involved U.S. based municipalities, including a major incident impacting Anne Arundel County in Maryland.

This week alone, residents of South Portland, Maine, lost access to critical city services due to a cyberattack, while Minnesota’s Otter Tail County notified its 61,000 residents of a data breach caused by a ransomware attack in July.

[51] The Record - US companies’ use of Chinese open weight AI draws rebuke from House chairmen
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 20:25:00 GMT
Link: https://therecord.media/chinese-open-weight-AI-use-by-US-companies-house-investigation

[TAM METİN - 542 kelime]
US companies’ use of Chinese open weight AI draws rebuke from House chairmen

A new congressional report focused on how some American companies are embedding China-developed open weight artificial intelligence models into their tech stacks calls the trend alarming and cautions U.S. firms against the practice.

Pointing to how Huawei and ZTE technology quickly found their place in the marketplace and threatened American networks, the new report warns that if China-developed open-weight models are allowed to take root, removing them down the road will take several years and cost taxpayers billions.

Open weight models’ numerical weights and biases are made public for download.

The joint investigative report — produced by the House Homeland Security Committee and the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party — focuses on Airbnb, DoorDash and Cursor coding platform owner Anysphere as examples of companies deploying Chinese open weight models. The companies were using them for customer assistance, coding projects and taking inventory.

None of the firms immediately responded to a request for comment.

Report co-authors Reps. Andrew Garbarino (R-NY) and John Moolenaar (R-NY) drew the 50-page-long report’s findings from hearings, classified briefings, and agency advisories. The lawmakers also received briefings from DoorDash, Airbnb and Anysphere about how they integrated China-developed open-weight models into their consumer platforms, enterprise software and other systems.

“The investigation uncovered risks that American businesses, policymakers, and national security officials can no longer afford to overlook or downplay,” the report said. “While America is investing billions and racing to build ‘Super Intelligence,’ Beijing is using stolen intelligence to close the gap.”

Silicon Valley startups and Fortune 500 companies alike are adopting Chinese open-weight models because they are cheap, easily customized and work well, according to the report.

But those benefits come with significant negatives, the report said, citing federal investigators’ findings showing that Chinese developers “used proxy networks and fraudulent accounts to harvest outputs from American frontier models and replicate their capabilities.”

The report features 12 policy recommendations, including the imperative to build an American open-weight AI initiative, establish a standard for where models are sourced from, create an AI bill of materials, bar China-developed models from federal contract work and sensitive critical infrastructure functions and evaluate Chinese models systematically.

The report is important because it identifies and explains the risks posed by the U.S. not competing seriously in the low cost open-source model marketplace, according to Mark Montgomery, a cybersecurity expert at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies.

Because China is more limited in the frontier model space — dominated by U.S. firms such as Anthropic and OpenAI — its leaders have pursued a strategy to expand global dependence on their open-source AI, using the “traditional Chinese model of state policy and capital” to kill competition, he said.

“Companies and utilities, driven by bottom line resource decisions will, as always, ignore security and safety issues in pursuit of a lower front end cost,” he said. “China knows this recipe well.”

Container Store restores systems after cyberattack

The Container Store on Friday said it is recovering from a cyberattack that forced it to shut down its online ordering systems and limited in-store transaction processing.

The firm’s parent company, Neighborhood Intelligence, said in a statement that The Container Store has “restored its website and systems following a cybersecurity incident this past weekend.” Neighborhood Intelligence — a rebrand of Bed Bath & Beyond — purchased The Container Store in July for $150 million.

While the stores remained open throughout the week, they had to use “alternative transaction-processing procedures,” according to the statement. The Texas-founded company has about 100 stores across the U.S.

Neighborhood Intelligence said the incident only impacted The Container Store and did not affect its other brands including Bed Bath & Beyond, Overstock, buybuy BABY or Kirkland’s. Neighborhood Intelligence reported $509 million in revenue for the third quarter earlier this month, with the increases driven primarily by the acquisition of The Container Store.

The company said it hired cybersecurity experts to contain the incident and restore the affected systems. So far, it does not appear the hackers stole customer financial data, but did not address claims made by the cybercriminal group n0n, which listed the company on its leak site earlier this month.

The n0n cybercriminal group emerged in September, and cybersecurity experts say they specialize in ransomware and data extortion. The group has attacked more than 100 victim organizations and demanded hundreds of millions of dollars in ransoms.

The group initially forced victims to pay a 10% fee just to access its negotiation portal, but now forces companies to pay the full ransom before viewing any sample of the stolen information, according to SOCradar.

Allan Liska, a ransomware expert at Recorded Future, said the group launched its data leak site in late September and tried to recruit affiliates on a Russian cybercrime forum called RehubcomPro Forum in late October.

Liska said the group’s cybercriminal post claimed affiliates were instructed to only target companies that earn more than $10 million annually in revenue and were banned from attacking organizations in the Commonwealth of Independent States. The Record is an independent unit of Recorded Future.

Cybersecurity firm LevelBlue said the group has primarily targeted healthcare and pharmaceuticals but recently claimed to have troves of data from financial services companies and retail firms.

LevelBlue noted that the group has used an AI coding agent and paid AI services to write and debug its attack scripts, helping it scale operations quickly.
