[53] The Record - Amazon says Chinese hackers used Cairn AI tool to discover apparent zero-day during attack on university
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 17:30:00 GMT
Link: https://therecord.media/amazon-research-cairn-ai-university-attacks-possible-zero-day

[TAM METİN - 825 kelime]
Amazon says Chinese hackers used Cairn AI tool to discover apparent zero-day during attack on university

Chinese hackers used an AI tool called Cairn to allegedly discover a zero-day while breaching several universities in Asia, according to a new report from Amazon’s Threat Intelligence team.

CJ Moses, CISO of Amazon Integrated Security, said their investigation began on September 10, when they discovered a publicly accessible server with a publicly hosted instance of Cairn — an open-source autonomous AI penetration-testing framework.

They were able to view the operational history of the platform, including previous prompts and more. The operator wrote their prompts in Simplified Chinese and the timestamps were configured to China Standard Time. The targeted victim organizations were universities in East Asia.

Moses explained that Cairn is ideal for attackers because, when given a starting point and objective in plain language, it can coordinate multiple AI agents to complete a task.

In this incident, the attacker provided IP addresses and asked Cairn to “obtain shell access” — meaning find a way to gain enough access to a system for various actions to be taken.

“Based on those inputs, the AI agents planned, executed, and adjusted their approach as they learned, without the operator choosing each next step,” Moses said.

One of the attempts involved 148 actions taken over 16 hours that were ultimately unsuccessful, including a failed attempt at exploiting the Log4Shell vulnerability. Another failed effort saw Cairn try for more than six hours to breach university servers by testing more than 30,000 credential combinations tied to 80 real usernames.

The only successful attempt occurred when the agents discovered a vulnerability in an open-source medical imaging AI application and exploited it.

“At the time of discovery, this path traversal vulnerability in the medical imaging application did not correspond to any assigned security advisory and was unpatched,” Moses said.

“Amazon Threat Intelligence assesses with high confidence that it was a zero-day based on the absence of any corresponding fix, issue, advisory, or prior mention in vulnerability databases for the affected open-source project.”

The attacker then used the same apparent zero-day to breach a second university.

Moses said Amazon Threat Intelligence contacted the maintainers behind the open-source medical imaging AI application and they fixed the bug that was discovered.

He added that AWS “worked with a government partner to notify the organizations about the activity.” AWS declined to name the universities or the country they are in.

Moses said the campaign stood out because of the speed and operational tempo of the AI agents.

An agent that discovers and exploits a zero-day in minutes “completes its activity faster than many security operations centers can manually triage an alert,” Moses warned, noting that the agents “ran continuously for 16 hours without breaks, sleep, or working-hour constraints.”

Cybersecurity researchers and law enforcement agencies have released multiple warnings in recent weeks about AI-backed offensive cyber tools that are being used by attackers, particularly those from China.

The FBI published an advisory about AI tool Artex one week ago, writing that it could take any large language model and turn it into a powerful hacking tool that can “automate multiple phases of cyber intrusions at machine speed, from reconnaissance through data exfiltration.”

Artex was implicated in multiple attacks on South Korean and Japanese financial institutions while Microsoft said Artex was used by Chinese state-backed actors in a recent supply chain attack on IT management software company ConnectWise. Moses said last week that Artex was seen used in credential theft attacks on AI models and in campaigns targeting crypto exchanges.

Cairn was also spotlighted by Google researchers on Tuesday in a report about the evolving use of autonomous multi-agent offensive frameworks like Artex, CyberStrikeAI, PentAGI and others.

Google noted that it saw Cairn used in intrusions of companies in the U.S. aerospace sector and wrote, like AWS found, that it was adept at starting with a target’s IP address and ending with an operational objective.

The AWS report on Cairn cites a study released in September by cybersecurity firm Gambit Security that documented the use of Cairn by a financially motivated hacking group using the tool to breach online retailers.

Eyal Sela, Director of Threat Intelligence at Gambit Security and the researcher behind the report, told Recorded Future News that Cairn is more significant than Artex because it is a general-purpose tool.

“While it is good at solving ‘red team’ or capture-the-flag tasks, it can also solve other problems and the main point is that it has no internal structuring for cybersecurity,” Sela said.

“When a tool is more generic, it is less predictable because it has less structuring around the way it solves a task.”

[55] Unit 42 - Dialing for Data: Inside the Com’s High-Profile Heists
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 22:00:25 +0000
Link: https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/com-affiliate-vishing-attacks/

[TAM METİN - 2689 kelime]
Threat Research Center

Dialing for Data: Inside the Com’s High-Profile Heists

Published:November 20, 2026

Categories:CybercrimeThreat Research

Tags:Bling LibraBrowser extensionExtortionSocial engineeringVishing

Unit 42 has tracked and responded to numerous waves of vishing attacks conducted by Com-affiliated threat actors in recent months. The attacks have led to data theft and extortion attempts. This activity has targeted data-rich industries, such as financial services, healthcare and legal services. Targeted organizations were primarily located in the U.S., UK and Australia.

Attribution for this broad activity includes:

Named actors such as Bling Libra (aka ShinyHunters)

Activity clusters CL-CRI-1116 (aka Redact, formerly BlackFile), CL-CRI-1147 (aka Pink), CL-CRI-1182 (aka Falcon), CL-CRI-1192 (aka Helix)

The newly uncovered CL-CRI-1264 (aka Vortex) and CL-CRI-1274 (aka Cinder), which overlap with activity Google tracks as UNC6671

This article details:

Our observations of persistent Com-affiliated threat activity since August 2026 based on unique telemetry analysis and incident response engagements

The different named actors and activity clusters we track, including unique observations not previously disclosed

Insights on victimology

Review of attacker tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs)

Allusions to future activity as we head into 2027

Palo Alto Networks customers are better protected from the threats discussed above through the following products and services:

Advanced URL Filtering, Advanced DNS Security and Advanced IP Defense

Cortex Agentic Endpoint Security

Idira Identity and Access Management (IAM)

Idira Identity Threat Detection and Response (ITDR)

Idira Secure Web Sessions (SWS)

Organizations can access tailored adversary intelligence, direct analyst consultations, and specialized exposure tracking through Unit 42 Threat Intel Services and its Deep and Dark Web Service.

If you think you might have been compromised or have an urgent matter, contact the Unit 42 Incident Response team.

Since early 2026, we have responded to numerous data theft and extortion attempts that we have attributed to Bling Libra and other Com-affiliated threat actors. More details on the typical playbook used by the attackers can be found in the Tactics, Techniques and Procedures section of this article.

We track these activities using the threat group and activity cluster naming conventions, which are noted in Table 1.

Table 1. Differentiation of Com-affiliated named actors and activity clusters.

Emerging Activity Cluster CL-CRI-1264 (Vortex)

In September 2026, we identified a new activity cluster that we track as CL-CRI-1264. The tradecraft used by the attackers largely follows the wider playbook used by Com-affiliated threat actors, but a few traits set it apart. Most notably, we observed this activity primarily targeting healthcare, pharmaceutical and other medical organizations.

Attackers associated with CL-CRI-1264 establish initial access through vishing, where they pose as internal IT support and direct employees to servers using subdomains tailored to each targeted organization. These servers act as adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) proxies that pass user credentials and multi-factor authentication (MFA) approvals to the attackers in real time. Attackers have targeted employees on both their corporate workstations and personal mobile devices.

We have observed attackers behind CL-CRI-1264 enrolling an unauthorized MFA device within minutes of authenticating to establish persistence. In multiple instances, the attackers have reused a single device named Pixel 10a across compromised accounts. They have also automated data exfiltration using Python scripts (python-httpx User Agent) to target Microsoft 365 mailbox, OneDrive and SharePoint content.

Following exfiltration, the attackers have sent Microsoft Teams messages directly to employees at victim organizations, claiming data theft and directing recipients to a Tor-hosted negotiation site.

Emerging Activity Cluster CL-CRI-1274 (Cinder)

In September 2026, we identified another new activity cluster that we track as CL-CRI-1274. Similar to other activity detailed throughout this report, the attackers used vishing for initial access and avoided re-prompting for Duo MFA by replaying a persistent “keep me signed in” session token. They then replayed that same session token from proxy infrastructure.

From there, they used scripted access through python-requests (python-requests/2.34.2) and the Microsoft Graph software development kit (SDK) to collect and exfiltrate data from the victim’s SharePoint and OneDrive environments. Afterwards, the attackers used a compromised account to send extortion messages internally via email and Microsoft Teams, ultimately directing recipients to a Tor-hosted negotiation site.

Malicious Browser Extension

During an investigation attributed to another activity cluster, CL-CRI-1192 (which Google tracks under UNC6671), we identified a malicious browser extension (manifest version 1.6.111) named Google Chrome.

The extension was not on the Chrome Web Store. It was downloaded from an attacker-controlled server at oskeysetup[.]com and required the victim to manually sideload it using Developer Mode. Naming the extension Google Chrome helps disguise the browser's built-in warning banner (Google Chrome started debugging this browser) when the extension is active.

This domain's registration information closely resembles attacker infrastructure previously disclosed by Google and ReliaQuest in relation to the activity that we track as CL-CRI-1192.

This browser extension performs several malicious actions:

Installs global keyloggers

Steals local/session storage and IndexedDB data across all sites

Scans pages for QR codes to capture login/MFA tokens

Furthermore, this browser extension implements a full command-and-control (C2) remote control module via Chrome DevTools Protocol (chrome.debugger). It allows operators to perform the following activities:

Capture hidden screenshots

Dispatch input events

Steal clipboard contents

Allow remote site navigation

We pivoted on this file and identified an additional browser extension also masquerading as Google Chrome (version 1.6.112) that communicates with the same C2 server. Both files share the same hard-coded API key.

We assess with moderate confidence that the attackers associated with CL-CRI-1192 developed this malicious browser extension as an alternative method to extract credentials from desktop and laptop devices running Chromium-based browsers such as Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge. The extension might also be shared with and used by other Com-affiliated attackers, although we currently have no evidence to suggest this.

We recognize Kevin Pham for his detailed investigation into this browser extension in a September 2026 write-up.

Our telemetry shows sustained campaigns by Com-affiliated threat actors accelerating significantly around August 2026. The victims share a common profile: they hold large volumes of high-impact corporate data where exposure carries severe regulatory, legal or market consequences. Financial services, healthcare and legal organizations were primary targets, though activity spans across other industries.

Rather than targeting generic mailboxes, actors systematically sought individuals or systems responsible for high-value files, documents and databases. These attacks focused on:

Legal and corporate strategy: Actors targeted partner communications, firm strategy, executive compensation and pending contracts. They explicitly threatened to publish client agreements and confidential casework.

Financial and investment records: Attackers prioritized private investment portfolios, deal pipelines and large-scale cloud data warehouses. They occasionally exfiltrated tens of millions of customer relationship management (CRM) and recruiting records.

Healthcare and life sciences: Attackers targeted cloud data platforms containing patient records and proprietary research. To maximize pressure, actors broadcast extortion notices across internal chat channels and threatened regulatory reporting.

The most targeted organizations have distributed workforces, centralized single sign-on (SSO) and extensive cloud collaboration platforms. They are also predominantly based in English-speaking countries. We have observed actors repeatedly targeting the same organization, sometimes returning weeks after a failed attempt.

Who Is Being Targeted: Industries and Countries

Our monitoring of domains linked to Com-related activity showed that their targeting shifted from financial services to healthcare in early September 2026. Figure 1 shows that these attackers targeted financial services organizations about twice as often as healthcare organizations in August 2026, but healthcare overtook financial services in September, around when we first observed CL-CRI-1264 activity. Healthcare continued to be the most targeted industry in October 2026, alongside financial services. Attackers also frequently targeted construction, high technology and transportation and logistics organizations.

Figure 2 shows that between August and October 2026, most targeted organizations were based in the U.S. However, we observed increased targeting of Australian organizations beginning in late September 2026. Australian organizations made up less than 1% of observed subdomains in August and September, rising to about 13% in October. Organizations in Australia are now the second most targeted.

Tactics, Techniques and Procedures

Infrastructure and Tooling

A key characteristic of Com-affiliated threat actors is their use of apex domains that pose as SSO portals, IT support pages and passkey configuration services. These domains often host short-lived subdomains that impersonate target organizations, such as {company}.mfaregister[.]com. We actively track this infrastructure, conduct threat hunting for identified domains and publish key findings as Timely Threat Intelligence (TTI) in our GitHub repository.

Across Com-affiliated cases, we have identified similarities in hosting infrastructure, attack chains and victimology. In some cases, these actors also share tooling, such as Doko's Panel, an operator-controlled AiTM phishing kit.

As previously reported by Push Security, some Okta-targeting variants of the kit replace the panel's default backend.php handler with the renamed endpoint api_FyekIDWY.php. We observed this endpoint on multiple domains associated with Com-affiliated cases.

In at least one financial services case, telemetry recorded a full AiTM sequence from credential entry to an MFA number-match prompt, indicating a likely successful session capture, as shown in Figure 3.

Domains consistent with Com-affiliated infrastructure have also been observed in campaigns that use different techniques to target victims. For example, Microsoft reported oskeyregister[.]com in its research into passkey-themed social engineering.

Building on this reporting, we identified Cloudflare Pages URLs following the pattern connect-pages-{company}.pages[.]dev that redirect to company-specific subdomains such as {company}.oskeyregister[.]com. These findings reflect the broader Com ecosystem, which comprises several activity clusters that frequently share infrastructure but can vary slightly in their tradecraft.

Beyond shared infrastructure, recurring patterns in the registration and deployment of tooling associated with Com-affiliated threat actors provide additional opportunities to identify related domains. Table 2 shows common registration patterns observed across this activity.

mfapasskeysetup[.]com

Table 2. Infrastructure registration patterns used by Com-affiliated threat actors.

We did not observe a standard playbook employed by Com-affiliated threat actors. Rather than employing custom tools, the threat actors primarily leveraged native cloud utilities and selectively limited executions and persistence deployments.

Intrusions typically begin with vishing, in which threat actors pose as IT staff resolving an authentication issue and direct the victim to a phishing page tailored to their organization. After the AiTM kit captures credentials and session tokens, the attackers quickly enroll their own MFA devices, misuse cloud utilities and, in some cases, deploy malicious browser extensions to exfiltrate data and extort victims.

Using the harvested authentication data, Com-affiliated threat actors authenticate to victim environments, typically routing through residential proxy networks and commercial VPNs. They then seek to establish multi-layered persistence, enumerate sensitive data and exfiltrate data from cloud platforms. We observed the following techniques across Com-affiliated threat actors:

Enrolling unauthorized MFA devices and workstation objects

Generating cloud infrastructure temporary credentials

Authorizing unapproved third-party OAuth applications or data-sync utilities

Staging secondary accounts or harvesting redundant credentials

Discovery and Defense Evasion

Monitoring authentications, permissions and mailboxes

Modifying calendar settings and mailbox rules

Clearing security alert events

Rotating infrastructure

Using open-source tools such as Rclone and cloud storage platforms

Exfiltrating via native SaaS and REST APIs or scripted HTTP-based exfiltration

Moving data via SaaS to SaaS transfers

Earlier this year, our 2026 Unit 42 Global Incident Response Report found that extortion incidents in 2025 not using encryption (at 78%) dropped below the 90% range for the first time in several years. This trend has continued into 2026 and we don’t expect a slowdown. Cybercriminals like Bling Libra and other Com-affiliated threat actors are pivoting away from encryption, enabling them to move at greater speed across their intrusion lifecycle while still achieving their objectives.

Another plausible motivation for the shift away from using encryption is to fly below the radar of law enforcement officials, given their crackdown on ransomware operators in recent years. However, shifting away from using encryption no longer seems to be enough to keep them under the radar. This is based on the reported arrests of suspected Bling Libra members such as “Rey” and “Umbreon” that occurred in proximity to the group’s claims of a breach of the FBI.

Recent arrests also include a person who allegedly ran Bling Libra’s extortion site.

Going forward, organizations must:

Tighten help desk verification processes

Transition to phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2/passkeys)

Implement browser extension allowlists

Establish visibility into identity actions

Alert on unauthorized data exports to mitigate the threat activity described in this article

Idira Identity and Access Management (IAM) can help enable secure, unified access across human, machine, and AI identities, balancing granular control with a seamless user experience. Powered by SSO, phishing-resistant MFA, passwordless login, and enterprise password management, Idira IAM extends intelligent privilege controls and session security across the broader workforce.

Idira Identity Threat Detection and Response (ITDR) can help enable security teams to counter identity-based attacks targeting Idira Next Generation Identity (NGI) Platform and the identities it secures. Using near real-time detection, powered by CORA AI, and leveraging Idira’s visibility across multiple contexts (like PAM, authentication, SSO, cloud, endpoints, browsers, and more), Idira ITP can apply automated, tailored non-disruptive in-session response to contain and minimize potential identity-based threats.

Idira Secure Web Sessions (SWS) is designed to provide client-side protection (blocking clipboards/downloads) and step-by-step audit logging for highly sensitive SaaS application sessions.

Organizations can access tailored adversary intelligence, direct analyst consultations, and specialized exposure tracking through Unit 42 Threat Intel Services and its Deep and Dark Web Service.

[56] Microsoft Security - Microsoft named a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for SIEM
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 17:00:00 +0000
Link: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/11/20/microsoft-named-a-leader-in-the-2026-gartner-magic-quadrant-for-siem/

[TAM METİN - 757 kelime]
We’re honored that Microsoft has once again been recognized as a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Security Information and Event Management (SIEM).

As security environments grow more complex and attackers move faster, organizations need more than the ability to collect and analyze data. They need comprehensive visibility, context to understand what is happening, and the ability to act before an attack causes further damage.

Comprehensive SIEM across the digital estate

Microsoft Sentinel is our cloud-native SIEM, bringing together security data, advanced analytics, automation, and threat intelligence to help organizations protect their digital estate.

With more than 500 connectors across Microsoft and third-party solutions, Microsoft Sentinel brings together signals from across complex, multicloud environments. Its rich library of out-of-the-box detections, informed by Microsoft’s threat intelligence and organizational context, helps defenders identify sophisticated threats without building every detection from scratch.

Microsoft Sentinel supports the core capabilities security teams depend on, from scalable security data management and advanced detection to threat hunting, investigation, and response. The Microsoft Sentinel data lake centralizes historical and real-time security data across platforms and clouds for cost-effective retention and advanced analytics at scale. Security operations center (SOC) optimization and cost management help teams improve coverage, identify detection gaps, and make informed decisions about the data they collect and retain.

Reimagining security operations for the agentic era

On September 23, 2026, Microsoft introduced the Integrated Security Operations Center (ISOC) in Microsoft Defender, reimagining security operations for the agentic era. As threats grow more sophisticated and security environments more complex, traditional approaches built on disconnected tools and workflows can no longer keep pace. ISOC brings security operations and threat protection together, creating a unified foundation where people and AI agents can see, understand, and act across the environment.

Through deep integration with Microsoft Sentinel, ISOC combines the full breadth of SIEM capabilities with extended detection and response (XDR), threat intelligence, posture management, and response. By connecting signals from Microsoft and third-party environments with rich security context and coordinated action, ISOC enables security teams to move beyond fragmented investigations toward faster, more proactive protection. Rather than operating as separate tools, the security stack works as one system, providing the foundation for agentic security.

Attack disruption demonstrates what this integrated approach makes possible. Microsoft Defender correlates signals across Microsoft and third-party environments with threat intelligence to identify high-confidence attacks in progress and automatically contain compromised users and devices before threats spread. This includes ransomware, business email compromise, and adversary-in-the-middle attacks. Across customers, ransomware attacks are disrupted in just 30 seconds on average.

Together, these capabilities demonstrate how Microsoft is moving security operations beyond detection and response toward an integrated, agentic approach that helps organizations anticipate, investigate, and stop threats faster.

A shared foundation for people and agents

AI is becoming part of how security teams work every day. Microsoft Sentinel combines advanced analytics, machine learning, and automation to help analysts use natural language to hunt for threats, generate response playbooks, support alert triage, analyze complex signals, and accelerate investigations. These capabilities reduce manual work and give defenders more time to focus on the threats and decisions that matter most.

By enabling SIEM and native protection to operate as one system, ISOC gives people and AI agents a shared foundation to see, understand, and act across the environment. Agents bring speed and scale to continuous security operations, while people provide expertise, judgment, and accountability.

Together, they can move beyond traditional, linear workflows toward continuous detection, investigation, and attack disruption. As agents take on more security operations workflows, comprehensive data, and rich context, the ability to act becomes even more important to helping organizations stop threats faster and deliver better security outcomes.

The future of SIEM is about more than managing security data. It’s about ensuring your SIEM is a core building block of the agentic SOC, bringing together security data, intelligence, AI, and native protection so people and agents can understand threats sooner, act faster, and stop attacks before they spread.

We’ll continue investing in the comprehensive SIEM capabilities customers rely on while advancing integrated, agentic security operations in Microsoft Defender. We’re grateful for the Gartner recognition and for the customers, partners, and security community whose feedback continues to shape Microsoft Sentinel.

[64] Industrial Cyber - Equinor thwarts cyberattack as separate intrusion at Skagerak Energi raises concerns across Norway’s energy sector
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 12:58:22 +0000
Link: https://industrialcyber.co/utilities-energy-power-water-waste/equinor-thwarts-cyberattack-as-separate-intrusion-at-skagerak-energi-raises-concerns-across-norways-energy-sector/

[TAM METİN - 1055 kelime]
Equinor thwarts cyberattack as separate intrusion at Skagerak Energi raises concerns across Norway’s energy sector

Norwegian energy major Equinor said Friday that the cyberattack it detected on its IT systems earlier in the week has been stopped, with production running as normal and no indication that data was stolen or altered. The announcement closes a four-day episode that began Nov. 17 and drew in a second Norwegian energy company, Skagerak Energi, which disclosed on Nov. 18 that outsiders had broken into some of its own IT systems. Skagerak said operations and production were unaffected and that there was no sign of information leaking, and it has notified the Norwegian Water Resources and Energy Directorate (NVE), KraftCERT, and the National Security Authority (NSM).

Unlike Equinor, Skagerak has not said the attack has been stopped, though on Thursday it said that it had taken the necessary measures and was still handling the incident.

Equinor first disclosed the incident on the evening of Nov. 17, saying it had detected an ongoing attack against certain IT systems and had mobilized resources to neutralize it and regain full system integrity. The company said then that operations and production were not affected and that relevant authorities were being informed.

By Nov. 18, Equinor said it had a clearer understanding of how the attack was carried out and which systems were affected. It stressed that the incident was not a virus attack, so there was no risk of it spreading, and that employees, partners, and suppliers showed no signs of impact. The company said the work to neutralize the attack and restore the affected systems was continuing in dialogue with national security authorities, though it was too early to say how long that would take.

However, in its Nov. 19 update, Equinor confirmed the attack was still ongoing and said restoring full integrity to the affected systems was still under way. It also noted that the attack did not appear to be specifically targeting the company, and that it was in continuous contact with the relevant national security authorities and had reported the matter to the police.

Then, at 08:55 CET on Nov. 20, the company confirmed the attack had been stopped, reiterating that production was normal and that there was no indication of negative consequences for employees, partners, or suppliers.

Equinor has not shared the nature of the attack, the systems affected, the actor behind it, or measures adopted to stop it.

On the Skagerak side, spokesperson Kjell Løyland told Energiteknikk that the company is routinely probed by outsiders, but that in this case someone had “come a bit further,” which the company takes seriously. He said the company had not notified the police, declined to comment on who was behind the attack, and said Skagerak is reserved about details of its IT systems.

Whether the two incidents are linked is unclear. Dark Reading noted that the disclosures read similarly and came within a day of each other, but reported no evidence yet that they are connected.

However, Equinor’s remark that its attack did not appear to target it specifically leaves open the possibility of a wider campaign, though neither company has said so, and the attack vector, actor type, and motivation all remain unknown in public reporting.

Other players in the sector are taking precautions. Aker BP said it has mobilized its emergency preparedness and strengthened monitoring, while Statkraft said it is closely monitoring the situation.

For now, both companies describe the damage as confined to IT, with operational technology and production untouched. That is the outcome every energy operator aims for, but the public statements do not explain whether segmentation held against an attacker who tried to go further or whether the intruders never got close to the plant floor. With the Equinor attack contained, Skagerak still working through its response, and the attribution questions unanswered, Norway’s energy sector is likely to stay on heightened watch in the weeks ahead.

Commenting on the recent incidents, John Strand, owner at Black Hills Information Security, wrote in an emailed statement that attackers clearly have absolutely no problem targeting the critical infrastructure of nation-states. “Whether we’re talking about power generation, healthcare, water treatment, transportation, or communications, nothing should be considered off-limits from an attacker’s perspective.”

“Every country and every organization responsible for critical infrastructure needs to be operating at the absolute highest level of vigilance right now. Just look at the current geopolitical situation around the world and then couple that with the emergence of agentic AI attack capabilities,” Strand said. “We’re seeing technology that can dramatically accelerate reconnaissance, vulnerability discovery, and exploitation, potentially allowing attackers to operate at a speed and scale that would have been incredibly difficult just a few years ago.”

He added, “When you combine those capabilities with geopolitical tensions and the willingness of attackers to target essential services, you have a situation that should make everyone responsible for critical infrastructure security extremely uncomfortable. We cannot afford to assume that these systems are somehow going to be spared simply because of how important they are to society.”

Prayukth K V identified in a Shieldworkz post that the more significant issue is the exposure of a major energy operator’s enterprise environment and potential consequences if an IT compromise affects the systems, personnel and processes that support industrial operations.

“Such incidents can slow down enterprises, impact operations and keep personnel occupied. When geopolitical actors activate the hybrid warfare playbook, such incidents can serve to keep strategic workforce tied up while threat actors carry out other attacks or intrusions,” he wrote in the blog post. “For energy companies, enterprise IT is not operationally irrelevant simply because it is separated from control systems. Corporate identity, engineering information, maintenance planning, procurement, logistics, contractor coordination and operational reporting can all contribute to the reliable management of industrial assets.”

The attacks on the Norwegian energy sector come as French and U.S. authorities suspect Iran, specifically the SHAHID KAVEH cyber offensive unit affiliated with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, was behind the overnight Oct. 11–12, 2026 cyberattacks on supermarket refrigeration controllers across Europe, affecting roughly 700 stores. The campaign exploited vulnerabilities in refrigeration control software and legacy systems, including Danfoss and Copeland/Dixell XWEB equipment, to raise temperatures, extend defrost cycles, spoil food, and cause equipment failures and tens of millions of euros or dollars in damage.

[65] Industrial Cyber - Federal cybersecurity gaps leave US food supply vulnerable to ransomware and operational disruptions, GAO warns
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 10:55:29 +0000
Link: https://industrialcyber.co/reports/federal-cybersecurity-gaps-leave-us-food-supply-vulnerable-to-ransomware-and-operational-disruptions-gao-warns/

[TAM METİN - 1899 kelime]
Federal cybersecurity gaps leave US food supply vulnerable to ransomware and operational disruptions, GAO warns

The U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) identified that federal efforts to strengthen cybersecurity across the food and agriculture sector remain incomplete, leaving gaps in information sharing and emergency preparedness despite growing risks to the nation’s food supply. It said the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) and the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) had met most cybersecurity-related requirements under the fiscal year 2021 National Defense Authorization Act, but only partially met or failed to meet five requirements. The GAO warned that staffing and resource constraints have created gaps in how the agencies share cyber threats and vulnerabilities, leaving the food supply vulnerable to attacks that could disrupt production and distribution, create unsafe conditions, and erode public confidence.

In its ‘Critical Infrastructure Protection: Further Action Needed to Enhance Cybersecurity of the Food and Agriculture Sector’ report published Thursday, GAO cited the 2021 ransomware attack on a global meat processing company that shut down some of the world’s largest slaughterhouses and contributed to meat shortages in the U.S. and other countries.

GAO reported increased use of technologies to produce food and agricultural products has introduced new potential vulnerabilities into the sector that can be exploited if adequate controls have not been put into place. “For example, failure to implement basic security measures, such as changing default passwords, can be exploited by threat actors. The threat actor could then manipulate data related to food quality, contamination testing, or traceability, potentially resulting in the distribution of unsafe or contaminated food products. This, in turn, can pose significant public health risks that could trigger product recalls and damage the reputation of food producers and suppliers.”

As another example, it also noted that farmers use GPS-guided tractors and real-time soil sensors to improve efficiency, but these technologies can have cybersecurity vulnerabilities when connected to the internet. A cyberattack that takes advantage of these weaknesses, such as by compromising credentials, can then threaten production, leading to food supply chain disruptions. While not every disruption on a farm will lead to supply chain disruption, if a threat actor compromised enough GPS-guided tractors and their data at the same time, it could potentially lead to a disruption of the food supply chain.

Further, while small-scale attacks may only have limited impact, large-scale attacks or those targeting one or two key facilities could carry the potential for hunger and economic devastation across different geographical areas, spanning from local to international levels.

Additionally, cybersecurity attacks can impact processing of food and agricultural products in a way that may cause financial consequences to the victim company. For example, the Food and Ag-ISAC reported in 2024 that a ransomware attack could impact or disrupt processes along agriculture production lines, such as seed production. Any downtime because of an attack could then lead to a chain reaction of delays, potentially causing late planting or harvesting windows. This delay could require crops to be moved to other regions with an active growing season, which is typically only done in cases of severe weather conditions such as flooding.

Ransomware has been the most commonly reported cyberattack type in the food and agriculture (FA) sector since 2021, with the Food and Ag-ISAC recording 167 ransomware incidents in 2023, 206 in 2024, and 295 in 2025. In August 2026, the Food and Ag-ISAC reported 227 ransomware incidents through July 2026 and noted that 2026 is on pace to be one of the highest-volume ransomware years on record for the sector. Most reported attacks sought ransom payments by shutting down food production and distribution systems across small and large companies as well as farms.

While USDA, FDA, and DHS’s 2024 draft sector risk assessment identified cybersecurity incidents and supply chain disruption as top sector concerns, USDA and FDA’s 2024 draft risk management plan noted that owners and operators struggle to accurately assess facility-level threat likelihood, complicating security prioritization and preparation.

The true volume and impact of FA sector cybersecurity incidents extend beyond voluntary public reports, as USDA and FDA lack authority to require sector-wide reporting and have no established voluntary incident-reporting mechanisms, while the Food and Ag-ISAC relies on voluntary member submissions, partner sharing, and open-source reporting, and CISA offers a voluntary reporting mechanism.

Publicly reported attacks between 2021 and 2026, most frequently involving ransomware and business email compromise, have caused costly operational and supply disruptions. Examples include a January 2021 U.S. farm attack via compromised administrator credentials that caused a $9 million production loss; a May 2021 ransomware attack on meat processor JBS that forced slaughterhouse shutdowns in the U.S. and abroad, caused meat supply shortages and a 25% meat price spike, and led to an $11 million bitcoin ransom payment; and a February 2022 business email compromise using nearly identical email domains and real employee names that cost a food manufacturer $600,000 in milk powder and non-fat dry milk.

Additional reported incidents include a March 2022 ransomware attack on a multi-state grain company that disrupted grain processing, seed, fertilizer, and logistics during spring planting preparations; an April 2022 business email compromise impersonating a food company and using a supplier president’s name and a nearly identical email address to cause a $100,000 whole milk powder loss; and a May 2022 ransomware and data exfiltration campaign targeting farming equipment maker AGCO’s websites and U.S. provider sites, halting operations for about two weeks including a tractor assembly facility.

Later examples include an August 2022 business email compromise using a distributor CFO’s name to place a fake order for two truckloads of powdered milk, costing a multinational snack food and beverage company $160,000; a February 2023 ransomware attack on Dole’s legacy servers and end-user computers that shut down production plants, disrupted U.S. grocery supplies, and cost $10.5 million; an April 2023 attack exploiting default passwords and other vulnerabilities in Jordan Valley farm irrigation controllers and Galil Sewage Corporation wastewater treatment controls, damaging controllers on systems not switched from remote to manual operation; and a July 2026 ransomware intrusion into Fairlife’s systems, including production systems, prompting production halts at U.S. plants during a Coca-Cola investigation.

GAO issued five recommendations, three to the Department of Health and Human Services and two to USDA, urging both agencies to fully implement information-sharing and emergency preparedness requirements and assess whether resources should be reprioritized or additional funding requested. HHS agreed with its recommendations, while USDA disagreed with its two recommendations. GAO maintained that all five recommendations are warranted.

The GAO review found that USDA and FDA met most of their cybersecurity responsibilities, though with gaps tied to stalled federal reviews and thin real-time visibility. On sector coordination, the agencies met all three requirements: they serve as day-to-day federal interfaces through joint sector meetings, chair the Government Coordinating Council, and sit on the Federal Senior Leadership Council. They also work with CISA on fact sheets, alerts and advisories.

On risk management, both requirements were met, even though the draft Food and Agriculture Sector Risk Management Plan, submitted to the National Security Council and CISA in early January 2025, remains unfinalized. USDA has received no feedback because Executive Order 14239 ordered a review of the underlying memoranda.

The agencies identified other ways of recommending security measures, including the March 2023 120-Day Food and Agriculture Interim Risk Review and a June 2026 advisory, coordinated with CISA, on hardening automatic tank gauge systems. Both risk assessment requirements were also met. The interim review flagged risks from automation, precision farming and digital agriculture; the agencies assessed potential AI risks, and a draft Sector-Specific Risk Assessment 2024 laid out cybersecurity scenarios, though it too is awaiting review because NSM-22 is paused. FDA also feeds sector vulnerability data into DHS’s national risk assessment efforts.

Information sharing was the weak spot, with three of four requirements met and one only partially met. USDA and FDA facilitate exchange through joint meetings, USDA’s biweekly emails (including a February 2026 alerts roundup) and FDA’s website, and they co-authored advisories such as the December 2022 warning on business email compromise used to steal food shipments. They also help identify sector intelligence needs, pass sector input to CISA, and support DHS’s annual reporting.

The partially met requirement concerns giving CISA and the sector awareness of ongoing and real-time threats, vulnerabilities and mitigations. USDA supplied input for CISA’s June 2026 tank gauge advisory and flagged how widely such gauges are used in agricultural facilities, but the co-SRMAs do not give CISA continuous real-time awareness. FDA has no structured mechanism for continuously collecting cybersecurity data and does not track how sector resources are used, so it is unclear how the agencies would receive and relay real-time threat or vulnerability information.

While USDA and FDA met most Sector Risk Management Agency (SRMA) requirements, they reported having limited resources to address critical cybersecurity activities, such as information sharing and cybersecurity emergency preparedness activities. Until USDA and FDA have assessed whether they can reprioritize their resources and staffing, or if they need additional resources to provide more support to meet the SRMA requirements, the FA sector will be more vulnerable to cybersecurity risks and attacks, potentially disrupting the nation’s food and agriculture supply chains and resulting in significant economic and environmental impact.

GAO made five recommendations to strengthen SRMA responsibilities across the two departments, beginning with two directed to the Department of Agriculture. Specifically, the Secretary of Agriculture should ensure that the Director of the Office of Homeland Security fully implements SRMA requirements for sharing cybersecurity threat and vulnerability information with CISA, as well as facilitating or conducting cybersecurity emergency preparedness exercises and simulations. Both recommendations call for assessing whether resources should be reprioritized or requested to continuously collect cyber threat information and carry out these preparedness activities.

The remaining three recommendations are directed to the Department of Health and Human Services, urging the Secretary to ensure that the Director of the Food and Drug Administration’s Office of Coordinated Outbreak Response fully implements key SRMA requirements. Like USDA, the FDA office should fulfill obligations to share cybersecurity threat and vulnerability data with CISA and facilitate or conduct emergency preparedness exercises and simulations, evaluating whether to reprioritize or request resources to support both efforts. Additionally, the Secretary should ensure the FDA office fully implements the SRMA requirement to develop planning documents for coordinated action during cybersecurity disasters or emergencies.

GAO concluded that the food and agriculture sector faces rising cybersecurity threats, with past incidents already costing millions of dollars in lost revenue and disrupting the nation’s food supply chain. The risk is amplified by the sector’s growing reliance on internet-connected technologies for producing, harvesting and storing food, which, when poorly secured, can be used to gain illicit access to systems and launch ransomware or supply chain disruption attacks. The sector’s critical dependencies on several other infrastructure sectors make it all the more important that food and agriculture equipment is as secure as possible.

In response, USDA and FDA, as the sector’s co-SRMAs, have taken steps to improve cybersecurity and have met most SRMA requirements. Both agencies, however, reported limited resources for critical activities, such as information sharing and cybersecurity emergency preparedness. GAO warned that until the agencies assess whether they can reprioritize existing resources and staff, or need additional resources, to better meet the SRMA requirements, the sector will remain more vulnerable to attacks. Such attacks could disrupt food and agriculture supply chains and carry significant economic and environmental consequences.

[66] Industrial Cyber - Intel 471 exposes ransomware groups, IABs targeting manufacturing and automotive supply chains
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 10:52:56 +0000
Link: https://industrialcyber.co/reports/intel-471-exposes-ransomware-groups-iabs-targeting-manufacturing-and-automotive-supply-chains/

[TAM METİN - 1873 kelime]
Intel 471 exposes ransomware groups, IABs targeting manufacturing and automotive supply chains

A new report from Intel 471 disclosed that the manufacturing sector remained a prime target for cybercriminals in 2026, accounting for 1,379 recorded ransomware and data extortion claims, or 16.8% of all monitored victims globally, between January and October. The industrial products and services industry represented 74.2% of the manufacturing claims, followed by chemicals and specialty materials at 11.5%, automotive at 11.3%, and aerospace and defense at 3%. The Qilin, The Gentlemen and Akira ransomware groups were the most active, accounting for 13.6%, 12.9% and 8.4%, respectively, of the monitored manufacturing victims.

The report, ‘From Aerospace to Assembly Lines: How Cybercriminals Are Targeting Manufacturing Supply Chains,’ also found that initial access brokers (IABs) offered unauthorized access affecting 172 manufacturing entities from January to October 2026, representing 10% of the worldwide access offers tracked by Intel 471. Vulnerability exploitation accounted for 25% of the examined access cases, while brute-force attacks represented 16.3%.

Additionally, small and medium-sized manufacturers faced disproportionate pressure, with about 68% of monitored ransomware and data extortion victim claims involving organizations with annual revenues below US$50 million.

Given the sector’s immense economic concentration and zero-tolerance threshold for operational downtime, manufacturing emerges as an exceptionally lucrative target for extortion.

“Interconnecting enterprise IT with plant floor operational technology (OT) has weakened traditional boundary defenses, exposing inherently insecure legacy controllers and assembly systems to enterprise-level threat vectors and lateral movement,” Intel 471 reported. “Financially motivated adversaries actively weaponize this exposure, knowing that halting an assembly or processing line costs millions of dollars per day and creates immense pressure for rapid extortion payouts. Concurrently, the sector’s reliance on multi-tier supply chains introduces critical third-party risk, where a compromise at an interconnected vendor, logistics partner or maintenance contractor provides adversaries with a trusted pivot into core networks or can trigger cascading cross-site operational shutdowns.”

Furthermore, the risk of having high-value IP leaked or auctioned across illicit underground channels exposes proprietary technical data to competitors, irreversibly devalues years of research and development (R&D) investments and provides threat actors with powerful extortion leverage to compel ransom payments. For the manufacturing sector, cybersecurity is not merely a data protection issue, but an existential operational risk

The report identified a key enabler of unauthorized access as the proliferation of IABs (initial access brokers), who are threat actors or groups that specialize in compromising networks via brute-force attacks, malware logs, vulnerability exploits and social engineering. “After gaining a foothold, IABs sell the access on underground channels to other threat actors seeking to carry out further attacks.”

“From Jan. 1 to Oct. 29, 2026, our internal data revealed IABs offered unauthorized access that impacted 172 entities in the manufacturing sector, representing about 10% of all accesses offered worldwide,” Intel 471 disclosed. “Manufacturing was the fifth most targeted sector behind professional services and consulting; public; consumer and industrial products; and technology, media and telecommunications. The five most impacted countries in descending order were the U.S., India, Italy, France and Spain.”

Furthermore, the five most prominent IABs identified during this period were the actors using the Pirat-Networks, Anon-WMG, Tamburino, IntegraGT and Saturned33 handles. Intel 471 categorized 66.8% of this access as wholesale offers involving multiple targets, while the remaining 33.2% was categorized as access to a specified target.

The report also analyzed advertised access targeting organizations operating in the manufacturing sector to understand how adversaries obtained their initial foothold. IABs gained initial access by exploiting vulnerabilities in 25% of the cases we examined, while they used brute-force techniques in 16.3% of cases.

“Actors obtained 10.5% of the advertised access through compromised credentials whose origin was not identified, while information stealers supplied the credentials used to obtain 0.6% of the access,” according to Intel 471. “We could not establish an acquisition method for 47.6%. Although the available information does not describe every compromise in equal detail, it demonstrates that vulnerability exploitation remains a substantial source of access targeting manufacturing organizations, alongside access obtained through credential compromise.”

The researchers assessed that gaps in identifying and remediating vulnerable internet-facing applications may help sustain this supply of access. Delays in applying available patches are one possible contributor, but the researchers could not determine whether a fix was available in each case or how quickly organizations responded.

“Access offers across the manufacturing sector are typically categorized by claimed corporate revenue, administrative permissions, host volume and access type. Analyzing the specific access mechanism is critical, as the compromised technology dictates an adversary’s initial foothold, privilege level and potential lateral reach into production environments,” Intel 471 reported. “While observed entry vectors spanned remote monitoring and management (RMM) utilities such as AnyDesk and BeyondTrust, remote shells deployed on vulnerable edge systems and information stealer-infected endpoints, perimeter remote access accounted for the majority of access listings.”

Also, virtual private network (VPN) services represented the largest share at 28.5% of examined cases, followed by Microsoft Remote Desktop Web Access (RDWeb) at 9.9%, file transfer protocol (FTP) servers at 7.6% and remote desktop protocol (RDP) hosts at 6.4%.

Manufacturing was the most targeted sector in ransomware and data extortion activity during the reporting period, with 1,379 recorded claims, or 16.8% of all monitored victims, according to Intel 471’s tracking of leak sites. Operators either buy access from initial access brokers or break in directly, then widen their foothold to stage extortion demands, often pairing data theft with system encryption, though sometimes skipping the encryption. Victims face downtime and the threat of stolen files going public. Industrial products and services made up 74.2% of the activity, followed by chemicals and specialty materials (11.5%), automotive (11.3%) and aerospace and defense (3%).

The U.S. led in victim counts, ahead of Germany, Canada, Italy and France. The headline-grabbing multimillion-dollar demands against giant corporations tell only part of the story, since the bulk of the damage landed on small and mid-sized manufacturers. Among victims with revenue estimates (about 66% of the total), firms earning $10–50 million were the largest group at 399, followed by 189 in the $5–10 million bracket, while only 66 victims topped $1 billion.

The pattern suggests attackers choose targets by how easy the access is and how little effort the intrusion takes, not by company size. These smaller players often serve as niche component makers and tier suppliers inside tightly woven production chains, bound by strict delivery contracts and often without a dedicated security team. That combination hands extortionists leverage: with downtime unaffordable, many pay mid-tier demands quickly rather than risk halting a supply line.

Automotive threat activity captured by Intel 471 centered on the supply chain. In May 2026, the actor zestix advertised a dataset allegedly exfiltrated from Taiwan-based electronics manufacturer Pegatron Corp., reportedly a key supplier to EV maker Lucid Motors. The offer described 416 unencrypted files totaling about 4.65 GB of engineering specifications and production assets tied mainly to Lucid’s Gravity and Air programs. The actor stressed that the data was technical intellectual property rather than customer records or PII, and framed it for direct use in CAD environments such as SolidWorks and CATIA.

It allegedly included production CAD schematics and board layouts for high-voltage and electronic architectures, among them the Gravity’s AC junction box, center information displays and instrument clusters, along with board-level schematics, Gerber files and pick-and-place data for the telematics control unit and layout files for the SVCU 2.0 module supporting ADAS. It also reportedly held engineering statements of work, preliminary bills of materials, PCBA designs, validation protocols adhering to LV-124 and IPC-A-610 standards, diagnostic statements of work, UDS reprogramming guides, supplier quality documentation and internal cybersecurity specifications.

On Aug. 8, 2026, the SovCali data extortion group listed Lucid Group Inc. on its DLS, and on Aug. 21, 2026, Lucid confirmed in an official statement that one of its vendors had suffered a cybersecurity event. The company said the vendor lacked access to customer databases or systems capable of interfering with vehicle operations or core business functions, that production and retail activities were unaffected, and that it was working with third-party investigators and law enforcement to protect its intellectual property and pursue legal remedies.

Intel 471 noted that a link between zestix and SovCali remains unconfirmed, but said the episode exemplifies the lifecycle of supply chain extortion in modern manufacturing, where an intrusion at an upstream technology supplier gave adversaries immediate access to proprietary design data.

Elsewhere in the sector, the picture was similarly varied. In industrial products and services, Intel 471 examined activity including purported supplier portal compromise, attempted movement into internal systems and ransomware-associated data theft.

In May 2026, Taiwan-based Hon Hai Precision Industry Co. Ltd., doing business as Foxconn, suffered a major breach attributed to the Nitrogen ransomware group. The company acknowledged the incident and said attacks affected several of its manufacturing facilities in North America. The group allegedly exfiltrated 8 TB of data, including internal project documentation, technical drawings and schematics related to multiple billion-dollar clients, and posted samples as proof.

In chemicals and specialty materials, which Intel 471 tracked across manufacturers and distributors, including alleged employee endpoint compromise and attempted sales of corporate network access, the firm reported in October 2026 that the actor Marge was actively recruiting social engineering specialists to obtain initial network access for downstream ransomware operations. That activity was linked to alleged employee endpoint access at Wanhua Chemical.

Intel 471 highlighted the risks posed by interconnected supply chains, where compromises involving vendors, logistics partners, or maintenance contractors can provide attackers with pathways into manufacturing networks and potentially disrupt operations across multiple sites. Deeply integrated supply chains add another opening, since breaching an upstream electronics supplier or engineering contractor yields the design files and operational data needed to extort the downstream enterprise without ever touching the OEM directly.

The report does not expect any major shift in the threat landscape for financially motivated adversaries targeting manufacturers. Attacks on the sector will stay at elevated rates, with extortion campaigns concentrated opportunistically on small and mid-sized manufacturers.

Ransomware and data extortion operators see middle market firms, tied to strict just-in-time production schedules and thin operating margins, as sources of faster, less-resisted payouts. They exploit that fragility through multi-layered extortion, pairing the threat of mounting losses from halted assembly or processing lines with the theft and auctioning of proprietary intellectual property such as CAD schematics, circuit board layouts and specialized chemical formulations. The model is amplified by fragile perimeter architectures and legacy OT environments: IABs and extortion groups routinely exploit exposed perimeter networking appliances, vendor-managed remote access gateways and compromised O&M credentials, and once inside, legacy OT assets that often lack native audit logging, automated patching or modern authentication leave control environments highly exposed.

To counter this, Intel 471 says manufacturers must move beyond perimeter-only defenses toward structural operational decoupling and proactive threat visibility. Industrial enterprises and their suppliers should enforce strict segmentation between corporate IT and plant floor OT, require multifactor authentication on all external vendor access pathways, and place hardware-level compensating controls around unpatchable brownfield controllers.

Cyber threat intelligence programs should extend into underground channels to catch early signs of activity. Incident response playbooks, meanwhile, need to account for third-party supply chain exposure, with enforceable vendor security standards and crisis management protocols designed to sustain minimum viable production during enterprise IT outages.

[67] Industrial Cyber - Texas Cyber Command adds 63 companies to Project Watershed 250 to bolster water utility security
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 10:44:30 +0000
Link: https://industrialcyber.co/utilities-energy-power-water-waste/texas-cyber-command-adds-63-companies-to-project-watershed-250-to-bolster-water-utility-security/

[TAM METİN - 808 kelime]
Texas Cyber Command adds 63 companies to Project Watershed 250 to bolster water utility security

Texas Cyber Command (TXCC) announced that 63 technology and cybersecurity companies have joined Project Watershed 250, a pilot initiative offering cybersecurity services, tools and technical expertise at no cost to Texas water and wastewater utilities. The industry partners are volunteering personnel and resources to strengthen the security and resilience of water infrastructure serving 31 million Texans.

This week’s announcement coincides with the inaugural Billington Critical Infrastructure CyberSecurity Summit in San Antonio, where TXCC Chief TJ White is among the featured speakers. The summit convenes leaders across four lifeline sectors (energy, communications, transportation, and water) on the premise that the systems Americans depend on are interconnected, and so is the work of defending them. Water is Texas’s most precious natural resource; our communities depend on reliable water service.

“Sixty-three companies raising their hands to help defend Texas water systems is a serious commitment from the private industry; it is what we mean at TXCC when we say, ‘Cybersecurity is a shared mission,’” White said in a statement. “Together, we are protecting the water systems that 31 million Texans depend on for their health, their safety, and their livelihood.”

Launched in August by the White House Office of the National Cyber Director in partnership with the Office of the Governor of Texas and TXCC, the initiative connects utilities with cybersecurity assessments, technical assistance, tools and remediation support based on their operational needs and priorities. The initiative targets cybersecurity gaps across Texas’ more than 7,400 public water systems and 3,000 wastewater treatment facilities, which provide essential public health, environmental and economic services but remain attractive targets for cybercriminals and hostile actors.

TXCC said the pilot is designed to support utilities of different operational scales, particularly under-resourced providers that lack the personnel, funding or technical expertise to obtain specialized cybersecurity assistance. The program is intended to establish a scalable framework for critical infrastructure protection, with the potential to serve as a model for other sectors in Texas and other states.

The 63 companies joining the initiative include 202 Group LLC, 4CORE Solutions, Abnormal AI, Akamai Technologies, Amazon Web Services, Applied Security Convergence, Armadin, ASC3ND Technologies Group, Belay Technologies, Booz Allen Hamilton, Breeze IT Services, ByteTrail, Centripetal, Cisco, Claroty Public Sector, Control Infotech, Cloudflare, CPLANE, CrunchAtlas, General Dynamics Information Technology, Deloitte & Touche, Demia, Diligent Innovations, Direnzic Technology, Dispel, Dragos, Elisity, ETK Consultant, Faction Networks, Forescout, Frenos, Galvanick, GB Tech, GFT Infrastructure and Global Solutions Group.

Other participating companies include IBM, Industrial Defender, KPMG, Kry10, Mahlet, MD Core Consulting, Method Security, NovaGuard Technologies, OnData, Palo Alto Networks, Parsons Transportation Group, Qinsight Technologies, Q-Net Security, RC4Vets, Red Trident, Reflection, Rilian, Sabari Tech Solutions, Sentinel Mosaics, Severnis, Signal Point Cyber Co., Spectrum Security, Tenable, The AI Cowboys, UTSI International Corporation, Xona Systems, Zecurity Technology Corporation and Zscaler. TXCC said this is the first group of industry partners to be onboarded, and the pilot remains open to additional applicants.

“Claroty is proud to support Project Watershed 250 and work alongside the Texas Cyber Command and our industry partners to strengthen the resilience of Texas’ water utilities,” Jen Sovada, general manager at Claroty Public Sector, wrote in an emailed statement. “As cyber risk increasingly intersects with the physical systems that underpin essential services, collaboration across the public and private sectors is critical to addressing these challenges, particularly as nation-state and other threat actors increasingly target critical infrastructure.”

She mentioned that water utilities face a growing threat landscape, while many smaller and rural providers have limited cybersecurity resources and aging infrastructure. “Providing these organizations with greater visibility into their cyber-physical environments and the expertise to identify and prioritize risk is essential to strengthening resilience. We are pleased to contribute our expertise to Project Watershed 250 and support an effort that helps protect the systems and services communities rely on every day.”

Elisity will offer assessments of utility networks and hands-on help implementing segmentation on compatible existing infrastructure, with plant operators controlling when policies take effect.

The offer includes engineering time and project management, along with the software needed for the pilot. Participating utilities will receive an inventory of in-scope assets, a map of network communications and prioritized remediation recommendations. Elisity IdentityGraph brings together identity, asset and risk context to inform access policies. Where infrastructure supports enforcement, engineers will work with operators to limit devices to the communications they need, testing policies in simulation before activation.

“Water utilities need to keep essential operations running while they strengthen security,” James Winebrenner, CEO of Elisity, said in a separate media statement. “Zero Trust starts with understanding what is connected and limiting access to what each device needs to do its job. We’re committing engineers and software to help utilities put those controls to work on the infrastructure they already own, at no cost during the pilot.”

[68] Industrial Cyber - LevelBlue finds cyberwarfare increasingly threatens critical infrastructure and connected industrial systems
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Tarih: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 10:40:03 +0000
Link: https://industrialcyber.co/industrial-cyber-attacks/levelblue-finds-cyberwarfare-increasingly-threatens-critical-infrastructure-and-connected-industrial-systems/

[TAM METİN - 1402 kelime]
LevelBlue finds cyberwarfare increasingly threatens critical infrastructure and connected industrial systems

A new report from LevelBlue SpiderLabs identified that cyber operations have become a standard component of geopolitical conflict, with attacks increasingly extending beyond military and government networks to businesses, utilities and critical infrastructure. Examining incidents from late 2025 through November 2026, the data documents how cyber operations have supported military strikes, sustained long-running espionage, disrupted water and food systems, and undermined public trust through the misuse of emergency alert applications. The findings highlight the growing convergence of cyber and conventional warfare, with digital attacks producing physical, financial and societal consequences.

In its 90-page report titled ‘How Cyberwarfare Is Reshaping the Connected World,’ LevelBlue identifies persistent access to telecommunications and critical infrastructure networks as a strategic priority for advanced threat actors, while noting that familiar techniques such as phishing, credential theft and exploitation of exposed systems remain central to cyber operations.

LevelBlue points to intrusions involving all four of Singapore’s major telecommunications operators, attacks affecting U.S. water utilities and European supermarket refrigeration systems, and using emergency-warning applications in Ukraine and Russia to distribute false nuclear and chemical alerts in November 2026. It also examines cyber and space operations conducted alongside U.S. strikes on Iran in February 2026, as well as drone and missile attacks targeting data centers from the Gulf region to Kyiv.

Interestingly, the most significant development is not necessarily emergence of new attack techniques, but expanding objectives and operational roles of familiar ones. Credential theft, phishing, and exploitation of exposed systems and malicious software remain widely used. However, these methods are increasingly combined with persistent espionage, intelligence collection supporting military activity, interference with physical processes, and manipulation of trusted communications.

The November 2026 compromises of emergency-warning applications in Ukraine and Russia, which distributed false nuclear and chemical threat alerts, illustrate how attackers can undermine public confidence without causing physical destruction. Meanwhile, increased abuse of legitimate cloud services, remote-access infrastructure, and connected devices makes malicious activity harder to distinguish from normal operations. Artificial intelligence is also accelerating reconnaissance and the development of offensive tools, although its role in fully autonomous attacks remains less established than some public claims suggest.

These attacks follow the December 2025 attacks against Polish energy infrastructure, which demonstrated potential for destructive interference with industrial control systems, while the U.S. publicly acknowledged using cyber capabilities to disrupt Iranian communications and sensors during the opening military strikes in February 2026. At the same time, attacks affecting commercial organizations, including Stryker, and water utilities in the U.S. highlighted how geopolitical tensions and weaknesses in critical infrastructure can translate into operational disruption, financial losses, and wider economic consequences. Not every such incident has a proven connection to a state or conflict, making reliable attribution an important part of understanding the threat.

Recent state-linked espionage and influence campaigns increasingly abuse the legitimate functions of trusted services instead of defeating their security. In March 2026, Dutch intelligence agencies warned that Russian state-linked operators were targeting Signal and WhatsApp accounts of government officials and military personnel, impersonating support staff to coax out verification codes and then abusing legitimate device-linking features, with no break in encryption required.

LevelBlue notes that the technique is old but now carries higher stakes, because a single compromised account, session, app permission or added device can unlock far more connected services and sensitive data, and the resulting activity can look like ordinary authorized access. Detection therefore leans less on spotting malware and more on scrutinizing authentication events, device registrations and application permissions. The same trust is being exploited to sway behavior: during the February 2026 strikes on Iran, the BadeSaba prayer app and several Iranian news sites were compromised to push surrender messages to military personnel, while a March 2026 fake Red Alert app spread Android spyware through spoofed Home Front Command texts, with possible but unconfirmed links to Arid Viper.

On Nov. 1 and 2, emergency warning apps in Ukraine and Russia were separately compromised to send false nuclear, chemical and missile alerts, prompting corrections from authorities, though the operators and any link between the incidents remain unconfirmed. Such cases aim to sow confusion and erode confidence rather than destroy systems, risks that availability or data-loss metrics fail to capture.

Alongside this, automation and AI are speeding operations.

In September 2026, Google Threat Intelligence Group described attackers moving from task-level AI use to broader automation, including an AI-assisted credential-harvesting operation built within six hours of a cloud compromise and attempts to manipulate AI coding assistants and security tools in supply chain attacks. The evidence still does not show autonomous AI replacing human operators, who continue to choose targets and interpret intelligence, but familiar attacks can now run faster and at greater scale, shrinking the window to detect and contain intrusions.

Flagging the growing threat to food preservation, LevelBlue identified that the refrigeration equipment involved included connected refrigeration management systems from Danfoss and other manufacturers, and investigations pointed to exposed management interfaces, outdated products, weak authentication and poor isolation from the public internet, with external contractors often maintaining installations and leaving store owners with little visibility into how they were connected. Contemporary reporting put French losses alone in the tens of millions of euros, and the concerns include food availability, disruption to local suppliers and unsafe products reaching the market if temperature failures go unnoticed, while discarding affected food reduces that risk but adds economic loss and waste. While no reliable public attribution exists, the attacks should not be presented as confirmed state-sponsored cyberwarfare.

LevelBlue stresses that a once-minor technical component can become the point where an intrusion causes physical and financial harm, a problem shared by water utilities, small power generators, cold-storage facilities and grain-management systems, whose operational importance often exceeds the security attention they receive. Protecting essential services therefore means understanding the connected equipment that physical operations depend on, controlling remote maintenance access, and ensuring operators can spot unsafe changes and recover control before a compromise becomes a public safety problem.

The report also notes the reverse of the usual cyberwarfare relationship, in which conventional weapons are increasingly used against the physical infrastructure that makes digital services possible. Data centers, telecommunications facilities, server infrastructure and logistics platforms have become important economic assets, some supporting military and government operations, so infrastructure once seen as primarily commercial is increasingly exposed to the consequences of armed conflict.

Ukraine offered early examples of logistics targeting: on August 28, 2025, a Russian missile strike damaged a Nova Post sorting facility in Kyiv, injuring three employees and causing delivery delays, though parcels were not damaged, and in January 2026 further strikes destroyed a Nova Post cargo terminal near Kharkiv, damaging postal operations and killing four employees. Nova Post described the facility as civilian infrastructure used to distribute food, medicines, humanitarian aid and ordinary goods.

These incidents show how physical attacks can interrupt services that depend on sophisticated digital sorting, inventory management and distribution networks, with the harm coming not from compromising software but from destroying the infrastructure, equipment and workforce needed to keep those services running.

Looking toward 2027, LevelBlue warns that organizations cannot rely on prevention alone against an evolving cyberwarfare landscape. Its report notes that while artificial intelligence accelerates offensive operations, organizations must separate documented capabilities from hype, verify confirmed attacks against unsubstantiated claims, and accurately attribute activity across blurred lines of state-sponsored groups, hacktivists, and cybercriminals. To build resilience, LevelBlue recommends prioritizing exposure reduction across operational technology (OT), remote access, identity security, supplier networks, and recovery planning.

Developments in 2025 and 2026 show cyberwarfare expanding beyond military and government targets into civilian infrastructure, commercial operations, and essential digital services.

“Cyber capabilities now support conventional military operations, intelligence gathering, industrial disruption, and information manipulation. At the same time, physical attacks against data centers, telecommunications, and logistics infrastructure have exposed the growing vulnerability of the digital economy,” according to the report. “The most significant change lies in the expanding objectives and consequences of established attack techniques. Credential theft, phishing, exploitation of exposed systems and malicious software remain common, but their use increasingly extends to military reconnaissance, and interference with physical processes.”

Recent incidents in energy, water, and refrigeration systems demonstrate how flaws in connected equipment trigger widespread operational and economic damage. Because not every wartime attack constitutes cyberwarfare, organizations must shift from defending isolated networks to detecting interference early, maintaining essential services, and containing technical incidents before they escalate into broader societal crises.
